children.name: Hymenoptera
Apidae
children.commonName: Honey Bees, Bumble Bees, and Allies

children.name: Nomada
children.description: Nomad bees are a fascinating group of cuckoo bees that don't build their own nests or collect pollen to feed their young. Instead, these crafty insects sneak into the nests of other solitary bees, laying their eggs alongside the host's eggs so their larvae can steal the stored food. They're often brightly colored with yellow and black markings that help them mimic their host bees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bees, nomad bees lack the fuzzy hairs (called scopae) that other bees use to collect pollen, since they don't need to gather food for their offspring. They're also typically more wasp-like in appearance with less body hair and shinier surfaces than their host bees.
children.funFact: Nomad bees are such skilled infiltrators that they often patrol around the nests of their host bees, waiting for the perfect moment when the host is away to slip inside and lay their eggs undetected.

children.name: Bombus
children.description: Bumble bees are large, fuzzy bees known for their distinctive black and yellow (or sometimes orange, white, or brown) banded patterns and their loud buzzing flight. These social bees live in colonies with a queen, workers, and males, though their colonies are much smaller than honeybee hives, typically containing just 50-400 individuals. They are exceptional pollinators, using a special technique called 'buzz pollination' where they grab onto flowers and vibrate their flight muscles to shake pollen loose.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bumble bees can be distinguished from other bees by their large, robust, densely fuzzy bodies and their ability to fly in cooler temperatures than most other bees. Unlike honeybees, they don't store large amounts of honey and their colonies die off each winter, with only new queens surviving to start fresh colonies in spring.
children.funFact: Some bumble bee species are 'cuckoo bees' that don't build their own nests—instead, they sneak into other bumble bee colonies, take over, and force the worker bees to raise their young!

children.name: Melissodes
children.description: Melissodes is a genus of native solitary bees commonly known as longhorn bees, named for the impressively long antennae of the males. These medium to large-sized bees are important pollinators that are especially active in late summer and fall when many flowers are blooming. They nest in the ground, with females digging burrows where they provision individual cells with pollen and nectar for their larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male longhorn bees can be easily identified by their distinctively long, thread-like antennae that extend well beyond their heads. The females have shorter antennae but can be recognized by their robust, fuzzy bodies and efficient pollen-collecting hairs on their legs and abdomen.
children.funFact: Many Melissodes species are specialists that prefer specific plant families - for example, the Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bee has a strong preference for thistle flowers, while the Pickerelweed Longhorn Bee specializes in pickerelweed blooms near wetlands.

children.name: Epeolus
children.description: Cellophane-cuckoo bees are parasitic bees that don't build their own nests or collect pollen for their young. Instead, they sneak into the nests of other ground-nesting bees (especially cellophane bees) and lay their eggs there, where their larvae consume the host's stored food provisions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These bees are recognized by their relatively hairless, wasp-like appearance with distinctive white or yellow markings on their dark bodies. Unlike their fuzzy host bees, they lack pollen-collecting structures since they don't gather food themselves.
children.funFact: Female cellophane-cuckoo bees have evolved thick, armor-like cuticles to protect themselves from the stings and bites of angry host bees when they invade their nests.

children.name: Triepeolus
children.description: Longhorn-cuckoo bees are a genus of parasitic bees that don't build their own nests or collect pollen for their young. Instead, they sneak into the nests of other native bees and lay their eggs there, leaving the host bee to unknowingly raise their offspring. These bees get their name from their relatively long antennae and their cuckoo-like parasitic lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be distinguished from other cuckoo bees by their longer antennae and often colorful, wasp-like appearance with yellow, white, or red markings on a dark body. Unlike their hard-working host bees, they lack pollen-collecting structures since they don't gather food themselves.
children.funFact: Many species in this genus are named after the plants where they're commonly found, like the Sunflower Cuckoo Nomad Bee and Goldenrod Longhorn-Cuckoo Bee, even though they're actually there to parasitize the specialist bees that visit those flowers.

children.name: Ceratina
children.description: Small carpenter bees are tiny, metallic-colored bees that create their nests by tunneling into the soft pith of plant stems like raspberry canes, elderberry, and sumac. Unlike their large carpenter bee cousins that bore into wood, these diminutive bees are only about 1/4 inch long and have a shiny, often greenish or bluish metallic sheen. They are solitary bees, with each female creating and provisioning her own nest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These bees can be distinguished from other small bees by their distinctive metallic coloration and their habit of nesting in plant stems rather than in the ground or existing cavities. They also have relatively sparse body hair compared to many other bee species.
children.funFact: Female small carpenter bees are excellent mothers who not only stock their nest cells with pollen and nectar for their young, but often remain with their developing offspring through the winter, making them one of the few semi-social small bees in our region.

children.name: Anthophora
children.description: Common Digger Bees are robust, fuzzy bees that excavate nests in soil, wood, or plant stems. These solitary bees are excellent pollinators that are often seen hovering around flowers during spring and summer, collecting nectar and pollen to provision their underground burrows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike social bees, these are solitary nesters that dig individual burrows rather than living in colonies. They're typically larger and more robust than many other solitary bees, with dense, often colorful body hair.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'digger bees,' some species in this genus actually excavate their nests in dead wood or hollow plant stems rather than digging in soil.

children.name: Apis
children.description: Honey bees are social insects that live in large colonies and are famous for producing honey and beeswax. These industrious bees are essential pollinators that visit flowers to collect nectar and pollen, which they bring back to their hive to feed the colony.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Honey bees can be distinguished from other bees by their ability to produce and store large quantities of honey, their complex social structure with a queen, workers, and drones, and their distinctive waggle dance communication.
children.funFact: A single honey bee colony can contain up to 60,000 individual bees during peak summer months, all working together as a superorganism.

children.name: Xylocopa
children.description: Large Carpenter Bees are robust, solitary bees that get their name from their habit of boring perfectly round holes into wood to create nests for their young. These impressive bees are among the largest native bees in North America, with shiny black bodies and often yellowish fur on their thorax. Unlike social bees, carpenter bee females work alone to excavate tunnels in dead wood, bamboo, or even deck railings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Carpenter bees can be distinguished from similar-looking bumblebees by their shiny, hairless black abdomens that have a metallic sheen, while bumblebees have fuzzy, hairy abdomens. They also have a distinctive hovering flight pattern and are often seen flying around wooden structures in spring.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating size and loud buzzing, male carpenter bees cannot sting and are mostly harmless - their aggressive hovering behavior is just for show to protect their territory.

children.name: Xenoglossa
children.description: Squash bees and allies are specialized native bees that have evolved a close relationship with squash, pumpkin, and gourd plants. These medium-sized bees are perfectly timed with their host plants' flowering schedule, emerging just as the blooms open in summer. They are among the most efficient pollinators of cucurbit crops, often completing their foraging before dawn.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other bees, squash bees collect pollen almost exclusively from squash family plants and nest in the ground near their host plants. They can be recognized by their rapid, buzzing flight between squash blossoms and their early morning activity when other bees are still inactive.
children.funFact: Squash bees actually arrived in North America before European colonists brought honeybees, having co-evolved with native wild gourds for thousands of years before adapting to cultivated squash and pumpkins.

children.name: Holcopasites
children.description: Holcopasites are small cuckoo bees that live as parasites in the nests of other bee species. Instead of collecting pollen and building their own nests, these bees sneak into host nests and lay their eggs alongside the host's eggs, where their larvae consume the food stores meant for the host's young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These bees can be identified by their relatively hairless, wasp-like bodies and their parasitic lifestyle. Unlike most bees, they lack pollen-collecting structures since they don't gather food for their own young.
children.funFact: The single New England species specifically targets Calliopsis bees as hosts, which is reflected in its scientific name 'calliopsidis' meaning 'of Calliopsis.'

children.name: Habropoda
children.description: Habropoda is a genus of large, robust bees known for their impressive digging abilities and specialized plant relationships. These solitary bees are excellent pollinators that create underground nests by excavating burrows in soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Habropoda bees are notably larger and more robust than most other digger bees, with strong legs adapted for extensive soil excavation. They have dense, often colorful body hair and distinctively large heads relative to other ground-nesting bee genera.
children.funFact: The Blueberry Digger Bee can buzz pollinate blueberry flowers using a special technique called 'buzz pollination,' where it grabs the flower and vibrates its flight muscles to shake pollen loose - the same technique used by bumblebees!

children.name: Ptilothrix
children.description: Ptilothrix is a small genus of specialized native bees known for their distinctive fuzzy, almost furry appearance. These solitary bees are excellent pollinators that create underground nests where females provision individual cells with pollen and nectar for their developing larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their exceptionally dense, plush-like hair covering their bodies, giving them a particularly fuzzy appearance compared to other native bees. They also have distinctive behavioral patterns, being closely associated with specific flowering plants.
children.funFact: The Hibiscus Turret Bee builds distinctive chimney-like turrets at the entrance to its underground nest, creating miniature clay towers that can be several inches tall above ground level.

children.name: Epeoloides
children.description: Epeoloides is a genus containing specialized cuckoo bees that are parasites of oil-collecting bees. These bees don't collect pollen or nectar themselves, but instead lay their eggs in the nests of other bees, where their larvae consume the host's provisions. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that specifically targets Macropis bees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cuckoo bees, Epeoloides species are specialized parasites of oil-collecting bees in the genus Macropis. They have evolved specific adaptations to infiltrate the nests of these unique hosts that collect floral oils instead of nectar.
children.funFact: The Macropis Cuckoo Bee is so specialized that it can only survive by parasitizing bees that collect oils from specific wildflowers like loosestrife, making it completely dependent on both the host bee and the host bee's preferred flowers.

children.name: Eucera
children.description: Eucera is a genus of large, robust bees known for their exceptionally long antennae, especially in males. These solitary bees are excellent pollinators that nest in the ground, creating tunnels where they raise their young on pollen and nectar provisions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male Eucera bees have remarkably long, thread-like antennae that are much longer than those of other bee genera. They are also notably large and fuzzy compared to most other native bee species.
children.funFact: The male's extraordinarily long antennae aren't just for show - they're packed with smell receptors that help them detect female pheromones from great distances during mating season.

children.name: Epimelissodes
children.description: Epimelissodes is a genus of solitary bees known as longhorn bees, named for the unusually long antennae found on the males. These medium-sized bees are important native pollinators that nest in the ground, creating burrows where females lay their eggs and provision them with pollen and nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Males of this genus have distinctively long, thread-like antennae that are much longer than those of most other bee species. They also have a more slender build compared to their close relatives in the genus Melissodes.
children.funFact: The males' extra-long antennae contain specialized scent receptors that help them detect female pheromones from greater distances during mating season.

children.description: The Apidae family includes some of our most familiar and important bees, from the fuzzy bumble bees that visit your garden flowers to the honey bees that pollinate crops and produce honey. These bees are generally robust, hairy insects that are excellent pollinators, though the family includes both social species that live in colonies and solitary species that nest alone. Many members are specialized for collecting pollen and nectar from flowers, while others are 'cuckoo bees' that lay their eggs in other bees' nests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Apidae bees typically have branched, feathery hairs that help them collect pollen, and many species have specialized structures like pollen baskets on their legs. They tend to be more robust and densely hairy compared to other bee families, with strong flying abilities.
children.funFact: This family includes both the highly social honey bees that communicate through waggle dances and sneaky cuckoo bees that have evolved to mimic their hosts so well they can infiltrate their nests undetected to lay parasitic eggs.

children.name: Andrenidae
children.commonName: Miner, Fairy, Allied Panurgine, and Oxaeine Bees

children.name: Andrena
children.description: Mining bees are solitary bees that create their nests by digging tunnels in the ground, earning their common name from their excavating behavior. Unlike honeybees that live in colonies, each female mining bee digs her own burrow where she provisions individual cells with pollen and nectar for her offspring. New England is home to an impressive 65 species of these industrious ground-nesters, many of which specialize in collecting pollen from specific types of flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mining bees can be distinguished from other ground-nesting bees by their branched, feathery body hairs that help them collect pollen, and the small mounds of excavated soil they create around their nest entrances. Many species are active early in the spring when few other bees are flying, and they often have specialized relationships with particular flowering plants.
children.funFact: Many mining bee species are named after the specific flowers they prefer - like the Spring Beauty Miner that specializes in spring beauty flowers, or the Violet Miner that focuses on violets - showing how these bees have evolved alongside their favorite plants over millions of years.

children.name: Perdita
children.description: Fairy bees are tiny, delicate native bees that are among the smallest bees in North America, often measuring less than a quarter inch long. These solitary bees nest in the ground and are typically very specialized, with many species collecting pollen from just one or a few closely related plant species. Despite their small size, they are important pollinators in their ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fairy bees can be distinguished from other small bees by their extremely tiny size, pale coloration (often yellow or whitish), and their highly specialized pollen-collecting habits. They lack the robust, hairy appearance of many other bee groups and have a more delicate, wasp-like build.
children.funFact: Some fairy bee species are so tiny that they can crawl through the mesh of a standard window screen, and their nests are so small that dozens could fit in the space of a single bumblebee nest.

children.name: Protandrena
children.description: Protandrena is a small genus of solitary mining bees that nest underground by digging tunnels in bare or sparsely vegetated soil. These medium-sized bees are important native pollinators that emerge in spring and early summer to collect pollen and nectar from wildflowers. Like other mining bees, females work alone to provision their underground nests with pollen balls for their developing larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Protandrena bees can be distinguished from other mining bee genera by their relatively robust build and specific facial hair patterns. They typically have dense, branched hairs on their bodies that help them collect pollen efficiently.
children.funFact: The name 'Protandrena' means 'first Andrena,' as these bees were once thought to represent an early evolutionary form of the more common mining bee genus Andrena.

children.name: Calliopsis
children.description: Calliopsis is a genus of small, solitary mining bees that nest in the ground by excavating tunnels in sandy or clay soils. These bees are specialized pollinators that primarily visit flowers in the sunflower family (Asteraceae), including asters, goldenrod, and other composite flowers. They are active during late summer and fall when their preferred host plants are in bloom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calliopsis bees can be identified by their distinctive yellow and black striped abdomens and their preference for collecting pollen almost exclusively from composite flowers. Unlike many other mining bees, they have relatively short tongues adapted specifically for accessing the shallow flowers of the sunflower family.
children.funFact: Female Calliopsis bees are so specialized that they will often ignore other types of flowers completely, even when their preferred aster and goldenrod blooms are scarce.

children.description: The Andrenidae family includes small to medium-sized solitary bees that are primarily ground-nesters, with most species digging burrows in soil to create their nests. These bees are important early-season pollinators, with many species emerging in spring to visit flowers like willows, maples, and fruit trees. They range from the tiny fairy bees, some smaller than a mosquito, to the more robust mining bees that create distinctive soil mounds around their nest entrances.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike social bees, all Andrenidae species are solitary, with each female constructing and provisioning her own nest. They can be distinguished from other bee families by their distinctive facial features and the way females carry pollen on specialized hairs (scopae) on their hind legs rather than in pollen baskets.
children.funFact: Fairy bees (Perdita) include some of the world's smallest bees, with some species measuring less than 4mm long - so tiny they could easily be mistaken for gnats or small flies!

children.name: Halictidae
Lasioglossum
children.description: Lasioglossum sweat bees are small, often metallic-colored native bees that are among the most common pollinators in New England. These hardworking bees get their name from their attraction to human sweat, which provides them with salt and moisture they need to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group are typically small bees with shiny, often greenish or bluish metallic bodies, though some species appear more bronze or black. They can be distinguished from other sweat bee groups by specific wing vein patterns and body proportions that require close examination to identify.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Lasioglossum sweat bees show remarkable diversity in their social behavior - some species are completely solitary, others form small cooperative groups, and a few even have primitive social colonies with a queen and workers.

children.name: Sphecodes
children.description: Blood bees are small, shiny bees with striking red and black coloration that earned them their dramatic name. These bees are actually cuckoo parasites, meaning they don't build their own nests but instead lay their eggs in the nests of other sweat bees, where their larvae consume the host's food supplies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blood bees can be identified by their glossy, often hairless bodies with distinctive red and black patterns, and their relatively small size compared to other sweat bees. Unlike their host bees, they lack pollen-collecting structures since they don't gather food for their own young.
children.funFact: Despite their sinister name and parasitic lifestyle, blood bees play an important ecological role by helping to regulate sweat bee populations, and the females are actually quite gentle and rarely sting humans.

children.name: Halictus
children.description: Furrow bees are small to medium-sized ground-nesting bees that get their name from the distinctive grooves or furrows that run across their abdomens. These metallic-looking bees are semi-social, with females often sharing nest burrows while maintaining separate brood cells for their young. They're important pollinators of wildflowers and crops throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Furrow bees can be identified by the parallel grooves that run horizontally across their abdominal segments, giving them a distinctly striped appearance. Unlike their close relatives the sweat bees, furrow bees are generally larger and have more pronounced metallic coloration.
children.funFact: Some furrow bee species can switch between solitary and social behavior depending on the season and local conditions, with sisters sometimes cooperating to share a nest in favorable years.

children.name: Agapostemon
children.description: Striped Sweat Bees are a group of metallic green bees with distinctive yellow and black striped abdomens that make them look like tiny flying jewels. These solitary bees are called 'sweat bees' because they're attracted to human perspiration for its salt content, though they're generally gentle and rarely sting. They're important native pollinators that nest in underground burrows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sweat bees, Agapostemon species have bright metallic green heads and thoraxes combined with distinctly striped yellow and black abdomens. The males and females often look quite different, with males typically having more yellow coloration.
children.funFact: Female striped sweat bees dig branching underground tunnels up to 8 inches deep, creating individual cells for each egg that they provision with pollen balls.

children.name: Dufourea
children.description: Short-faced bees are small, solitary native bees that get their name from their notably short tongues compared to other bee species. These ground-nesting bees are important pollinators that collect pollen and nectar from flowers to provision their underground nests for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their unusually short tongues make them easily distinguishable from most other bee genera, limiting them to feeding on flowers with easily accessible nectar. They are typically dark-colored, compact bees that are much smaller than honeybees.
children.funFact: Each of New England's two short-faced bee species has evolved to specialize on specific host plants - one prefers pickerelweed while the other favors beebalm flowers, making them highly specialized pollinators.

children.name: Augochlora
children.description: Augochlora is a genus of metallic green sweat bees that are among the most brilliantly colored native bees in New England. These small, solitary bees get their name from their attraction to human perspiration, which they visit to collect salts and moisture. They are important pollinators of wildflowers and crops throughout their range.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sweat bees that may be dull or have subtle metallic hints, Augochlora bees shine with an unmistakable bright emerald green coloration that makes them look like tiny flying jewels. Their metallic sheen is more vivid and consistent than related genera.
children.funFact: The Pure Green Sweat bee is one of the few native bee species that can be active on cloudy days when most other bees stay home, thanks to their ability to navigate using polarized light patterns invisible to human eyes.

children.name: Augochloropsis
children.description: Augochloropsis is a genus of metallic green sweat bees known for their brilliant emerald coloration and solitary nesting habits. These bees are important native pollinators that visit a wide variety of flowering plants throughout the growing season. They get their common name from their attraction to human perspiration, which provides them with essential salts and minerals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Augochloropsis bees are distinguished from other sweat bees by their larger size and particularly vibrant metallic green sheen that covers their entire body. Unlike many other sweat bee genera, they have a more robust build and distinctly longer antennae.
children.funFact: Female Augochloropsis bees excavate their own underground nests in sandy or loose soil, creating branching tunnels up to 8 inches deep where they provision individual cells with pollen balls for their developing larvae.

children.name: Augochlorella
children.description: Augochlorella is a small genus of metallic green sweat bees that are important native pollinators. These solitary bees are known for their brilliant emerald coloration and their habit of being attracted to human perspiration, which gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other metallic green bees by their smaller size and specific wing venation patterns. They have a more compact, robust build compared to the closely related Augochlora genus.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sweat bees,' these insects are actually beneficial - they're attracted to the salt in human sweat but rarely sting unless directly handled or trapped against skin.

children.description: Sweat bees are a diverse family of small to medium-sized bees that get their name from their attraction to human perspiration, which they visit to obtain salt and moisture. These native bees are important pollinators found in gardens, meadows, and forests throughout New England, with many species being ground-nesters that create burrows in soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most sweat bees are metallic green, blue, or bronze in color, though some are black or have yellow markings. They can be distinguished from other bee families by their distinctive wing venation pattern and relatively hairless, often shiny appearance.
children.funFact: Some sweat bee species exhibit fascinating social behaviors ranging from solitary living to complex societies where multiple generations share the same nest, with some acting as workers while others reproduce.

children.name: Megachilidae
children.commonName: Mason, Leafcutter, Carder, and Resin Bees

children.name: Megachile
children.description: Leafcutter, mortar, and resin bees are industrious solitary bees known for their remarkable building skills. These medium to large-sized bees create individual nests by cutting circular pieces from leaves, collecting plant resins, or gathering mud and other materials to construct protective chambers for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other bees that carry pollen on their legs, Megachile bees have specialized pollen-carrying hairs called scopa on the underside of their abdomen. They also have powerful mandibles (jaws) perfectly adapted for cutting through plant materials.
children.funFact: A single female leafcutter bee can cut up to 1,000 leaf circles in her lifetime, creating neat circular holes in rose, lilac, and other plant leaves that gardeners sometimes mistake for plant disease!

children.name: Osmia
children.description: Mason bees are solitary bees that get their name from their habit of using mud, clay, or other materials to build compartmented nests in hollow stems, wood cavities, or other protected spaces. Unlike honeybees, each female mason bee works alone to provision her nest with pollen and nectar for her offspring. These industrious bees are excellent pollinators and are especially active in spring and early summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mason bees carry pollen on specialized hairs under their abdomen (called a scopa) rather than on their legs like many other bees. They are also known for their habit of constructing individual brood cells separated by mud or leaf partitions.
children.funFact: A single female mason bee can do the pollination work of about 100 honeybees, making them incredibly efficient pollinators for fruit trees and other crops.

children.name: Coelioxys
children.description: Sharptail bees are a distinctive group of solitary bees known for their pointed, cone-shaped abdomens that give them their common name. These bees are cuckoo parasites, meaning they don't build their own nests but instead lay their eggs in the nests of other bee species, particularly leafcutter bees. The sharptail bee larvae then consume the food stores meant for the host's offspring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bees, sharptail bees have dramatically tapered, spear-like abdomens that end in sharp points or teeth. They also lack pollen-collecting structures since they don't gather food for their own young, instead relying on their parasitic lifestyle.
children.funFact: Female sharptail bees use their pointed abdomens like tiny daggers to pierce through the leaf caps that leafcutter bees use to seal their nest cells, allowing them to slip inside and lay their eggs.

children.name: Hoplitis
children.description: Small Mason Bees are tiny, solitary bees that build their nests using mud, plant materials, or other natural substances. These industrious insects are excellent pollinators that work alone rather than in colonies, with each female constructing and provisioning her own nest chambers for her offspring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike larger mason bees, Hoplitis species are quite small and often have distinctive facial markings or hair patterns, as suggested by names like 'white-fronted' and 'hairy-fronted.' They typically nest in pre-existing cavities like hollow plant stems or beetle holes rather than excavating their own burrows.
children.funFact: Some Hoplitis species are so specialized that they collect pollen from just one type of flower - the Viper's Bugloss Small-Mason bee primarily visits the blue flowers of viper's bugloss plants!

children.name: Stelis
children.description: Dark bees are small, metallic-colored bees that have earned the nickname 'cuckoo bees' for their sneaky lifestyle. Instead of building their own nests and collecting pollen, these bees are kleptoparasites that lay their eggs in the nests of other bee species, where their larvae steal the food provisions meant for the host's offspring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dark bees can be identified by their dark, often metallic blue or green coloration and their lack of pollen-carrying structures like scopae or corbiculae, since they don't collect pollen themselves. They tend to be smaller and more slender than their host bees.
children.funFact: Female dark bees are like tiny bee burglars - they carefully watch leafcutter and mason bees to learn the locations of their nests, then sneak in when the host is away to deposit their own eggs.

children.name: Anthidium
children.description: Wool carder bees are medium-sized, robust solitary bees known for their unique nesting behavior of collecting plant fibers to line their nest cells. These bees scrape fuzzy hairs from plant leaves and stems, especially from lamb's ear and other woolly plants, earning them their common name. They are part of the leafcutter bee family but have evolved this specialized fiber-collecting habit.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other leafcutter bees that cut circular pieces of leaves for nesting, wool carder bees scrape and collect plant hairs and fibers. Males are notably aggressive and territorial, often larger than females, and will chase away other bees from their preferred flowers.
children.funFact: Male wool carder bees have sharp spines on their abdomen that they use as weapons when defending their territory, making them some of the most aggressive bees you might encounter in a garden.

children.name: Chelostoma
children.description: Scissor bees are small, dark-colored solitary bees that get their name from their scissor-like mandibles (jaws) which they use to cut plant material. These specialized bees are cavity nesters, meaning they build their nests in hollow stems, beetle holes in wood, or other small cavities. Unlike honeybees or bumblebees, scissor bees work alone rather than in colonies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scissor bees can be identified by their elongated bodies, strong cutting mandibles, and their habit of carrying pollen on the underside of their abdomen rather than on their legs like many other bees. They are also notably smaller and more slender than most other cavity-nesting bees.
children.funFact: Each of New England's two scissor bee species has evolved to specialize on specific plant families - the Mock-orange Scissor Bee focuses on plants in the rose family, while the Rampion Scissor Bee prefers bellflowers and their relatives.

children.name: Anthidiellum
children.description: Anthidiellum is a genus of small, solitary bees known for their unique nesting behavior of collecting plant resins to build their brood cells. These bees are part of the leafcutter bee family and are important pollinators of wildflowers and garden plants. They are typically dark-colored with subtle markings and have a compact, rounded body shape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other resin bees that may use various materials, Anthidiellum bees specialize in collecting sticky plant resins and oils to construct their nest cells. They can be distinguished from similar bees by their particularly rounded, robust build and their preference for resinous building materials.
children.funFact: The Northern Rotund-Resin Bee gets its name from its unusually round, chubby appearance compared to other resin bees, making it look almost spherical when viewed from the side.

children.name: Pseudoanthidium
children.description: Small Carder Bees are tiny, solitary bees that get their name from their unique habit of collecting plant fibers and 'carding' them (combing and arranging) to build their nests. These industrious little bees are part of the leafcutter and mason bee family, but instead of cutting leaves, they gather soft plant materials like fuzzy hairs from stems and leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bees in their family that cut circular pieces from leaves, Small Carder Bees specialize in collecting plant fibers and woolly materials. They're also notably smaller than most other carder bees, with compact bodies well-suited for their fiber-collecting lifestyle.
children.funFact: The single New England species, the European Small-Woolcarder, is actually an introduced species that has successfully established itself in North America, showing remarkable adaptability to new environments.

children.name: Paranthidium
children.description: Paranthidium is a small genus of solitary bees that specialize in collecting plant resins to build their nests. These bees are part of the leafcutter bee family and are known for their unique nesting behavior of creating resin-lined burrows in the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other resin bees that nest in cavities above ground, Paranthidium bees dig their own burrows in soil and line them with collected plant resins and oils.
children.funFact: The single New England species, the Sunflower Burrowing-Resin bee, has a strong preference for sunflowers and other composite flowers, making it an important pollinator in areas where these plants grow.

children.name: Dianthidium
children.description: Pebble bees are small, solitary bees that get their name from their unique nesting behavior of using small pebbles and stones to build protective walls around their nest entrances. These industrious little architects are part of the leafcutter and mason bee family, but instead of cutting leaves or using mud, they carefully select and arrange tiny rocks. They are important pollinators of various wildflowers and garden plants throughout their range.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mason bees that use mud or leafcutter bees that use plant materials, pebble bees are distinguished by their remarkable ability to manipulate small stones and pebbles with their mandibles to construct nest closures. They are also notably smaller than most other mason bees and have a more metallic sheen to their bodies.
children.funFact: A single female pebble bee can move stones that weigh up to 40 times her own body weight, making her proportionally stronger than an ant when it comes to construction work!

children.name: Heriades
children.description: Armored Resin bees are small, dark-colored solitary bees that get their name from their tough, armor-like appearance and their habit of using plant resins to build their nests. These industrious bees collect sticky tree saps and resins to construct protective walls and partitions in their nest cavities. They are cavity-nesting bees that typically use hollow plant stems or small holes in wood for their homes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small dark bees, Armored Resin bees have a distinctly robust, heavily-built appearance with strong mandibles adapted for working with sticky resins. They can be distinguished from similar bees by their compact body shape and their specialized resin-collecting behavior.
children.funFact: These bees are so skilled at working with plant resins that they can manipulate the sticky material without getting permanently stuck to it themselves, using special techniques to handle the gooey substances while building their nests.

children.description: Mason, Leafcutter, Carder, and Resin Bees are a diverse family of solitary bees known for their remarkable building skills. Unlike honeybees that live in colonies, these bees work alone to construct individual nests using materials they gather from their environment. They are master architects, cutting leaves, collecting mud and resin, or carding plant fibers to create protective chambers for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These bees carry pollen on specialized hairs (scopa) located on the underside of their abdomen, rather than on their legs like many other bees. They are also characterized by their solitary nesting behavior and their use of various natural materials as building supplies.
children.funFact: Leafcutter bees can cut perfectly circular or oval pieces from leaves in just a few seconds, using their sharp mandibles like tiny scissors to create custom-fitted building materials for their nest cells.

children.name: Colletidae
Colletes
children.description: Cellophane bees are solitary bees that get their name from the thin, waterproof cellophane-like material they secrete to line their underground nest cells. These medium-sized bees are important native pollinators that nest in sandy or loose soil, creating branched tunnels where females provision individual cells with pollen and nectar for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike social bees, cellophane bees work alone and can be identified by their distinctive nest-lining behavior and the shiny, transparent secretion that waterproofs their brood cells. They tend to be less fuzzy than many other bee species and often have a somewhat shiny appearance.
children.funFact: The cellophane-like nest lining that gives these bees their name is actually a natural plastic-like substance that's completely biodegradable, making them some of nature's earliest eco-friendly engineers!

children.name: Hylaeus
children.description: Masked bees are small, slender native bees that get their name from the distinctive yellow or white markings on their faces that look like tiny masks. These solitary bees are important pollinators that nest in hollow plant stems, beetle burrows in wood, or other small cavities. Unlike many other bees, they don't have branched hairs for collecting pollen and instead swallow pollen and nectar to transport it back to their nests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Masked bees lack the fuzzy, branched hairs (scopa) that most other bees use to collect pollen on their bodies. Instead, they have a smooth, almost hairless appearance and carry pollen internally in a special crop.
children.funFact: Female masked bees regurgitate a mixture of pollen and nectar to create a liquid provision ball for their larvae, making them one of the few bee groups that essentially 'throw up' food for their babies.

children.description: Plasterer bees are solitary bees known for their unique nesting behavior - they line their underground nest cells with a waterproof, cellophane-like secretion that they produce from special glands. Unlike social bees that live in colonies, each female plasterer bee creates and provisions her own nest. They are important native pollinators that collect pollen and nectar from a wide variety of flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plasterer bees can be identified by their distinctive cell-lining behavior and their relatively short, forked tongues compared to other bee families. Many species have a shiny, hairless appearance, especially the masked bees which often have yellow or white facial markings.
children.funFact: The cellophane-like material that plasterer bees use to waterproof their nest cells is so effective that scientists have studied it as inspiration for developing new biodegradable packaging materials.

children.name: Melittidae
Melitta
children.description: Blunt-horn Bees are small, dark-colored native bees named for their distinctively blunt or rounded antennae tips. These solitary bees are specialist pollinators that have evolved close relationships with specific plant families, particularly members of the heath family like blueberries and cranberries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other bees, Blunt-horn Bees have antennae that end in blunt, club-like tips rather than pointed ones. They are also much smaller than honey bees and lack the branched hairs that many other native bees use for pollen collection.
children.funFact: These tiny bees are so specialized that some species, like the Blueberry Blunt-horn, have synchronized their life cycles perfectly with their host plants' blooming periods and are among the most efficient pollinators of wild blueberries in New England.

children.name: Macropis
children.description: Loosestrife bees are specialized solitary bees that have formed an exclusive partnership with yellow loosestrife flowers. These medium-sized bees collect both pollen and floral oils from their host plants, using the oils to waterproof their underground nest cells and as food for their larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bees that only collect pollen and nectar, loosestrife bees have special branched hairs on their legs specifically adapted for collecting and carrying floral oils from loosestrife flowers.
children.funFact: Loosestrife bees are so dependent on yellow loosestrife that they time their entire life cycle to match the blooming period of these flowers, emerging as adults only when the plants are in peak flower.

children.description: Melittid bees are a small but distinctive family of solitary bees that are often specialists, with many species closely tied to specific types of flowers. These ground-nesting bees are medium-sized and typically have a somewhat fuzzy appearance, collecting pollen to provision their underground nests for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Melittid bees can be recognized by their unique branched hairs (plumose setae) and distinctive wing venation patterns that differ from other bee families. They also have specialized pollen-collecting structures that are adapted to their preferred flower types.
children.funFact: Loosestrife bees (Macropis) are so specialized that they collect both pollen and floral oils exclusively from loosestrife flowers, using the oils to waterproof their underground nest cells!

children.description: Hymenoptera is one of the largest and most diverse insect orders, including all ants, bees, wasps, and sawflies. These insects share a distinctive narrow 'wasp waist' (except sawflies) and typically have two pairs of membranous wings that hook together during flight. Many species are incredibly important as pollinators, predators, or social insects that build complex colonies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most hymenopterans have a constricted connection between their thorax and abdomen, creating the classic 'wasp waist,' and their wings have a unique coupling system where tiny hooks link the front and back wings together. They also undergo complete metamorphosis and many species have specialized mouthparts for their particular lifestyle.
children.funFact: Hymenoptera includes some of the most intelligent insects on Earth - honeybees can communicate the location of flowers through complex 'waggle dances' and some wasps can recognize individual faces of their colony mates!

children.name: Lepidoptera
Nymphalidae
Polygonia
children.description: Commas are a group of medium-sized butterflies known for the distinctive jagged, irregular edges of their wings that look like they've been cut with pinking shears. They get their name from the small white or silver comma-shaped mark found on the underside of their hindwings. These butterflies are masters of camouflage, with mottled brown undersides that make them nearly invisible when resting on tree bark or dead leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other anglewing butterflies, commas have particularly raggedy wing edges and that characteristic comma punctuation mark on their underwings. Their wing shape is more angular and irregular compared to the smoother curves of other butterfly groups.
children.funFact: Many comma butterflies have two different seasonal forms - spring individuals often have lighter coloring while fall individuals are darker and more heavily marked, helping them blend in with changing foliage.

children.name: Boloria
children.description: Lesser Fritillaries are a group of small to medium-sized orange butterflies decorated with intricate black markings and distinctive silver spots on their underwings. These hardy butterflies are well-adapted to cooler climates and can be found in a variety of habitats from meadows and bogs to arctic tundra. All species in this genus have a close relationship with violet plants, which serve as the primary food source for their caterpillars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger cousins in the Greater Fritillary group, Lesser Fritillaries are generally smaller in size and tend to prefer cooler, more northern habitats. They can be distinguished by their more compact wing patterns and their preference for violets as host plants rather than the diverse plant families used by other fritillaries.
children.funFact: Some Lesser Fritillaries, like the Arctic Fritillary, can survive in extremely harsh conditions and may take two years to complete their life cycle in the coldest parts of their range, with caterpillars overwintering twice before becoming adults.

children.name: Vanessa
children.description: The Vanessa genus includes some of our most familiar and widespread butterflies, commonly known as ladies and admirals. These medium-sized butterflies are characterized by their orange, black, and white wing patterns, often with distinctive eyespots on the undersides of their wings. All three New England species are strong fliers and can be found in gardens, fields, and open areas throughout the region.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vanessa butterflies can be distinguished from other brush-footed butterflies by their angular wing shapes and specific color patterns that typically include orange or reddish-brown base colors with black markings and white spots. The undersides of their wings often display intricate eyespot patterns that help identify individual species.
children.funFact: The Painted Lady holds the record for the longest butterfly migration in the world, with some individuals traveling over 9,000 miles from tropical Africa to the Arctic Circle and back across multiple generations.

children.name: Argynnis
children.description: Greater Fritillaries are medium to large orange butterflies with intricate black markings on their wings and distinctive silver spots on their undersides. These robust butterflies are among the most spectacular fritillaries in New England, with wingspans typically ranging from 2.5 to 4 inches. All members of this genus have a strong, powerful flight and are often seen visiting flowers in open meadows, fields, and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Greater Fritillaries are larger and more robust than their Lesser Fritillary cousins, with more prominent silver spots on the underside of their hindwings. They also tend to have darker, more contrasting black markings on their orange wings compared to other fritillary groups.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Greater Fritillaries have an unusual strategy - they hatch in late summer but immediately go into hibernation without feeding, waiting until spring to wake up and search for violet plants to eat.

children.name: Phyciodes
children.description: Crescents are small, orange-brown butterflies that belong to the brushfoot family. These delicate butterflies typically have intricate patterns of black markings and pale crescents along their wing edges, which gives them their common name. They are often seen fluttering low to the ground in sunny, open areas like fields and meadows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crescents can be distinguished from other small orange butterflies by their distinctive crescent-shaped pale markings along the outer edges of their wings and their habit of flying close to the ground with a quick, erratic flight pattern.
children.funFact: Male crescents are known to be territorial and will chase away other butterflies that enter their chosen sunny patches, even pursuing much larger species that pose no real threat to them.

children.name: Lethe
children.description: Pearly-eyes and allies are a group of woodland butterflies known for their distinctive eyespots and brown, earth-toned coloring. These butterflies prefer shaded forest environments and have a somewhat secretive nature, often flying close to the ground among trees and shrubs. All members of this genus share similar wing patterns featuring prominent eyespots that help startle predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other butterflies, Lethe species have prominent eyespots on both their upper and lower wing surfaces, and they prefer shaded woodland habitats rather than open sunny areas. Their flight pattern is typically weaker and more erratic compared to other butterfly groups.
children.funFact: These butterflies get their 'pearly' name from the silvery, iridescent sheen that appears on their eyespots when light hits them at just the right angle.

children.name: Oeneis
children.description: Arctics are a group of butterflies perfectly adapted to life in cold, northern environments. These hardy butterflies are typically brown or grayish with subtle patterns, and they fly low to the ground in open areas like bogs, meadows, and tundra. All three New England species are considered rare and are found only in the region's coldest, most northern habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arctic butterflies are distinguished from other satyrs by their muted earth-tone coloration and their preference for extremely cold climates. They also tend to have a slower, more deliberate flight pattern compared to their warmer-climate relatives.
children.funFact: Arctic butterflies can survive freezing temperatures as caterpillars, and some species may take two full years to complete their life cycle due to the short growing seasons in their harsh northern habitats.

children.name: Limenitis
children.description: Limenitis is a genus of medium-sized butterflies commonly known as admirals and viceroys. These butterflies are characterized by their dark wings marked with distinctive white bands or spots, and they're often seen gliding gracefully through woodlands and open areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other butterflies by their bold white markings on dark wings and their characteristic sailing flight pattern with wings held in a shallow V-shape.
children.funFact: The Viceroy butterfly is famous for mimicking the toxic Monarch butterfly's orange coloration as protection from predators, even though it's not closely related to monarchs at all.

children.name: Nymphalis
children.description: Tortoiseshells are large, robust butterflies known for their distinctive angular wing shapes and rich, dark coloration with intricate patterns. These hardy butterflies are among the longest-lived of all North American butterflies, with adults capable of surviving harsh New England winters by hibernating in sheltered spots like tree crevices or woodpiles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other brush-footed butterflies, tortoiseshells have notably jagged, scalloped wing edges and tend to be darker overall with less bright orange coloration. They're also much larger and more powerful fliers than most related species.
children.funFact: The Mourning Cloak can live up to 11 months as an adult butterfly - longer than almost any other North American butterfly species - by hibernating through winter and emerging on warm days to bask in the sun.

children.name: Chlosyne
children.description: Patches and Allies are a group of medium-sized butterflies known for their intricate checkered wing patterns in orange, black, and white. These butterflies are closely tied to specific host plants, with their caterpillars feeding on particular wildflowers and herbs in meadows and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive checkerboard wing patterns and their tendency to have more angular, geometric markings compared to the rounder spots found on many other checkerspots.
children.funFact: Harris's Checkerspot is considered one of New England's rarest butterflies and depends entirely on white turtlehead plants for reproduction, making it an indicator species for healthy wetland ecosystems.

children.name: Aglais
children.description: Tortoiseshells are medium-sized butterflies known for their distinctive wing patterns featuring warm colors like orange, red, and brown, often with dark borders and intricate markings. These hardy butterflies are among the few species that overwinter as adults, hiding in protected spots like tree crevices or buildings during the cold months. Members of this genus are found across northern regions and are well-adapted to cooler climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tortoiseshells can be identified by their angular, scalloped wing edges and their characteristic habit of basking with wings spread wide in sunny spots. Unlike many other butterflies, they have a jerky, erratic flight pattern and often land with wings fully open rather than folded.
children.funFact: Milbert's Tortoiseshell caterpillars live communally in silk webs on stinging nettles, working together to strip entire branches bare before moving on to the next food source.

children.name: Asterocampa
children.description: Hackberry butterflies are a small group of woodland butterflies whose caterpillars feed exclusively on hackberry trees. These medium-sized butterflies are known for their earthy brown and orange coloration with distinctive eyespots on their wings. Both New England species prefer forest edges and clearings where their host trees grow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other butterflies, hackberry butterflies rarely visit flowers for nectar, instead preferring to feed on rotting fruit, tree sap, dung, and carrion. Their dependence on hackberry trees as the sole food source for their caterpillars makes them more localized than many other butterfly species.
children.funFact: Male hackberry butterflies are highly territorial and will chase away other butterflies, birds, and even small animals that enter their chosen perching spots, often returning to the exact same branch or leaf day after day.

children.name: Danaus
children.description: Tiger Milkweed Butterflies are large, orange butterflies known for their incredible long-distance migrations and their toxic nature from feeding on milkweed plants as caterpillars. These butterflies have distinctive orange wings with black veining and borders, and white-spotted black bodies that warn predators of their poisonous qualities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other orange butterflies, Tiger Milkweed Butterflies have thick black wing borders with white spots along the edges, and males have distinctive black scent patches on their hindwings that other similar species lack.
children.funFact: The Monarch butterfly can travel up to 3,000 miles during migration, with individual butterflies somehow navigating to the exact same winter roosting sites their great-great-grandparents used, despite never having been there before.

children.name: Coenonympha
children.description: Coenonympha is a genus of small, brownish butterflies commonly known as heaths or ringlets. These butterflies are characterized by their subtle earth-toned coloration and the distinctive eye-spots or 'ringlets' that often appear on their wings, particularly on the undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other satyr butterflies by their smaller size and the specific pattern of eye-spots on their wings, which are typically more prominent on the hindwings and often surrounded by pale rings.
children.funFact: Despite their modest appearance, Coenonympha butterflies have excellent eyesight and can see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are completely invisible to humans.

children.name: Cercyonis
children.description: Wood-nymphs are medium to large brown butterflies that prefer woodland edges, meadows, and grassy areas. They are characterized by their earthy brown coloration with distinctive eyespots on their wings, which help them blend into their natural surroundings while also startling potential predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wood-nymphs can be distinguished from other brown butterflies by their prominent eyespots surrounded by yellow or orange patches, particularly on the forewings, and their relatively large size compared to other grassland butterflies.
children.funFact: Wood-nymphs have a unique flight pattern where they often fly low to the ground with an irregular, bouncing motion, making them appear to 'dance' through tall grasses and wildflowers.

children.name: Megisto
children.description: Megisto is a small genus of woodland butterflies known as wood satyrs. These butterflies are characterized by their brown, earth-toned wings with distinctive eyespots that help them blend into their forest habitats. They prefer shaded woodland areas and have a slow, bouncing flight pattern.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wood satyrs in the genus Megisto are distinguished from other satyr butterflies by their smaller size and the specific pattern of eyespots on their wings, typically featuring prominent spots on both the forewings and hindwings.
children.funFact: The eyespots on wood satyr wings aren't just for show - they help startle predators and can redirect attacks away from vital body parts, giving the butterfly a better chance to escape.

children.name: Euphydryas
children.description: Euphydryas is a genus of medium-sized butterflies known as checkerspots, named for their distinctive checkerboard wing patterns of orange, black, and white patches. These butterflies are closely tied to specific host plants where their caterpillars feed, making them important indicators of ecosystem health.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Checkerspots in this genus have particularly bold, contrasting wing patterns with clearly defined rectangular patches that create a true checkerboard appearance, unlike the more mottled patterns of many other butterfly species.
children.funFact: Baltimore Checkerspots were once thought to be extinct in New England but have made a comeback in recent decades, with their caterpillars feeding exclusively on white turtlehead plants found in wetland areas.

children.name: Junonia
children.description: Junonia is a genus of medium-sized butterflies known for their striking eyespots and colorful wing patterns. These butterflies are strong fliers that prefer open, sunny areas like fields, gardens, and roadsides where they can easily spot potential mates and threats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their prominent eyespots on both the upper and lower wing surfaces, which serve as a defense mechanism to startle predators. They also have distinctive orange bars and bands across their wings.
children.funFact: Common Buckeyes can't survive freezing temperatures, so northern populations migrate south each fall, then recolonize New England each spring and summer by flying hundreds of miles north.

children.name: Euptoieta
children.description: Euptoieta is a small genus of medium-sized orange butterflies known as longwing fritillaries. These butterflies are characterized by their bright orange wings decorated with black markings and distinctive silvery spots on the undersides of their hindwings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fritillaries, Euptoieta species lack the prominent black stripes along their wing veins and have more elongated forewings, giving them their 'longwing' common name.
children.funFact: The Variegated Fritillary is one of the most widely distributed butterflies in North America, found from southern Canada all the way to South America, though it's only an occasional visitor to New England.

children.name: Libytheana
children.description: New World Snouts are a small genus of distinctive butterflies found only in the Americas. These medium-sized butterflies are most famous for their unusually long, protruding mouthparts called palps that stick out like a snout from the front of their head. They belong to the brush-footed butterfly family and are closely tied to hackberry trees, which serve as their primary host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The dramatically elongated labial palps that extend forward like a beak make these butterflies unmistakable among North American species. Their angular wing shape and mottled brown coloration also help distinguish them from other brush-footed butterflies.
children.funFact: American Snout butterflies can undergo massive population explosions and migrations involving millions of individuals, sometimes creating such dense swarms that they show up on weather radar and pile up several inches deep on car windshields.

children.name: Dione
children.description: Dione is a small genus of orange butterflies in the longwing family, with only a few species found in the Americas. These medium-sized butterflies are known for their bright orange wings with distinctive black markings and their strong, direct flight patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dione butterflies can be distinguished from other fritillaries by their more elongated forewings and the presence of distinctive silvery spots on the underside of their hindwings.
children.funFact: The Gulf Fritillary's caterpillars feed exclusively on passion vines and have bright orange spines that make them look intimidating to predators, even though they're actually harmless.

children.name: Anartia
children.description: Peacock butterflies are a small genus of medium-sized butterflies known for their distinctive eyespot patterns that resemble peacock feathers. These tropical and subtropical butterflies are strong fliers with relatively broad wings and are typically found in open, sunny areas like gardens, fields, and forest edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be identified by their prominent eyespots on the wings and their white, brown, and orange coloration patterns that differ from other brush-footed butterflies in the region.
children.funFact: The White Peacock is actually more common in Florida and the Gulf Coast states, making any New England sighting quite rare and likely representing a stray individual that has wandered far north of its usual range.

children.description: Brush-footed butterflies are one of the largest butterfly families, named for their unique front legs that are reduced to small, brush-like structures used for tasting rather than walking. These butterflies essentially walk on just four legs, using their front pair like tiny chemical sensors to detect suitable places to land and lay eggs. The family includes many of our most familiar and colorful butterflies, from the iconic Monarch to the intricate fritillaries and bold admirals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other butterflies that walk on all six legs, brush-footed butterflies have greatly reduced front legs that are held close to their body and covered in sensory hairs. This gives them the appearance of having only four functional legs for walking.
children.funFact: The famous Monarch butterfly's incredible 3,000-mile migration to Mexico is guided partly by a sun compass in their antennae and an internal clock that helps them navigate across multiple generations.

children.name: Hesperiidae
Erynnis
children.description: Duskywings are a group of small, brownish-gray skipper butterflies that are among the most challenging butterflies to identify in New England. These fast-flying butterflies have mottled brown wings with subtle patterns of light and dark spots, and they're often seen basking on sunny trails or visiting flowers in open woodlands and fields.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other skippers, duskywings lack the bright orange or golden colors typical of the group, instead sporting earthy brown and gray tones that help them blend into their surroundings. They can be distinguished from other brown butterflies by their characteristic skipper flight pattern - quick, darting movements followed by brief glides.
children.funFact: Many duskywing species have wonderfully sleepy-sounding names like 'Dreamy' and 'Sleepy,' which may reflect their habit of resting motionlessly on the ground or low vegetation during cooler parts of the day.

children.name: Euphyes
children.description: Euphyes is a genus of small to medium-sized skipper butterflies known for their brownish coloration and quick, darting flight patterns. These woodland and wetland butterflies are often called 'sedge skippers' because their caterpillars feed primarily on sedges and other grasses in marshy habitats. Adults have relatively short, triangular wings and hold them at distinctive angles when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euphyes skippers are distinguished from other skipper genera by their preference for wetland habitats and their generally dull, brownish wing coloration with subtle markings. Unlike many other skippers, they rarely have bright orange or yellow patches, instead displaying more muted tones that help them blend into their marshy environments.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Euphyes skippers create silk shelters by rolling or tying together sedge leaves, living hidden inside these protective tubes while they feed.

children.name: Hesperia
children.description: Branded Skippers are a group of small, fast-flying butterflies that get their name from the distinctive dark patches or 'brands' found on the wings of males. These compact butterflies have relatively short, triangular wings and are typically golden-brown or orange in color. They're often seen darting quickly between flowers or perching on grasses in open meadows and fields.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male Branded Skippers can be identified by the dark scent patches (brands) on their forewings, which they use to release pheromones during courtship. Unlike many other skipper groups, Hesperia species tend to have more vibrant orange-gold coloration and prefer open grassland habitats.
children.funFact: Leonard's Skipper has one of the latest flight periods of any New England butterfly, often not appearing until late August and flying well into October when most other butterflies have finished their season.

children.name: Polites
children.description: Polites is a genus of small, orange-brown skipper butterflies that are common throughout New England's grassy areas. These compact butterflies have distinctive triangular wings and a quick, darting flight pattern that earned them the name 'skippers.' All three New England species prefer open habitats like meadows, fields, and lawn edges where their caterpillars feed on various grasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Polites skippers are distinguished from other skipper genera by their warm orange-brown wing coloration and specific patterns of light spots or dashes on their wings. They tend to be smaller and more orange-toned than many other common New England skippers.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Polites skippers are surprisingly strong fliers and can quickly zip between flowers, making them challenging to photograph as they rarely sit still for more than a few seconds.

children.name: Cecropterus
children.description: Cloudywings are a genus of skipper butterflies known for their distinctive wing patterns that feature cloudy or mottled markings, giving them their common name. These medium-sized butterflies have robust bodies and relatively small wings compared to other butterfly families, with forewings that often display silvery or translucent spots against darker backgrounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cloudywings can be distinguished from other skippers by their characteristic wing patterns that include prominent hyaline (clear or translucent) spots on the forewings and often have a frosted or cloudy appearance to their wing borders.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, cloudywings are powerful fliers that can quickly dart between flowers and are often seen basking with their wings spread wide to absorb maximum sunlight.

children.name: Lon
children.description: Lon is a small genus of skipper butterflies found in eastern North America, including New England's woodlands and fields. These medium-sized skippers are known for their rapid, darting flight patterns and their habit of perching with wings held at angles rather than flat like other butterflies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lon skippers can be distinguished from other skipper genera by their distinctive wing patterns and sexual dimorphism, where males and females often look quite different from each other.
children.funFact: The Hobomok Skipper has a rare dark form called 'Pocahontas' that was once thought to be a completely separate species until scientists discovered it was just a color variant of the same butterfly!

children.name: Limochores
children.description: Limochores is a small genus of grass skipper butterflies found in New England's meadows, fields, and woodland edges. These medium-sized skippers are closely associated with grasses, where their caterpillars feed and develop. Both species in this genus have distinctive wing patterns that help distinguish them from other grass skippers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Limochores skippers can be identified by their specific wing markings - the Long Dash has a prominent dark dash mark on its forewings, while the Crossline Skipper displays distinctive pale crosslines on its underwings.
children.funFact: The Long Dash skipper gets its name from the bold, dark line that streaks across its orange forewings, making it one of the most easily recognizable grass skippers in flight.

children.name: Poanes
children.description: Poanes is a small genus of grass skippers found in wetland habitats across North America. These medium-sized butterflies are closely associated with sedges and grasses in marshes, wet meadows, and along waterways. Both New England species are brownish-orange with distinctive wing patterns and prefer moist environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Poanes can be distinguished from other grass skippers by their relatively broad wings and preference for wetland habitats rather than dry grasslands. They typically have more rounded forewings compared to the narrower-winged skippers in related genera.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Poanes skippers are so specialized that they feed exclusively on sedges, making them excellent indicators of healthy wetland ecosystems.

children.name: Amblyscirtes
children.description: Roadside-Skippers are small, brownish butterflies that get their name from their habit of perching along roadsides, trails, and woodland edges. These compact skippers have relatively short, triangular wings and tend to stay close to the ground, often darting quickly between patches of sunlight and shade. They're generally less colorful than other skipper groups, preferring earth tones that help them blend into their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other skipper groups, Roadside-Skippers are notably small and drab, with muted brown and gray coloration that lacks the bright orange or yellow markings seen in many related species. They also have a distinctive low, darting flight pattern and prefer shadier habitats than most other skippers.
children.funFact: Despite their plain appearance, Roadside-Skippers have excellent eyesight and can detect the slightest movement from potential predators, allowing them to instantly disappear into nearby vegetation with lightning-fast reflexes.

children.name: Epargyreus
children.description: Silverdrops are a genus of robust, fast-flying skipper butterflies known for their distinctive metallic markings. These butterflies are larger than most other skippers and have powerful flight capabilities, often seen darting quickly between flowers and perching with their wings held at angles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Silverdrops are distinguished from other skippers by their prominent silvery-white spots on the undersides of their hindwings, which give them their common name. They are also notably larger and more robust than most other skipper species.
children.funFact: The Silver-spotted Skipper can fly at speeds up to 20 miles per hour, making it one of the fastest butterflies in North America.

children.name: Atalopedes
children.description: Sachems and Allies is a small genus of grass skipper butterflies known for their warm orange and brown coloration. These medium-sized skippers are typically found in open, grassy areas where they feed on nectar from various wildflowers and their caterpillars develop on grasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other grass skippers by their distinctive wing patterns, with males showing prominent dark patches on their forewings and both sexes displaying characteristic orange-brown base colors.
children.funFact: The Sachem skipper gets its common name from a Native American term for chief or leader, possibly referring to the male's bold, prominent wing markings that make it stand out among other grass skippers.

children.name: Ancyloxypha
children.description: Ancyloxypha is a small genus of tiny skipper butterflies known for their diminutive size and grass-loving habits. These butterflies are among the smallest skippers in North America, with wings that barely span an inch across. They're closely tied to wetland environments where their caterpillars feed on various grass species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their exceptionally small size compared to other skippers, along with their bright orange-yellow coloration and preference for moist, grassy habitats near water sources.
children.funFact: The Least Skipper is so small that it's often mistaken for a moth rather than a butterfly, and its flight pattern resembles a tiny orange spark dancing just above the grass tops.

children.name: Thymelicus
children.description: Thymelicus is a genus of small, golden-orange butterflies commonly known as small skippers. These delicate butterflies are characterized by their rapid, darting flight patterns and their habit of holding their wings at distinctive angles when at rest - forewings held upward and hindwings horizontal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other skippers by their bright orange-gold coloration and the males' distinctive black scent patches on their forewings. They are typically smaller and more brightly colored than most other skipper species.
children.funFact: The Essex Skipper was accidentally introduced to North America from Europe and wasn't discovered here until 1910, likely arriving as eggs on imported grass seeds.

children.name: Anatrytone
children.description: Anatrytone is a small genus of grass skipper butterflies found in North America. These medium-sized skippers are closely associated with wetland habitats where their caterpillars feed on sedges and grasses. They are part of the larger skipper butterfly family, which are known for their quick, darting flight patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anatrytone skippers can be distinguished from other grass skippers by their relatively large size and their preference for wet meadows and marsh edges rather than dry grasslands.
