children.funFact: The Delaware Skipper gets its name not from the state of Delaware, but from early butterfly collectors who first studied specimens along the Delaware River valley.

children.name: Carterocephalus
children.description: Carterocephalus is a small genus of skipper butterflies known for their robust build and distinctive flight patterns. These butterflies are characterized by their orange and brown coloration with checkered patterns, and they have relatively broad wings compared to other skippers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other skipper butterflies, Carterocephalus species have a more moth-like appearance with broader wings and a less erratic flight pattern. They also tend to hold their wings horizontally when at rest, rather than the typical skipper position.
children.funFact: The Arctic Skipper is one of the most northern-ranging butterflies in North America, able to survive in conditions where few other butterfly species can thrive.

children.name: Vernia
children.description: Vernia is a small genus of skipper butterflies found in North America. These butterflies are characterized by their relatively small size and quick, darting flight patterns typical of the skipper family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vernia skippers can be distinguished from other skipper genera by their specific wing patterns and markings, though detailed examination is often needed for proper identification.
children.funFact: The Little Glassywing gets its name from the translucent, glass-like spots on its wings that help distinguish it from other small brown skippers.

children.name: Atrytonopsis
children.description: Atrytonopsis is a genus of small, brownish skipper butterflies known for their dusty, mottled appearance and relatively inconspicuous nature. These butterflies are part of the grass skipper family and are typically found in open grasslands, prairies, and woodland edges where their caterpillars feed on various grasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their dusty brown coloration with pale spots and checkered wing fringes, giving them excellent camouflage among dried grasses and leaf litter. They tend to be more secretive and less flashy than many other skipper species.
children.funFact: The Dusted Skipper gets its name from its powdery, dust-covered appearance, which helps it blend in so well with its surroundings that it's often overlooked by casual observers despite being active during the day.

children.name: Hylephila
children.description: Hylephila is a small genus of skipper butterflies known for their rapid, darting flight patterns and vibrant orange coloration. These compact butterflies have thick bodies and relatively small wings compared to other butterfly families, giving them a moth-like appearance when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hylephila are distinguished from other skippers by their bright orange-yellow wings with dark borders and their preference for open, sunny habitats like fields and gardens.
children.funFact: The Fiery Skipper gets its name not just from its flame-colored wings, but also from its incredibly fast flight speed - it can zip around at speeds that make it difficult for the human eye to follow!

children.name: Pholisora
children.description: Pholisora is a small genus of skipper butterflies known for their dark, sooty-colored wings and compact size. These butterflies are part of the spread-wing skipper family and are characterized by their relatively broad wings and distinctive flight patterns. They typically prefer open, disturbed habitats like fields, roadsides, and gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pholisora skippers can be distinguished from other skipper genera by their predominantly dark brown to black wing coloration with small white spots, giving them their 'sooty' appearance. Unlike many other skippers, they tend to hold their wings horizontally when at rest rather than in a tent-like position.
children.funFact: The genus name Pholisora comes from Greek words meaning 'scale' and 'heap,' likely referring to the dense, dark scales that cover their wings and give them their characteristic dusky appearance.

children.name: Panoquina
children.description: Panoquina is a genus of grass skipper butterflies known for their strong flying abilities and preference for wetland habitats. These medium-sized skippers have relatively long, pointed forewings and are typically brown or orange-brown in color with subtle markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Panoquina skippers can be distinguished from other grass skippers by their longer, more pointed forewings and their association with wet, marshy areas rather than dry grasslands.
children.funFact: The Ocola Skipper is a strong migrant that regularly travels northward from the southern United States, sometimes reaching New England in late summer and fall.

children.name: Urbanus
children.description: Urbanus is a genus of skipper butterflies known for their distinctive long tails extending from their hindwings. These medium-sized butterflies are strong fliers with robust bodies and relatively narrow wings compared to other butterfly families.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by the prominent tail-like projections on their hindwings, which set them apart from most other skipper butterflies that typically have rounded wing edges.
children.funFact: The Long-tailed Skipper caterpillars are sometimes called 'bean leaf rollers' because they fold and silk together the edges of bean leaves to create protective shelters while they feed.

children.name: Nastra
children.description: Nastra is a small genus of grass skippers, which are tiny butterflies that get their name from their quick, darting flight patterns. These small brown butterflies are closely associated with grassland habitats where they feed on various grasses as caterpillars and nectar from flowers as adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nastra skippers are distinguished from other grass skippers by their particularly small size and uniformly dark brown coloration with minimal markings. They lack the prominent light spots or patches found on many related skipper species.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Swarthy Skipper, these tiny butterflies are so small and quick that they're often mistaken for moths rather than butterflies by casual observers.

children.name: Burnsius
children.description: New World Checkered-Skippers are small, fast-flying butterflies known for their distinctive black and white checkered wing patterns. These compact butterflies belong to the skipper family and are found throughout North and South America, with one species making its home in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be identified by their bold checkerboard pattern of white spots on dark wings and their characteristic skipper flight pattern of quick, darting movements followed by brief glides.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Common Checkered-Skippers are remarkable migrants that can travel hundreds of miles, with northern populations often boosted by butterflies flying up from southern regions each summer.

children.description: Skippers are a large family of small to medium-sized butterflies that get their name from their quick, darting flight pattern that looks like they're skipping through the air. They have stocky bodies, relatively small wings, and large eyes, giving them a moth-like appearance compared to other butterflies. Most skippers are brown, orange, or golden in color with simple patterns, though some species have distinctive spots or markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Skippers can be distinguished from other butterflies by their thick, robust bodies, hooked antennae clubs, and their characteristic rapid, erratic flight style. Unlike most butterflies that hold their wings vertically when at rest, many skippers hold their forewings at an angle while keeping their hindwings horizontal.
children.funFact: Skipper caterpillars are unique among butterflies because they create silk shelters by rolling or folding grass blades and leaves, living inside these protective hideouts while they feed and grow.

children.name: Lycaenidae
Callophrys
children.description: Green Hairstreaks are a group of small, delicate butterflies that get their name from their distinctive greenish undersides and the thin, hair-like tails extending from their hindwings. These compact butterflies are closely tied to specific host plants, with each species often depending on just one or a few plant species for their caterpillars to develop.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hairstreak butterflies, members of this genus have predominantly green or brown undersides that provide excellent camouflage when they rest on vegetation. Many species also have intricate patterns of spots and lines on their wing undersides.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Green Hairstreaks,' several species in this genus like the Brown Elfin and Frosted Elfin are actually more brownish than green, showing the diversity within this closely related group.

children.name: Satyrium
children.description: Satyrid Hairstreaks are a genus of small, delicate butterflies that belong to the larger hairstreak family. These butterflies are characterized by their brownish or grayish wing colors with intricate patterns of lines, spots, and bands, plus the distinctive 'tails' on their hindwings that give hairstreaks their name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other hairstreak genera, Satyrium species typically have more subdued earth-tone coloring and often display prominent striping or banding patterns on their underwings. Many species in this genus also have a close relationship with specific host trees, with their common names often reflecting these plant associations.
children.funFact: The tiny 'tails' on their hindwings aren't just decorative - they work with eyespots to create a fake head that confuses predators into attacking the wrong end of the butterfly, giving it a better chance to escape!

children.name: Celastrina
children.description: The Holarctic Azures are a group of small, delicate butterflies known for their beautiful blue wings that shimmer in the sunlight. These butterflies are found across northern regions of both North America and Eurasia, with all four New England species displaying various shades of blue on their upper wings and intricate patterns of spots and bands on their undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Azures can be distinguished from other blue butterflies by their relatively small size, typically measuring less than an inch across, and their distinctive underwing patterns featuring rows of dark spots and crescents on a pale background. Unlike some other blues, azure caterpillars have special relationships with ants that protect them in exchange for sweet secretions.
children.funFact: Azure butterflies are notoriously difficult to tell apart, with some species only recently recognized as separate - the Summer Azure wasn't officially distinguished from the Spring Azure until the 1970s!

children.name: Tharsalea
children.description: Tharsalea is a genus of small, colorful butterflies commonly known as copper butterflies. These butterflies are characterized by their metallic, copper-colored wings that often shimmer in sunlight, and they're typically found in wet or boggy habitats throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Copper butterflies can be distinguished from other small butterflies by their distinctive metallic copper, bronze, or orange wing coloration, often with dark spots or borders.
children.funFact: Despite their name, copper butterflies don't actually contain copper - their metallic sheen comes from microscopic scales on their wings that reflect light in special ways.

children.name: Cupido
children.description: Tailed-Blues are small, delicate butterflies in the hairstreak family that get their name from the tiny tail-like projections on their hindwings. These petite butterflies are typically blue on top (males) or brownish-gray (females) with intricate spotted patterns on their undersides. They're common visitors to gardens and meadows where they feed on flower nectar and lay their eggs on legume plants like clover and beans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other blue butterflies, Tailed-Blues have distinctive small tails extending from their hindwings and orange spots near these tails. They're also notably smaller than most other blues, with wingspans typically under an inch.
children.funFact: The tiny tails and eye-spots on their hindwings create a false head that confuses predators into attacking the wrong end, allowing the butterfly to escape while losing only a small piece of wing instead of vital body parts.

children.name: Plebejus
children.description: Plebejus is a genus of small, delicate butterflies commonly known as blues. These butterflies are characterized by their compact size and beautiful blue coloration on the upper wings, though females may appear more brownish or grayish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plebejus blues can be distinguished from other blue butterflies by their specific wing patterns and the arrangement of spots on their undersides. They also have distinctive host plant relationships, particularly with legumes and other specific plant families.
children.funFact: The Karner Blue butterfly was named after the Karner Pine Barrens in New York, and it has such a specialized relationship with wild lupine that the caterpillars can only survive by eating this one plant species.

children.name: Lycaena
children.description: Lycaena butterflies are small, vibrant copper butterflies known for their metallic orange, red, and bronze wing colors. These compact butterflies are part of the larger gossamer-wing family and are often seen fluttering close to the ground in open areas like fields and meadows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small butterflies, Lycaena species display distinctive coppery-metallic wing coloration with dark spots and borders. Their wings often show iridescent qualities that shimmer in sunlight, making them easily recognizable among other gossamer-wings.
children.funFact: The American Copper butterfly found in New England is actually the same species found across Europe and Asia, making it one of the most widely distributed butterflies in the world.

children.name: Strymon
children.description: Scrub-Hairstreaks are small, delicate butterflies in the gossamer-wing family known for their soft gray-brown coloration and hair-like projections called 'tails' on their hindwings. These butterflies get their name from their preference for scrubby, open habitats like fields, gardens, and woodland edges where they flutter close to the ground in search of flowers and host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their subtle gray coloration with intricate patterns of spots and lines on the underwings, plus the distinctive thin 'tails' extending from the rear of their hindwings that help confuse predators.
children.funFact: The Gray Hairstreak is one of North America's most widespread butterflies, with caterpillars that can feed on over 100 different plant species - from beans and clover to cotton and strawberries!

children.name: Calycopis
children.description: Calycopis is a small genus of butterflies known as hairstreak butterflies, characterized by their delicate appearance and small size. These butterflies are part of the gossamer-wing family and are recognized for their intricate wing patterns and the thin, hair-like tails extending from their hindwings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calycopis hairstreaks can be distinguished from other hairstreak genera by their distinctive reddish-orange bands on the underside of their wings and their relatively robust build compared to other gossamer-wings.
children.funFact: The Red-banded Hairstreak gets its name from the prominent reddish-orange stripe that runs across the underside of both its forewings and hindwings, creating a distinctive banded pattern that makes it easily recognizable among New England's small butterflies.

children.name: Glaucopsyche
children.description: Glaucopsyche is a genus of small blue butterflies known for their delicate, metallic wing coloration and close relationships with ants. These butterflies are part of the copper and blue family and are found across temperate regions of North America, Europe, and Asia. Their caterpillars often have special relationships with ant colonies, receiving protection in exchange for sweet secretions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their silvery-blue wing coloration with distinctive white-ringed black spots on the undersides of their wings. They typically lack the orange markings found on many related blue butterflies.
children.funFact: Glaucopsyche caterpillars can actually communicate with ants through chemical signals and vibrations, essentially "speaking" ant language to gain protection and care from their hosts.

children.name: Feniseca
children.description: North American Harvesters are a unique group of butterflies with only one species found in our region. These small, orange and brown butterflies are carnivorous as caterpillars, making them completely different from other butterfly larvae that eat plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike all other North American butterflies, Harvester caterpillars are predators that feed exclusively on woolly aphids rather than plants. The adults are also distinctive with their rapid, erratic flight pattern and preference for tree sap over flower nectar.
children.funFact: The Harvester is the only carnivorous butterfly in North America - its caterpillars actually hunt and eat aphids instead of munching on leaves like other butterfly larvae.

children.name: Parrhasius
children.description: Parrhasius is a genus of small butterflies known as hairstreak butterflies, characterized by their delicate wing tails and intricate patterns. These butterflies are part of the larger hairstreak family and are known for their quick, darting flight patterns and tendency to perch with their wings closed, displaying their detailed undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Parrhasius can be distinguished from other hairstreaks by their distinctive white 'M' marking on the underside of their hindwings, along with their relatively larger size compared to many other hairstreak species.
children.funFact: White M Hairstreaks often perch head-down on tree trunks and move their hindwing tails in a way that mimics antennae, potentially confusing predators about which end is the head!

children.name: Polyommatus
children.description: Polyommatus is a genus of small, delicate butterflies commonly known as blues due to their brilliant blue wing coloration, particularly in males. These butterflies are part of the copper and blue family and are typically found in open grasslands, meadows, and other sunny habitats where they feed on flower nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their metallic blue upper wing surfaces in males, while females often display brown or purple-tinged wings with orange spots along the wing edges.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Polyommatus butterflies often have a special relationship with ants, secreting sweet substances that attract the ants, who in return protect the caterpillars from predators.

children.name: Erora
children.description: Erora is a small genus of delicate butterflies known as hairstreaks, characterized by their diminutive size and subtle beauty. These tiny butterflies are among the smallest members of the hairstreak family, with wings that rarely exceed an inch in span.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Erora butterflies are distinguished from other hairstreaks by their exceptionally small size and relatively plain wing patterns, lacking the bold colors and prominent tail-like projections found on many of their relatives.
children.funFact: The Early Hairstreak is so small and flies so early in the season that it's often mistaken for a moth rather than a butterfly by casual observers.

children.name: Leptotes
children.description: Zebra Blues are tiny butterflies in the genus Leptotes, known for their delicate size and distinctive wing patterns. These small butterflies typically have grayish or brownish wings with intricate striping patterns that give them their zebra-like appearance, along with small tail-like projections on their hindwings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zebra Blues can be distinguished from other small blues by their characteristic zebra-striped patterns on the undersides of their wings and the presence of small, thread-like tails on their hindwings that help confuse predators.
children.funFact: The Marine Blue is actually more common in warmer regions and is considered a rare vagrant to New England, occasionally appearing during unusually warm periods or migration events.

children.name: Icaricia
children.description: Icaricia is a small genus of butterflies in the blues family, known for their delicate wings and close association with specific host plants. These butterflies are typically found in open habitats like meadows and fields where their caterpillars feed on legumes such as clovers and vetches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Icaricia blues are distinguished from other blue butterflies by their wing patterns and the specific arrangement of spots on their underwings. They tend to be smaller and more closely tied to particular plant communities than many of their relatives.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Icaricia butterflies have a fascinating relationship with ants - they produce sweet secretions that attract ants, which then protect the caterpillars from predators in exchange for the sugary treat.

children.description: Gossamer-winged butterflies are small to medium-sized butterflies known for their delicate, shimmering wings that often display brilliant blues, coppers, and greens with an almost metallic sheen. Many species have thin, thread-like tails extending from their hindwings, and their caterpillars are often compact and slug-like in appearance. This diverse family includes hairstreaks, blues, and coppers that are commonly seen in gardens, meadows, and woodland edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other butterfly families, gossamer-wings have small, compact bodies relative to their wingspan and many species display iridescent scales that create their characteristic metallic luster. Their caterpillars are also unique in being short and broad rather than long and cylindrical like most other butterfly larvae.
children.funFact: Many gossamer-winged butterfly caterpillars have developed fascinating relationships with ants - some species produce sweet secretions that ants harvest in exchange for protection from predators, while others actually trick ants into caring for them in their nests.

children.name: Geometridae
Macaria
children.description: Macaria is a genus of geometric moths whose caterpillars are known as inchworms or spanworms because of their distinctive looping movement. These moths are typically small to medium-sized with delicate wings that often display subtle patterns of lines, spots, or bands. The adults are active at night and are commonly attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Macaria moths can be distinguished from other geometric moths by their specific wing patterns and the host plants their caterpillars prefer, often feeding on trees like maples, birches, and other deciduous species.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Macaria moths move by arching their bodies into a loop because they lack the middle pairs of prolegs that most other caterpillars have, giving them their characteristic 'measuring worm' appearance.

children.name: Caripeta
children.description: Caripeta is a small genus of moths known as looper moths, whose caterpillars move in a distinctive arching motion by bringing their back end up to meet their front end. These medium-sized moths are primarily associated with coniferous forests, where their larvae feed on pine, spruce, and other evergreen trees. Both New England species are important parts of the forest ecosystem, serving as food for birds and other wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caripeta moths can be distinguished from other looper moths by their relatively large size and the intricate wavy patterns on their wings that often include subtle shades of gray and brown. Their caterpillars are particularly specialized for feeding on coniferous trees, unlike many other loopers that prefer deciduous plants.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Caripeta moths are such convincing mimics of twigs that they will freeze motionless with their bodies extended at an angle when threatened, making them nearly impossible to spot among the branches of their host trees.

children.name: Campaea
children.description: Campaea is a small genus of moths in the geometer moth family, known for their delicate, pale-colored wings with subtle markings. These moths are medium-sized with relatively broad wings and are active during the night, often attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Campaea moths are distinguished from other geometers by their particularly pale, almost translucent wing coloration and their distinctive wing patterns featuring fine, wavy lines rather than bold markings.
children.funFact: The Pale Beauty moth gets its name from its ethereal, almost ghostly appearance - its wings are so pale they can appear nearly transparent in certain lighting conditions.

children.name: Prochoerodes
children.description: Prochoerodes is a small genus of moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as geometrid or measuring worms moths. These moths are characterized by their delicate wing patterns and their caterpillars' distinctive looping movement as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their relatively large size for geometrid moths and distinctive wing patterns featuring fine lines and subtle coloration that often provides excellent camouflage against tree bark.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Prochoerodes moths are called 'inchworms' or 'loopers' because they move by arching their bodies into loops, appearing to measure the ground as they go.

children.name: Lambdina
children.description: Lambdina is a genus of moths whose caterpillars are known as loopers because they move by arching their bodies in a characteristic loop-like motion. These moths are closely associated with coniferous forests, where their larvae feed primarily on the needles of evergreen trees like hemlocks, firs, and spruces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lambdina moths can be distinguished from other looper moths by their relatively large size and their caterpillars' strong preference for coniferous trees rather than deciduous plants.
children.funFact: The Hemlock Looper's caterpillars can completely defoliate hemlock trees during population outbreaks, causing the trees to appear bare and brown as if damaged by fire.

children.name: Scopula
children.description: Scopula is a genus of small, delicate moths known as wave moths or carpet moths. These moths are characterized by their thin, relatively broad wings that often display intricate patterns of fine lines and geometric designs that resemble lace or embroidery.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scopula moths can be distinguished from other geometrid moths by their particularly delicate wing structure and the characteristic wavy or scalloped patterns along their wing edges, which give them their common name of 'wave moths.'
children.funFact: The name 'Scopula' comes from the Latin word meaning 'little broom,' referring to the brush-like tufts of scales found on the legs of these moths.

children.name: Protoboarmia
children.description: Protoboarmia is a genus of moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their broad wings and the caterpillars' distinctive looping method of movement, where they arch their backs as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Protoboarmia moths have relatively large, broad wings with subtle gray and white patterns that help them blend in with tree bark and lichens. They differ from other geometer moths by their specific wing patterns and the porcelain-like appearance of their coloration.
children.funFact: The name 'Protoboarmia' means 'first Boarmia,' referring to its relationship to another genus of geometer moths, and the single New England species gets its common name 'Porcelain Gray' from its delicate, ceramic-like wing coloration.

children.name: Cyclophora
children.description: Mochas are a small genus of delicate geometer moths known for their subtle, earth-toned wing patterns. These moths are part of the large Geometridae family, which includes the familiar inchworm caterpillars that loop along as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mochas can be identified by their relatively small size and muted brown, tan, and gray wing coloration with fine crosslines. They tend to be more subdued in appearance compared to many of their more boldly patterned geometer moth relatives.
children.funFact: The Sweetfern Geometer Moth gets its name because its caterpillars feed specifically on sweetfern, a low-growing shrub that's actually more closely related to walnuts than to true ferns.

children.name: Eutrapela
children.description: Eutrapela is a small genus of moths in the geometer family, represented in New England by just one species. These moths are part of the large group of 'inchworm moths' whose caterpillars move in a distinctive looping motion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eutrapela moths are characterized by their relatively large size for geometers and their distinctive wing patterns with curved or scalloped edges that give them their common name reference to 'curved teeth.'
children.funFact: The genus name Eutrapela comes from Greek meaning 'well-turned' or 'graceful,' referring to their elegant wing shapes and flight patterns.

children.name: Nematocampa
children.description: Nematocampa is a small genus of moths known for their distinctive wing patterns and unique larval appearance. These moths belong to the Geometridae family, commonly called geometrid moths or inchworms, and are characterized by their relatively small size and delicate wing structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their intricate wing markings and the distinctive horn-like projections found on their caterpillars, which give the Horned Spanworm Moth its common name.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Nematocampa species have remarkable camouflage abilities, resembling tiny twigs or bark fragments so perfectly that they're nearly invisible when resting motionless on tree branches.

children.name: Pleuroprucha
children.description: Pleuroprucha is a small genus of moths belonging to the Geometridae family, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their delicate build and relatively broad wings that they hold horizontally when at rest. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the Common Tan Wave.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pleuroprucha moths can be distinguished from other geometer moths by their distinctive wing patterns featuring wavy or undulating lines across tan or brownish wings. They have a more robust body compared to many other members of the wave moth group.
children.funFact: The name 'Pleuroprucha' comes from Greek words meaning 'side-colored,' referring to the distinctive lateral markings on these moths' wings.

children.name: Costaconvexa
children.description: Costaconvexa is a small genus of moths in the geometrid family, known for their distinctive wing patterns and medium size. These moths are part of the large group called carpet moths, which get their name from the intricate, carpet-like patterns on their wings. Only one species from this genus is found in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Costaconvexa can be identified by their characteristic bent or curved lines that run across their forewings, giving them a distinctive geometric appearance that differs from the more regular patterns of other carpet moths.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Costaconvexa' literally means 'curved coast,' referring to the curved lines along the wing edges that look like a winding coastline when viewed up close.

children.name: Nepytia
children.description: Nepytia is a genus of geometrid moths known as loopers, named for the distinctive way their caterpillars move by arching their backs in loops. These moths are typically medium-sized with wings that often display intricate patterns of lines and bands. The adults are generally active at night and are attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nepytia moths can be distinguished from other looper moths by their specific wing patterns and the fact that their caterpillars often feed on coniferous trees like hemlocks and firs. The False Hemlock Looper gets its name because it mimics the appearance of the true Hemlock Looper but feeds on different host plants.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Nepytia moths are masters of camouflage, often resembling twigs or bark so closely that they can remain motionless on branches during the day and be nearly impossible to spot.

children.name: Epirrhoe
children.description: Epirrhoe is a genus of small to medium-sized moths known as carpet moths, named for their intricate wing patterns that resemble woven carpet designs. These moths are part of the large Geometridae family and are active during both day and night hours. Their caterpillars are typically green and feed on plants in the bedstraw family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Epirrhoe moths can be distinguished from other carpet moths by their specific wing patterns featuring alternating light and dark bands or zigzag markings. They tend to have more geometric, regular patterns compared to the more irregular markings of related genera.
children.funFact: The Common Carpet Moth gets its name 'alternata' from the alternating light and dark bands across its wings, which create a distinctive striped pattern that helps it blend in perfectly with tree bark and shadows.

children.name: Pasiphila
children.description: Pasiphila is a genus of small moths commonly known as pugs, which are part of the large Geometridae family of moths. These delicate moths are typically small to medium-sized with intricate patterns on their wings and are active during twilight hours. They get their common name 'pug' from their compact, somewhat flattened appearance when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pasiphila pugs can be distinguished from other pug moth genera by their specific wing patterns and the arrangement of veins in their wings. The Green Pug found in New England has distinctive greenish coloration that helps it blend in with foliage.
children.funFact: The larvae of Pasiphila moths are often called 'inchworms' or 'loopers' because they move by arching their bodies in a characteristic measuring motion, appearing to measure the ground as they crawl.

children.name: Trichodezia
children.description: Trichodezia is a small genus of moths in the Geometridae family, known as geometer moths or measuring worms. These moths are characterized by their delicate wings and the caterpillars' distinctive looping movement as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus typically have slender bodies and relatively broad wings with distinctive striping patterns that help distinguish them from other geometer moths.
children.funFact: The name Trichodezia comes from Greek words meaning 'hairy' and 'to bind,' likely referring to the fuzzy scales on their wings and body.

children.name: Homochlodes
children.description: Homochlodes is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometers or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their delicate appearance and subtle coloration that helps them blend in with their surroundings. Like other geometers, their caterpillars move in a distinctive looping motion, arching their bodies as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Homochlodes moths are distinguished by their pale, muted wing patterns with fine cross-lines and subtle markings that create excellent camouflage against tree bark and lichens.
children.funFact: The genus name Homochlodes means 'uniform green,' referring to the subtle greenish tints that can be seen on fresh specimens of these otherwise pale-colored moths.

children.name: Patalene
children.description: Patalene is a small genus of moths in the geometer family, known for their delicate wing patterns and relatively small size. These moths are part of the large group of 'inchworm moths' whose caterpillars move in a distinctive looping motion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Patalene can be distinguished from other geometer moths by their specific wing venation patterns and the arrangement of scales on their wings that create their characteristic markings.
children.funFact: The only New England species in this genus, the Juniper Geometer Moth, has caterpillars that specialize in feeding on juniper and cedar trees, making them perfectly camouflaged against the needle-like foliage.

children.name: Euphyia
children.description: Euphyia is a small genus of geometric moths in the carpet moth family, with delicate wings marked by distinctive angular patterns. These moths are part of the large group of Geometridae moths, which are known for their broad, often colorfully patterned wings that they hold horizontally when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Euphyia are characterized by their sharp, angular wing patterns that give them their common name reference to 'sharp-angled.' The wing markings create distinctive geometric designs that help distinguish them from other carpet moth genera.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Euphyia moths are 'inchworms' or 'loopers' that move by arching their bodies into loops, as they lack the middle pairs of legs that most caterpillars have.

children.name: Chlorochlamys
children.description: Chlorochlamys is a small genus of delicate green moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as emerald moths. These moths are characterized by their bright green coloration that helps them blend in with foliage during the day. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the Blackberry Looper Moth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chlorochlamys moths are distinguished from other emerald moths by their specific wing patterns and the tendency for their green coloration to fade to white or pale yellow over time when preserved in collections.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Blackberry Looper Moth, Chlorochlamys chloroleucaria caterpillars actually feed on a variety of plants including wild cherry, elderberry, and other shrubs - not just blackberries!

children.name: Tetracis
children.description: Slant-Lines are a genus of geometrid moths known for their distinctive wing patterns featuring diagonal lines that give them their common name. These medium-sized moths are part of the large family of geometric moths, which are characterized by their caterpillars that move in a looping motion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Slant-Lines can be identified by the prominent oblique or diagonal lines that cross their forewings at an angle, creating their characteristic slanted appearance that sets them apart from other geometric moths.
children.funFact: The White Slant-line moth is active during both day and night, making it one of the few geometric moths that can be spotted flying around during daylight hours.

children.name: Ennomos
children.description: Ennomos is a genus of moths in the geometer family, known for their distinctive angular wing shapes and earth-toned coloration. These moths are medium to large-sized with wings that often have scalloped or notched edges, giving them an irregular outline when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ennomos can be identified by their characteristic wing shape with pronounced angles and indentations along the wing margins, unlike the smoother wing edges of most other geometer moths.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Ennomos moths are accomplished mimics, holding themselves rigid at an angle to perfectly resemble twigs or small branches of their host trees.

children.name: Ectropis
children.description: Engrailed moths are a genus of geometric moths known for their distinctive wing patterns featuring jagged, tooth-like edges that give them their 'engrailed' name. These moths are typically medium-sized with mottled brown and gray coloration that provides excellent camouflage against tree bark during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Engrailed moths can be identified by their characteristic scalloped or dentate wing margins and their complex pattern of wavy crosslines across both forewings and hindwings. Unlike many other geometrid moths, they have relatively robust bodies and broader wings.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of engrailed moths are classic 'inchworms' or 'loopers' that move by arching their bodies in a distinctive measuring motion, earning them the nickname 'measuring worms.'

children.name: Iridopsis
children.description: Iridopsis is a genus of moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as inchworms or loopers. These moths are characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and their caterpillars' unique way of moving by arching their bodies in loops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Iridopsis moths can be identified by their intricate, wavy line patterns across their wings that often appear to shimmer or change slightly depending on the viewing angle. Their forewings typically display complex geometric designs that help distinguish them from other geometrid moths.
children.funFact: The name 'Iridopsis' comes from the Greek words for 'rainbow' and 'appearance,' referring to the subtle iridescent quality of their wing patterns that can catch light in fascinating ways.

children.name: Phigalia
children.description: Phigalia is a small genus of moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as geometrid or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their winter activity patterns and distinctive wing patterns, with males typically having fully developed wings while females often have reduced or absent wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phigalia moths are distinguished from other geometrids by their late fall to early spring flight period and sexual dimorphism in wing development. The males have broad, well-developed wings while females are often flightless with greatly reduced wings.
children.funFact: Unlike most moths that fly during warmer months, Phigalia moths are active during the coldest parts of the year, with adults emerging and mating during late fall through early spring when temperatures are near freezing.

children.name: Xanthorhoe
children.description: Xanthorhoe is a genus of moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as carpet moths due to their intricate wing patterns that resemble woven carpets. These medium-sized moths are active at night and are attracted to lights, with their caterpillars feeding on various plants including bedstraws and cleavers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive cross-banded wing patterns with wavy lines and their relatively broad, triangular forewings when at rest.
children.funFact: The name 'Xanthorhoe' comes from Greek words meaning 'yellow flow,' referring to the yellowish bands that often flow across their wings like streams of color.

children.name: Biston
children.description: Biston is a genus of moths in the geometer family, known for their large size and distinctive wing patterns. These moths are typically active at night and have wings that often feature intricate patterns of lines, spots, and bands that help them blend in with tree bark and other surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Biston moths are distinguished from other geometer moths by their robust build and relatively large wingspan, often exceeding 2 inches across. Their forewings typically display complex mottled patterns while their hindwings are usually lighter with simpler markings.
children.funFact: The genus Biston is home to the famous Peppered Moth, which became a textbook example of natural selection when dark-colored individuals became more common during the Industrial Revolution due to their better camouflage on soot-darkened trees.

children.name: Idaea
children.description: Idaea is a genus of small, delicate moths known as wave moths, characterized by their thin, fragile wings and subtle geometric patterns. These moths are part of the large Geometridae family and are typically active at night, drawn to artificial lights. They have slender bodies and relatively broad wingspans compared to their body size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wave moths in the genus Idaea can be distinguished from other geometrid moths by their particularly delicate wing structure and fine, wavy crosslines that give them their common name. Their forewings and hindwings are usually similar in color and pattern, creating a cohesive appearance when at rest.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Idaea moths are called 'loopers' or 'inchworms' because they move by arching their bodies in a distinctive loop-like motion, as they lack the middle pairs of legs that most caterpillars have.

children.name: Orthonama
children.description: Orthonama is a small genus of moths in the geometrid family, known for their delicate appearance and intricate wing patterns. These moths are typically small to medium-sized with wings that often display subtle but beautiful geometric designs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Orthonama can be distinguished from other geometrid moths by their specific wing venation patterns and the arrangement of markings on their forewings and hindwings.
children.funFact: The name 'Gem Moth' for the single New England species reflects the jewel-like quality of its wing patterns, which can shimmer subtly in the right light.

children.name: Anavitrinella
children.description: Anavitrinella is a small genus of moths in the geometer moth family, known for their delicate wings and earth-toned coloration. These moths are part of the large group of caterpillars called "inchworms" or "loopers" that move by arching their bodies as they crawl. The adults are typically active at night and are attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their grayish-brown wing patterns with subtle wavy lines and relatively small size compared to other geometer moths. Their wing patterns often provide excellent camouflage against tree bark and lichens.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Anavitrinella moths are masters of disguise, often resembling small twigs or bark fragments so perfectly that they can remain motionless on branches and go completely unnoticed by predators.

children.name: Eusarca
children.description: Eusarca is a genus of moths in the geometrid family, known as measuring worms or inchworms in their caterpillar stage. These moths are part of the large group of geometric moths that get their name from how their larvae move by arching their bodies in a looping motion. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species with distinctively patterned wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eusarca moths can be distinguished from other geometrids by their specific wing patterns and coloration, though identification often requires close examination of wing markings and body characteristics.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this genus is called the 'Confused' Eusarca Moth, likely named because it can be easily mistaken for other similar-looking geometric moths, making field identification particularly challenging even for experienced moth watchers.

children.name: Nemoria
children.description: Nemoria is a genus of small, delicate moths known as emerald moths due to their beautiful green coloration. These moths are part of the Geometridae family and are characterized by their slender bodies and broad, often translucent wings that help them blend in perfectly with foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nemoria moths can be distinguished from other emerald moths by their distinctive wing patterns and coloration, often featuring subtle lines, bands, or fringed edges that give them their common names.
children.funFact: The bright green color of Nemoria moths comes from pigments that can fade over time, so museum specimens often appear much paler than the vibrant emerald green of living moths.

children.name: Plagodis
children.description: Plagodis is a genus of moths in the Geometridae family, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their delicate wings and the caterpillars' distinctive looping movement as they crawl. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that displays subtle but beautiful wing patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plagodis moths can be distinguished from other geometrid moths by their relatively pale coloration and the presence of straight or nearly straight lines running across their wings, which gives the New England species its common name.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Plagodis moths are master mimics that can stretch their bodies stiffly away from branches to perfectly imitate twigs, complete with the right angle and bark-like coloration.

children.name: Metanema
children.description: Metanema is a small genus of moths in the geometrid family, known for their delicate appearance and relatively large wingspan. These moths are part of the group commonly called "geometers" because their caterpillars move in a distinctive looping motion, appearing to measure the earth as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Metanema moths can be identified by their pale, translucent wings with subtle brown and gray markings that create an almost ghostly appearance. They have relatively broad wings compared to their body size and tend to hold their wings horizontally when at rest.
children.funFact: The scientific name Metanema comes from Greek words meaning "spinning thread," likely referring to the silken threads these moths use during their life cycle.

children.description: Geometer moths are a large family of moths whose caterpillars are known as "inchworms" or "loopers" because they move by arching their bodies in a characteristic loop-like motion. These moths typically have broad, delicate wings held horizontally when at rest, and many species are active during the day or evening hours. The family includes both small, delicate species and larger, more robust moths with intricate wing patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Geometer moth caterpillars can be easily identified by their unique looping locomotion, caused by having fewer prolegs (false legs) than other moth larvae. Adult geometers typically rest with their wings spread horizontally rather than folded over their backs like many other moth families.
children.funFact: The name "geometer" means "earth measurer" in Greek, referring to how the caterpillars appear to be measuring the ground as they move along in their distinctive looping gait.

children.name: Erebidae
children.commonName: Underwing, Tiger, Tussock, and Allied Moths

children.name: Lophocampa
children.description: Lophocampa is a genus of striking moths known as tussock moths, named for the distinctive tufts of hair on their caterpillars. These medium-sized moths are part of the family Erebidae and are found throughout North America. Both the adult moths and their fuzzy caterpillars are relatively common sights in New England's forests and suburban areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Lophocampa apart from other tussock moths is their caterpillars' particularly dense and prominent hair tufts, along with the adults' relatively robust build and distinctive wing patterns that often include spots or stripes.
children.funFact: The fuzzy caterpillars of Lophocampa moths can cause skin irritation in humans who handle them, as their hairs contain mild toxins that serve as protection against predators.

children.name: Hypena
children.description: Hypena is a genus of moths known for their distinctive snout-like projections formed by extended mouthparts called palps. These medium-sized moths are part of the owlet moth family and are active at night, often attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The prominent forward-projecting palps that create a snout-like appearance easily separate Hypena moths from most other moth genera. Their forewings typically have subtle but distinctive patterns of lines and markings.
children.funFact: The Green Cloverworm Moth caterpillars are unusual among moths because they move by looping their bodies like inchworms, despite not being geometrid moths.

children.name: Orgyia
children.description: Orgyia is a genus of moths known as tussock moths, named for the distinctive tufts or 'tussocks' of colorful hairs found on their caterpillars. These moths are part of the family Erebidae and are commonly found throughout North America. The caterpillars are often more conspicuous than the adult moths, with their fuzzy, bristly appearance making them easily recognizable.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Orgyia moths show extreme sexual dimorphism - males have feathery antennae and can fly, while females are wingless or have very reduced wings and cannot fly. The caterpillars have characteristic dense tufts of hair, including pencil-like tufts at the head and tail ends.
children.funFact: Female Orgyia moths are flightless and often lay their eggs directly on their own empty cocoons, staying close to where they developed as caterpillars.

children.name: Idia
children.description: Idia is a genus of small, delicate moths in the snout moth family (Crambidae). These moths are typically brown or gray with intricate patterns and have a distinctive triangular resting posture with their wings held tent-like over their bodies. They are nocturnal creatures that are often attracted to lights at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Idia moths can be identified by their relatively small size, muted earth-tone coloration, and the characteristic way they hold their wings in a steep triangular shape when at rest. They have prominent labial palps (mouthpart projections) that give them a somewhat 'snouted' appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Idia moths are excellent at camouflage - when resting on tree bark or dead leaves during the day, their mottled brown and gray patterns make them nearly invisible to predators.

children.name: Palthis
children.description: Palthis moths are small, delicate moths in the family Erebidae that are active during twilight and nighttime hours. These moths are characterized by their relatively small size and subtle wing patterns featuring various spots and markings. Both New England species are drawn to lights and can often be found resting on tree trunks or other surfaces during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Palthis moths can be distinguished from other small moths by their specific wing pattern combinations of spots and angular markings, along with their relatively narrow forewings. The two New England species are separated primarily by the intensity and clarity of their spotting patterns.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and inconspicuous appearance, Palthis moths are actually part of the diverse Erebidae family, which includes some of the largest and most colorful moths in North America.

children.name: Catocala
children.description: Underwing moths are large, nocturnal moths known for their dramatic wing patterns. Their forewings are typically mottled in browns and grays that provide excellent camouflage against tree bark, while their hindwings are brightly colored with bold bands of red, orange, or yellow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets underwing moths apart is their striking defense mechanism - when startled, they flash their colorful hindwings to startle predators before quickly hiding them again. This creates a confusing 'now you see it, now you don't' effect.
children.funFact: Underwing moths are sometimes called 'sweetheart moths' because their colorful hindwings often display heart-shaped patterns when viewed up close.

children.name: Pyrrharctia
children.description: Pyrrharctia is a small genus of tiger moths known for their fuzzy caterpillars and attractive adult moths. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species - the Isabella Tiger Moth, whose caterpillar is the famous woolly bear that many people encounter crossing roads in fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctive orange and cream-colored wings as adults, and their caterpillars are covered in dense bands of black and reddish-brown bristles that give them a fuzzy, bear-like appearance.
children.funFact: The width of the brown band on a woolly bear caterpillar was once thought to predict winter weather, but this old folklore isn't scientifically accurate - the band size actually depends on the caterpillar's age and species variety.

children.name: Lymantria
children.description: Lymantria is a genus of moths in the tussock moth family, known for their fuzzy caterpillars and often destructive feeding habits on trees. These moths are characterized by their robust bodies and relatively broad wings, with females typically being larger and less capable of flight than males.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lymantria moths can be distinguished from other tussock moths by their specific wing patterns and the dense, colorful tufts of hair on their caterpillars. The females are notably flightless or poor fliers compared to the active, day-flying males.
children.funFact: Female Spongy Moths are so heavy with eggs that they cannot fly, instead attracting males from miles away using powerful chemical signals called pheromones.

children.name: Halysidota
children.description: Halysidota is a genus of moths known for their fuzzy, colorful caterpillars that are often called tussock moths. These moths are part of the tiger moth family and are characterized by their hairy larvae that feed on a variety of trees and shrubs. The adult moths are typically pale colored with subtle patterns on their wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Halysidota moths can be distinguished from other tussock moths by their less dramatically tufted caterpillars and their preference for deciduous trees as host plants. The adults are generally more muted in coloration compared to their bright, fuzzy caterpillars.
children.funFact: Despite their soft, cuddly appearance, Halysidota caterpillars have urticating hairs that can cause skin irritation in some people, making them a classic example of warning coloration in nature.

children.name: Euchaetes
children.description: Euchaetes is a small genus of moths in the tiger moth family, with species that have developed a special relationship with milkweed plants. These moths are known for their fuzzy, colorful caterpillars that feed exclusively on toxic milkweed plants, absorbing the plant's poisonous compounds for protection.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other tiger moths, Euchaetes species are specifically adapted to feed on milkweeds and incorporate the plant's toxic cardiac glycosides into their bodies. The adults are relatively small and have distinctive wing patterns with white or cream-colored forewings marked with dark spots.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Euchaetes moths are immune to the toxic chemicals in milkweed that would kill most other insects, and they advertise their toxicity with bright warning colors to potential predators.

children.name: Spilosoma
children.description: Spilosoma is a genus of tiger moths known for their fuzzy, woolly caterpillars and relatively plain white or cream-colored adult moths. These moths are part of the larger tiger moth family and are closely related to the familiar woolly bear caterpillars that many people encounter in gardens and along pathways.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many of their more colorful tiger moth relatives, Spilosoma moths tend to have predominantly white or pale wings with minimal markings, giving them a clean, simple appearance.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Spilosoma' means 'spotted body' in Greek, referring to the small dark spots often found on their thorax and abdomen, even though their wings appear mostly unmarked.

children.name: Hyphantria
children.description: Hyphantria is a small genus of moths in the tiger moth family, represented in New England by just one species - the Fall Webworm Moth. These moths are known for their larvae that create distinctive silky webs around tree branches and leaves where they feed in groups. The adult moths are typically white or cream-colored with variable dark spotting.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike tent caterpillars that build webs in tree forks, Fall Webworm larvae create their webs around the ends of branches, enclosing leaves within their silky shelters. The webs are expanded as the caterpillars grow and need more food.
children.funFact: Fall Webworm caterpillars can vary dramatically in appearance even within the same web - some are pale yellow with black spots while others are nearly black with orange markings, representing different color forms of the same species.

children.name: Ctenucha
children.description: Ctenucha is a genus of colorful day-flying moths that are often mistaken for butterflies due to their bright colors and active daytime behavior. These moths have metallic blue-black wings with vibrant orange or red markings on their bodies, making them some of the most striking moths in North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths, Ctenucha species are active during the day and have clubbed antennae similar to butterflies, though their antennae are more feathery. They can be distinguished from butterflies by their wing-folding pattern and their more robust, fuzzy bodies.
children.funFact: Virginia Ctenucha moths are excellent mimics of wasps, using their bright warning colors and buzzing flight pattern to deter predators even though they are completely harmless.

children.name: Hypercompe
children.description: Hypercompe is a genus of large, colorful moths known as tiger moths that are found throughout the Americas. These moths are characterized by their dramatic wing patterns, often featuring bold spots, stripes, or other eye-catching markings that serve as warning signals to predators. Members of this genus typically have fuzzy, robust bodies and are active at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hypercompe moths can be distinguished from other tiger moth genera by their particularly large size and distinctive wing patterns that often include leopard-like spots or tiger-like stripes. They also tend to have more vibrant coloration compared to many of their relatives.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Hypercompe moths are often called 'woolly bears' due to their extremely fuzzy appearance, and they can survive freezing temperatures by producing a natural antifreeze in their body fluids.

children.name: Cisseps
children.description: Cisseps is a small genus of moths in the tiger moth family, known for their distinctive day-flying behavior and wasp-like appearance. These moths are active during daylight hours rather than at night like most moths, making them easier to spot as they visit flowers for nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths, Cisseps species fly during the day and have bright warning colors that mimic wasps, helping to deter predators. They have narrow wings and slender bodies that enhance their wasp-like appearance.
children.funFact: The Yellow-collared Scape Moth is often mistaken for a wasp because of its bright yellow collar, dark body, and daytime flying habits - a clever case of Batesian mimicry that helps protect it from hungry birds!

children.name: Hypoprepia
children.description: Hypoprepia is a small genus of colorful moths known as painted lichen moths. These delicate moths are characterized by their vibrant wing patterns and their caterpillars' specialized diet of lichens growing on trees and rocks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other moth species, Hypoprepia moths have distinctively bright, contrasting wing colors and their larvae feed exclusively on lichens rather than typical plant material.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of painted lichen moths are so specialized that they can only survive by eating specific types of lichens, making them important indicators of healthy forest ecosystems.

children.name: Haploa
children.description: Haploa is a genus of moths in the tiger moth family known for their distinctive wing patterns and colors. These moths are medium-sized with wings that typically display bold contrasts between light and dark areas, often featuring intricate geometric designs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Haploa moths can be distinguished from other tiger moths by their specific wing pattern combinations of cream, yellow, and dark markings that form unique geometric shapes rather than spots or stripes.
children.funFact: The Clymene Moth, New England's only Haploa species, is sometimes called a 'hybrid' moth because it appears to combine features of two other moth species, though it's actually a distinct species in its own right.

children.name: Parallelia
children.description: Parallelia is a small genus of moths in the geometer family, represented in New England by just one species - the Maple Looper Moth. These are medium-sized moths with distinctive wing patterns that help them blend in with tree bark during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Parallelia moths can be recognized by their brownish wings with parallel lines running across them, which gives the genus its name. Their caterpillars are classic 'inchworms' that move in a characteristic looping motion.
children.funFact: The Maple Looper Moth gets its name because its caterpillars primarily feed on maple trees and are important defoliators in maple forests during outbreak years.

children.name: Panopoda
children.description: Panopoda moths are a small genus of nocturnal moths known for their relatively large size and distinctive wing patterns. These moths are part of the owlet moth family and are characterized by their robust build and earth-toned coloration that helps them blend with tree bark during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Panopoda moths can be distinguished from other owlet moths by their larger size, broader wings, and distinctive linear markings that often include reddish or rusty-colored lines across their forewings.
children.funFact: Despite being nocturnal, Panopoda moths are sometimes attracted to tree sap and fermenting fruit, where they can occasionally be spotted feeding during daylight hours alongside butterflies.

children.name: Rivula
children.description: Rivula is a small genus of moths in the family Erebidae, represented in New England by just one species - the Spotted Grass Moth. These are small, delicate moths with distinctive spotted wing patterns that help them blend in with their grassy habitats. They are typically active at night and are attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rivula moths can be identified by their characteristic spotted forewings and their preference for grassy areas where their caterpillars feed on various grasses and sedges.
children.funFact: The Spotted Grass Moth gets its name from the small dark spots scattered across its pale forewings, which create perfect camouflage when the moth rests among dried grasses during the day.

children.name: Euproctis
children.description: Euproctis is a genus of moths in the tussock moth family, known for their distinctive fuzzy appearance and the irritating hairs found on their caterpillars. These moths are characterized by their white or pale-colored wings and the dense, hair-like scales that cover their bodies. The caterpillars are particularly notable for having urticating hairs that can cause skin irritation in humans and animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Euproctis are distinguished from other tussock moths by their predominantly white or cream-colored wings and the toxic, barbed hairs on their larvae that cause severe skin reactions. The adult moths also have a characteristic dense covering of hair-like scales that gives them a woolly appearance.
children.funFact: The Brown-tail Moth caterpillars have such potent irritating hairs that even old, abandoned nests can cause skin rashes years later, as the microscopic barbed hairs remain airborne and active for extended periods.

children.name: Chytolita
children.description: Chytolita is a small genus of moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae). These are medium-sized moths with distinctive wing patterns that help them blend in with their surroundings during the day when they rest on tree bark or other surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Chytolita can be identified by their mottled brown and gray wing patterns with subtle lighter markings that create excellent camouflage against tree bark and lichen.
children.funFact: Despite its dramatic common name 'Morbid Owlet,' the single New England species in this genus is actually quite beautiful, with intricate wing patterns that look like abstract art when viewed up close.

children.name: Lascoria
children.description: Lascoria is a small genus of moths in the family Crambidae, commonly known as grass moths or snout moths. These moths are part of a large family that includes many species whose caterpillars feed on grasses and other plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive wing patterns and coloration that help them blend in with their surroundings when at rest.
children.funFact: The genus name Lascoria is represented by only one species in New England - the Ambiguous Moth - which gets its common name from the difficulty scientists initially had in properly identifying and classifying it.

children.name: Zanclognatha
children.description: Zanclognatha is a genus of small to medium-sized moths commonly known as fan-foot moths. These nocturnal insects are part of the erebid moth family and are characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and resting posture where they hold their wings in a tent-like position over their bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fan-foot moths can be identified by their triangular forewings with intricate wavy or zigzag patterns, and their habit of extending their front legs forward when at rest, giving them a distinctive fan-like appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Zanclognatha' comes from Greek words meaning 'sickle jaw,' referring to the curved shape of their specialized mouthparts used for feeding on fermenting fruit and tree sap.

children.name: Caenurgina
children.description: Caenurgina is a genus of moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae) known for their distinctive wing patterns and caterpillar feeding habits. These medium-sized moths are characterized by their mottled brown and gray coloration that provides excellent camouflage when resting on tree bark during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other owlet moths by their specific wing markings, including distinctive lines and patterns that create a marbled appearance. Their caterpillars are semi-loopers, meaning they arch their backs while crawling in a characteristic measuring worm motion.
children.funFact: The Clover Looper Moth caterpillar gets its name from its unusual way of moving - it pulls its hind end up to meet its front end, creating a loop, then stretches forward again to 'measure' its way across plants.

children.name: Estigmene
children.description: Ermine moths are a genus of fuzzy white moths in the tiger moth family, known for their distinctive woolly appearance and bold patterns. These moths get their name from their resemblance to the white winter coat of an ermine, with their wings typically displaying white or cream coloring marked by black spots or lines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are recognized by their robust, hairy bodies and predominantly white wings with contrasting dark markings, along with their relatively large size compared to other white moths in the region.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of ermine moths are called "woolly bears" and are covered in dense, bristly hairs that can cause skin irritation - a defense mechanism that helps protect them from predators.

children.name: Phalaenophana
children.description: Phalaenophana is a small genus of moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae) that contains just a handful of species worldwide. These are typically small to medium-sized moths with relatively plain wing patterns compared to their flashier relatives. They are nocturnal creatures that are attracted to lights at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their relatively subdued coloration and the distinctive dark bands that cross their forewings, giving them a more understated appearance than many other owlet moths.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'owlet moths,' members of Phalaenophana and their relatives got this name not because they hunt like owls, but because many species have large, prominent eyespots on their wings that can resemble owl eyes when the moth is at rest.

children.description: The Erebidae family is a diverse group of moths that includes some of New England's most recognizable night-flying insects. These moths range from the dramatically patterned underwing moths that flash bright colors when startled, to the fuzzy tussock moths whose caterpillars sport distinctive hair tufts, to the boldly striped tiger moths that often fly during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This family is incredibly varied in appearance, but many members have robust, hairy bodies and relatively broad wings. Unlike many other moth families, Erebidae includes species that are active during both day and night, and their caterpillars often have prominent hairs or bristles.
children.funFact: Many tiger moths in this family can produce ultrasonic clicks to jam bat sonar, essentially giving them a cloaking device against their main predators!

children.name: Noctuidae
Panthea
children.description: Panthea moths are medium-sized nocturnal moths with distinctive zigzag or wavy patterns across their wings. These moths are part of the owlet moth family and are known for their cryptic coloration that helps them blend in with tree bark during the day. Both New England species have caterpillars that feed on coniferous trees, particularly pine and spruce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Panthea moths can be recognized by their prominent zigzag wing patterns and their relatively robust build compared to other owlet moths. Their forewings typically show contrasting light and dark bands that create their characteristic wavy appearance.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Panthea moths are sometimes called 'pine devils' due to their spiky appearance and their habit of feeding on pine needles, where they can occasionally become minor forest pests.

children.name: Feltia
children.description: Feltia is a genus of nocturnal moths commonly known as dart moths or cutworm moths. These medium-sized brown and gray moths are part of the large owlet moth family and are active during nighttime hours. Their caterpillars are agricultural pests that cut through plant stems at soil level, earning them the name 'cutworms.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Feltia moths can be identified by their earth-toned coloration with distinctive dart-like markings on their forewings. They have robust bodies and relatively narrow wings compared to other owlet moths in their size range.
children.funFact: Despite being considered agricultural pests, Feltia moth caterpillars play an important ecological role by aerating soil as they burrow and serving as food for many birds, spiders, and ground beetles.

children.name: Eudryas
children.description: Eudryas is a small genus of moths commonly known as wood-nymphs, belonging to the family Erebidae. These medium-sized moths are known for their distinctive wing patterns and colors that help them blend into their woodland habitats. Both species in this genus are found in forested areas where their caterpillars feed on various plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wood-nymph moths can be distinguished from other similar moths by their unique combination of wing coloration and patterns - the Beautiful Wood-nymph has striking white and dark markings, while the Pearly Wood-nymph displays more subdued grayish tones with pearly highlights.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting delicate forest spirits, wood-nymph moths are actually quite hardy and their caterpillars can feed on a variety of plants including grapes, making them occasionally noticed by gardeners.

children.name: Schinia
children.description: Schinia is a genus of small, colorful moths known as flower moths because their caterpillars feed specifically on flowers and developing seeds of certain plants. These moths are often beautifully patterned with bright colors that help them blend in with the flowers they visit. Adults are typically active during the day and evening hours, making them more visible than many other moth species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths that feed on leaves, Schinia caterpillars are highly specialized to feed on flowers and seeds of specific host plants. Their bright, intricate wing patterns often mimic or complement the colors of their preferred flowers.
children.funFact: Primrose Moths have such a close relationship with evening primrose flowers that they time their life cycle perfectly - the caterpillars emerge just as the flowers are blooming and the seeds are developing.

children.name: Acronicta
children.description: Dagger Moths are a genus of fuzzy, medium-sized moths whose caterpillars are more famous than the adults. The caterpillars are covered in distinctive hair-like setae and often have dramatic warning coloration, while the adult moths are typically gray or brown with intricate patterns on their wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dagger moth caterpillars are easily recognized by their dense, fuzzy appearance and often bright yellow or black coloration with long pencil-like hair tufts. The adults can be distinguished from other moths by their relatively plain coloring and the dagger-like markings on their forewings.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating appearance, dagger moth caterpillars' fuzzy hairs can cause skin irritation in humans, making them one of the few New England caterpillars you shouldn't handle with bare hands.

children.name: Noctua
