children.description: Yellow Underwings are a genus of robust moths in the owlet moth family known for their distinctive wing pattern. These nocturnal moths have dull, camouflaged forewings that help them blend in during the day, but when they fly or are disturbed, they flash bright yellow or orange hindwings with dark bands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The dramatic contrast between their cryptic brown forewings and bright yellow hindwings with black borders makes Yellow Underwings instantly recognizable when in flight. This startling color display is used as a defense mechanism against predators.
children.funFact: The Large Yellow Underwing is actually a European species that was accidentally introduced to North America and has become so well-established that it's now one of the most common moths in many areas.

children.name: Amphipyra
children.description: Amphipyra is a genus of medium-sized moths known for their distinctive underwings that are often brightly colored or patterned, contrasting with their more subdued forewings. These nocturnal moths are typically brown or gray on top, helping them blend in when resting during the day. They belong to the owlet moth family and are active fliers at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their contrasting wing patterns - dull, camouflaged forewings that hide bright orange, yellow, or copper-colored underwings that flash when the moth takes flight.
children.funFact: The 'copper underwing' gets its name from the brilliant metallic copper coloration of its hindwings, which it uses as a startle display to confuse predators when it suddenly takes flight.

children.name: Ochropleura
children.description: Ochropleura is a small genus of nocturnal moths in the cutworm family. These moths are characterized by their earth-toned coloration and distinctive wing patterns that help them blend in with tree bark and soil during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their flame-colored shoulder patches on the forewings and their robust, medium-sized build typical of dart moths.
children.funFact: The Flame-shouldered Dart gets its name from the bright orange or reddish patches on its forewings that resemble flickering flames when the moth is at rest.

children.name: Cucullia
children.description: Hooded Owlets are a genus of medium-sized moths known for their distinctive hood-like markings and nocturnal habits. These moths are part of the cutworm and dart moth family, and their caterpillars typically feed on various flowering plants including asters and goldenrod.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hooded Owlets can be recognized by their characteristic dark hood or cap-like pattern on their forewings, which gives them their common name. They have more elongated wings compared to many other owlet moths and tend to hold their wings in a distinctive tent-like position when at rest.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'owlets,' these moths are not related to owls at all - they got their name because their large, prominent eyes and mottled brown coloration reminded early naturalists of small owls.

children.name: Lacinipolia
children.description: Lacinipolia is a genus of moths in the cutworm family that includes medium-sized nocturnal species with earth-toned wings. These moths are part of the large owlet moth family and are typically active at night when they're attracted to lights. Their caterpillars are known as cutworms because they often cut through plant stems at ground level.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished by their mottled brown and gray wing patterns with distinctive kidney-shaped and round spots on the forewings. They have a robust build typical of cutworm moths and relatively narrow forewings compared to some related genera.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they only cut plants, cutworm caterpillars often feed by climbing up plants at night and then hiding in soil during the day, making them surprisingly sneaky nighttime gardeners.

children.name: Agrotis
children.description: Agrotis is a genus of moths commonly known as dart moths, belonging to the large cutworm moth family. These are typically medium-sized, brownish or grayish moths that are active at night and are attracted to lights. The adults have forewings with distinctive markings and relatively plain hindwings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dart moths in the genus Agrotis can be distinguished from other cutworm moths by their specific wing patterns, including characteristic kidney-shaped and oval spots on their forewings. They tend to be more robust and darker than many related genera.
children.funFact: The Ipsilon Dart Moth found in New England is actually a cosmopolitan species - one of the most widely distributed moths in the world, found on every continent except Antarctica!

children.name: Pseudaletia
children.description: Pseudaletia is a genus of moths in the cutworm and armyworm family, known for containing some of the most economically important agricultural pest species. These medium-sized moths are characterized by their relatively plain, brownish coloration and strong flying abilities that allow them to migrate long distances.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other armyworm moths by their specific wing patterns, including distinctive spots and markings on the forewings, and their particular host plant preferences for grasses and cereal crops.
children.funFact: The Armyworm Moth in this genus gets its name from the caterpillars' behavior of moving across fields in large groups like marching armies, sometimes completely stripping crops bare before moving on to the next area.

children.name: Leuconycta
children.description: Leuconycta is a small genus of moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae) that includes species with distinctively marked forewings. These medium-sized moths are typically active at night and are attracted to lights, like many of their nocturid relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be recognized by their characteristic wing patterns that often include contrasting light and dark markings, giving them their name which means 'white night.'
children.funFact: The genus name Leuconycta literally translates to 'white night,' referring to the pale markings that stand out against the darker portions of their wings.

children.name: Pseudeustrotia
children.description: Pseudeustrotia is a small genus of moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae) that contains just a handful of species worldwide. These are relatively small, delicate moths with distinctive wing patterns that help distinguish them from other nocturnal species. In New England, we have only one representative of this genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Pseudeustrotia are characterized by their specific wing venation patterns and the unique arrangement of scales on their wings that create their distinctive markings. They can be separated from similar genera by subtle differences in their antennae structure and wing shape.
children.funFact: The Pink-barred Pseudeustrotia Moth, our only New England species, is so small and inconspicuous that it was likely overlooked by early moth collectors, making it a relatively recent addition to regional species lists despite probably being present all along.

children.name: Sunira
children.description: Sunira is a small genus of moths in the cutworm and dart moth family (Noctuidae). These medium-sized moths are known for their subtle, earth-toned wing patterns that help them blend in with tree bark and fallen leaves during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sunira can be distinguished from other noctuid moths by their distinctive wing markings and coloration patterns, which typically feature muted browns and grays with subtle banding.
children.funFact: The name 'Sunira' comes from a combination of Latin roots, and these moths are most active during late fall and early spring when many other moth species are dormant.

children.name: Maliattha
children.description: Maliattha is a small genus of moths in the family Noctuidae, represented in New England by just one species. These are medium-sized moths that are active at night and are attracted to lights, like many of their noctuid relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive wing patterns and markings that help separate them from other noctuids in the region.
children.funFact: The Black-dotted Glyph gets its common name from the small dark spots that create a distinctive pattern on its forewings, almost like nature's own morse code.

children.name: Chytonix
children.description: Chytonix is a genus of moths in the cutworm family known for their distinctive wing patterns and nocturnal habits. These medium-sized moths are typically found in woodland areas where they feed on tree sap and rotting fruit as adults, while their caterpillars feed on various deciduous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their mottled brown and gray wing patterns that provide excellent camouflage against tree bark. They have relatively robust bodies and hold their wings in a distinctive tent-like position when at rest.
children.funFact: The name 'Cloaked Marvel' comes from the moth's remarkable ability to blend seamlessly with tree bark during the day, making it nearly invisible to predators and human observers alike.

children.name: Nephelodes
children.description: Nephelodes is a small genus of moths in the cutworm family, with only one species found in New England. These are medium-sized nocturnal moths with wings that display distinctive bronze and brown coloring patterns that help them blend in with tree bark and fallen leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their metallic bronze wing coloration and specific wing pattern markings that distinguish them from other cutworm moths in the region.
children.funFact: The Bronzed Cutworm Moth gets its name from the beautiful bronze sheen on its forewings that catches the light, making it one of the more attractive members of the often drab-colored cutworm moth family.

children.name: Alypia
children.description: Alypia is a small genus of day-flying moths known for their bold, colorful patterns that mimic butterflies. These moths are active during daylight hours and feed on flower nectar, making them easy to spot in gardens and meadows. They're part of the tiger moth family but look quite different from their fuzzy, typically night-flying relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths, Alypia species fly during the day and have bright, contrasting wing patterns with metallic spots that help them mimic butterflies. Their wings are held horizontally when at rest, and they have a more slender body compared to typical tiger moths.
children.funFact: The Eight-spotted Forester gets its name from the bright white and yellow spots on its dark wings, but it's actually a master of deception - it mimics toxic butterflies to avoid being eaten by predators, even though it's completely harmless itself.

children.name: Protodeltote
children.description: Protodeltote is a small genus of nocturnal moths in the owlet moth family. These moths are characterized by their relatively small size and distinctive wing patterns that help them blend in with their surroundings during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their specific wing markings and coloration patterns that differ from other owlet moth genera. They have a unique combination of markings that includes distinctive glyphs or symbols on their forewings.
children.funFact: The Large Mossy Glyph gets its name from the moss-like appearance of its wing patterns, which provide excellent camouflage when the moth rests on tree bark or lichen-covered surfaces during the day.

children.name: Phlogophora
children.description: Phlogophora is a small genus of nocturnal moths known for their distinctive angular wing patterns and earth-toned coloration. These moths are part of the owlet moth family and are typically medium-sized with wings that display intricate geometric markings. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the Brown Angle Shades moth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Phlogophora are recognized by their characteristic angular, zigzag patterns on the forewings that create distinctive 'shades' or shadow-like markings. Their wing shape tends to be more triangular when at rest compared to many other owlet moths.
children.funFact: The name 'Phlogophora' comes from Greek words meaning 'flame-bearing,' referring to the fiery orange and brown colors that often appear in their wing patterns.

children.name: Papaipema
children.description: Papaipema is a genus of moths whose caterpillars are specialized plant borers, tunneling inside the stems and roots of specific host plants. These moths are part of the larger cutworm and dart moth family, but have evolved to live intimately with particular plant species. In New England, we have just one species - the Sensitive Fern Borer Moth, whose larvae develop exclusively inside sensitive fern plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many related moths whose caterpillars feed on leaves or live in soil, Papaipema larvae are internal plant borers that spend their development hidden inside plant stems or roots. Each species typically specializes on just one or a few closely related host plants.
children.funFact: The Sensitive Fern Borer Moth caterpillars spend their entire larval stage living inside the underground rhizomes of sensitive ferns, making them nearly impossible to find without digging up and dissecting the fern's root system.

children.name: Autographa
children.description: Autographa is a genus of moths in the looper family, known for their caterpillars that move in a distinctive arching motion by bringing their back legs up to meet their front legs. These medium-sized moths are typically active at night and are attracted to lights. The adults have forewings with metallic silvery or golden markings that give them their distinctive appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Autographa moths can be distinguished from other loopers by the characteristic metallic spots or patches on their forewings, which often appear silver or gold in color. These shiny markings create a striking contrast against the darker wing background.
children.funFact: The name 'Autographa' means 'self-writing' in Greek, referring to the metallic markings on their wings that resemble cursive writing or signatures.

children.name: Callopistria
children.description: Fern Moths are a small genus of nocturnal moths whose caterpillars feed specifically on ferns, particularly sensitive fern and other woodland fern species. These moths are part of the larger owlet moth family and are typically active during summer nights. They're closely tied to moist, shaded forest habitats where their host ferns thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fern Moths can be distinguished from other owlet moths by their specialized diet as caterpillars, feeding exclusively on ferns rather than flowering plants. They also tend to have more delicate wing patterns and are generally smaller than many of their owlet moth relatives.
children.funFact: The Pink-shaded Fern Moth is one of the few moths in New England whose caterpillars have evolved to digest ferns, which contain compounds that are toxic or indigestible to most other insects.

children.name: Euplexia
children.description: Euplexia is a small genus of nocturnal moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae). These medium-sized moths are known for their distinctive wing patterns and are primarily active during nighttime hours when they're attracted to lights and feed on flower nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euplexia moths can be identified by their characteristic mottled wing patterns with angular, zigzag markings that give them excellent camouflage against tree bark and lichen. Their forewings typically display a mix of browns, grays, and subtle purples that create their signature "angle shades" appearance.
children.funFact: The common name "Angle Shades" comes from the moth's unique resting posture where it holds its wings at sharp angles, creating geometric shadows that help it blend perfectly with its surroundings during the day.

children.name: Raphia
children.description: Raphia is a genus of moths in the owlet moth family (Noctuidae) that includes medium-sized, robustly built species. These moths are typically brown or grayish in color with intricate patterns on their wings that help them blend in with tree bark and other natural surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Raphia moths can be distinguished from other noctuids by their distinctive wing patterns, which often include kidney-shaped spots and wavy lines across the forewings. They tend to be more heavily built than many related genera.
children.funFact: The Brother Moth gets its common name from its close resemblance to several other moth species, making them look like 'brothers' in the same family.

children.description: Cutworm Moths and Allies make up one of the largest families of moths in the world, with many species being active at night and attracted to lights. These moths are incredibly diverse in appearance, ranging from drab brown and gray species to colorful ones with intricate patterns, and their caterpillars feed on a wide variety of plants including crops, wildflowers, and trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most noctuids have a distinctive kidney-shaped spot and triangular marking on their forewings, and their antennae are typically thread-like rather than feathery. Many species hold their wings in a tent-like position when at rest, and they generally have robust, medium-sized bodies.
children.funFact: Many species in this family get their name 'cutworm' because their caterpillars have the habit of cutting through plant stems at ground level, often toppling entire seedlings overnight.

children.name: Sphingidae
Paonias
children.description: Paonias is a small genus of sphinx moths known for their distinctive eye-spot patterns on their hindwings. These medium-sized moths are nocturnal and are often called 'eyed sphinxes' because of the prominent eyespots that they flash when threatened to startle predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Paonias moths can be distinguished from other sphinx moths by their characteristic eye-spots on the hindwings and their relatively broad, rounded forewings with muted brown and gray coloration.
children.funFact: When disturbed, Paonias moths will suddenly expose their hindwings to reveal large, intimidating eyespots that mimic the eyes of a much larger animal, causing potential predators to hesitate long enough for the moth to escape.

children.name: Hemaris
children.description: Clearwings and Bee Hawkmoths are day-flying moths that look remarkably like hummingbirds or large bees when hovering at flowers. These chunky, fast-flying insects have mostly transparent wings and feed on nectar with their long proboscis while hovering in front of blooms. They're often mistaken for hummingbirds due to their similar size, flight pattern, and feeding behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sphinx moths that are typically night-flying, Hemaris species are active during the day and have large areas of clear, scale-free wings that make them transparent. Their bee-like or hummingbird-like appearance and hovering flight distinguish them from other moths.
children.funFact: These moths lose most of their wing scales on their first flight, revealing the transparent windows that give them their 'clearwing' name and help them mimic hummingbirds.

children.name: Ceratomia
children.description: Ceratomia is a genus of large, robust sphinx moths known for their impressive size and distinctive wing patterns. These moths are part of the hawkmoth family and are characterized by their powerful flight capabilities and thick, streamlined bodies that help them hover while feeding on nectar from flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ceratomia moths can be distinguished from other sphinx moths by their particularly large size and the characteristic wavy or undulating patterns on their forewings that give some species their common names.
children.funFact: Despite their large size and moth-like appearance, Ceratomia species are often mistaken for hummingbirds when seen hovering at flowers during their feeding flights at dusk.

children.name: Hyles
children.description: Hyles is a genus of large, robust sphinx moths known for their powerful flight and distinctive wing patterns. These moths are strong migrants, capable of traveling hundreds of miles, and are often called hawkmoths due to their swift, hovering flight similar to hummingbirds. They are active at dusk and night, feeding on flower nectar with their long proboscis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hyles moths can be distinguished from other sphinx moths by their relatively broad forewings with distinctive banding patterns and their ability to undertake long-distance migrations. They typically have more colorful and contrasting wing markings compared to many other hawkmoth genera.
children.funFact: Some Hyles species can fly at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour and have been tracked migrating over 1,000 miles from their breeding grounds to overwintering sites.

children.name: Manduca
children.description: Manduca is a genus of large, heavy-bodied moths commonly known as sphinx moths or hawkmoths. These impressive insects are powerful fliers with streamlined bodies and long, narrow wings that allow them to hover like hummingbirds while feeding on flower nectar. They are most active during twilight hours and are important pollinators of many plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Manduca moths are distinguished from other sphinx moths by their robust size, typically measuring 4-5 inches across, and their characteristic wing patterns featuring zigzag lines and eyespots. They have exceptionally long proboscis (tongue) that can extend several inches to reach deep into tubular flowers.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Manduca moths, known as hornworms, are famous garden pests that can strip tomato plants bare overnight, but the adult moths are actually beneficial pollinators that help fertilize tobacco, tomato, and other nightshade family plants.

children.name: Darapsa
children.description: Darapsa is a small genus of sphinx moths known for their robust bodies and strong flying abilities. These moths are medium-sized hawkmoths that are active during twilight hours, hovering at flowers to feed on nectar much like hummingbirds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Darapsa moths can be identified by their distinctive wing patterns and their preference for feeding on plants in the grape family (Vitaceae) during their caterpillar stage.
children.funFact: The Virginia Creeper Sphinx gets its name because its caterpillars primarily feed on Virginia creeper vines, and the adult moths are such strong fliers they can hover motionless while feeding, earning them the nickname 'hummingbird moths.'

children.name: Lapara
children.description: Lapara is a small genus of sphinx moths known for their close association with pine trees. These medium-sized moths are specialized feeders, with their caterpillars developing exclusively on pine needles. They are part of the larger sphinx moth family, known for their strong flight abilities and hovering behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lapara moths can be distinguished from other sphinx moths by their pine-specific feeding habits and their more subdued, bark-like coloration that helps them blend in with pine tree trunks.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Lapara moths are so well-camouflaged that they look exactly like pine needles, complete with the right color and texture to fool predators while they feed.

children.name: Eumorpha
children.description: Eumorpha is a genus of large, robust sphinx moths known for their impressive size and powerful flight abilities. These moths are typically active at dusk and night, when they hover at flowers to feed on nectar using their long proboscis, much like hummingbirds during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eumorpha moths are characterized by their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies and relatively narrow, pointed forewings that give them excellent aerodynamic efficiency. They tend to be larger and more robust than many other sphinx moth genera, with distinctive wing patterns that often include olive, pink, or brown coloration.
children.funFact: The Pandorus Sphinx can fly at speeds up to 12 miles per hour and has such precise flight control that it can hover motionless in front of flowers while feeding, earning sphinx moths the nickname 'hummingbird moths.'

children.name: Pachysphinx
children.description: Pachysphinx is a small genus of sphinx moths, also known as hawkmoths, that are medium to large-sized nocturnal fliers. These robust moths are characterized by their streamlined bodies and strong flight capabilities, typical of the sphinx moth family. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species, the Modest Sphinx.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pachysphinx moths can be distinguished from other sphinx moths by their relatively modest size and subtle coloration patterns, lacking the bold markings found in many of their relatives. They have a more understated appearance compared to the flashier members of the sphinx moth family.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting modesty, Pachysphinx moths are powerful fliers that can hover like hummingbirds while feeding on flower nectar with their long proboscis.

children.name: Sphinx
children.description: Sphinx is a genus of large, robust moths known for their powerful flight and ability to hover like hummingbirds while feeding on flowers. These moths are characterized by their streamlined bodies, long narrow wings, and distinctive feeding behavior where they use their long proboscis to drink nectar without landing on the flower.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sphinx moths can be distinguished from other hawkmoths by their particularly heavy, torpedo-shaped bodies and their preference for feeding at dusk and dawn rather than deep night.
children.funFact: Sphinx moths are often mistaken for small hummingbirds because of their similar size, hovering flight pattern, and daytime feeding habits around flowers.

children.description: Sphinx moths are medium to large-sized moths known for their powerful flight and ability to hover while feeding on flowers, much like hummingbirds. They have streamlined bodies, narrow pointed wings, and long proboscis (feeding tubes) that they use to sip nectar from deep flowers. Most species are active at dusk or night, though some fly during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sphinx moths can be distinguished from other moth families by their distinctive triangular wing shape when at rest, their rapid hovering flight pattern, and their characteristically long, pointed forewings that give them excellent aerodynamic abilities.
children.funFact: Some sphinx moths, like the White-lined Sphinx, can fly over 25 miles per hour and migrate hundreds of miles, making them among the fastest and most athletic of all moths.

children.name: Pieridae
Pieris
children.description: Garden Whites are small to medium-sized butterflies with predominantly white wings marked by black spots or borders. All three New England species have caterpillars that feed on plants in the mustard family, including both wild species and garden crops like cabbage and broccoli.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other white butterflies in the region, Garden Whites have relatively simple wing patterns with clean black markings on bright white backgrounds, and their caterpillars are specialist feeders on mustard family plants.
children.funFact: The Small White butterfly was accidentally introduced from Europe and has become so common that many people assume it's a native species!

children.name: Colias
children.description: Clouded Yellows are medium-sized butterflies known for their bright yellow or orange wings with distinctive dark borders. These active butterflies are commonly seen in open areas like fields, meadows, and roadsides throughout New England, where they feed on clover, alfalfa, and other legumes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other yellow butterflies, Clouded Yellows have solid dark borders around their wing edges and often show a silvery spot with a pink ring on the underside of their hindwings.
children.funFact: Male Clouded Yellows can see ultraviolet patterns on females' wings that are completely invisible to human eyes, helping them identify the right species for mating.

children.name: Eurema
children.description: Grass Yellows are small, bright butterflies in the sulfur family known for their vibrant yellow and orange coloration. These delicate butterflies are often seen fluttering low over fields, gardens, and open areas where they feed on flower nectar and search for host plants in the pea family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger sulfur cousins, Grass Yellows are notably smaller with more delicate wing structures and tend to have more intense, saturated yellow and orange colors with distinctive dark borders.
children.funFact: The Sleepy Orange gets its name from its habit of resting with wings closed during the heat of the day, appearing drowsy as it perches motionless on vegetation.

children.name: Phoebis
children.description: Phoebis is a genus of large, bright yellow butterflies commonly known as sulphurs or cloudless sulphurs. These butterflies are strong fliers with vibrant coloration and are typically found in open areas like fields, gardens, and roadsides where they feed on nectar from various flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phoebis butterflies are distinguished from other sulphur butterflies by their larger size, cleaner yellow coloration without heavy black borders, and their powerful, sustained flight patterns.
children.funFact: Cloudless Sulphurs are impressive migrants that can travel hundreds of miles, with some individuals flying from as far south as Central America to reach New England during their seasonal movements.

children.name: Anthocharis
children.description: Orangetips are a genus of small to medium-sized butterflies known for the distinctive orange patches on the tips of their forewings, though this feature is usually only present in males. These delicate butterflies are typically white or pale yellow with intricate patterns of dark spots and veining on their wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The bright orange wingtips on males are the most distinctive feature of this genus, setting them apart from other white butterflies in the region. Their wings also have a characteristic marbled or mottled pattern on the undersides.
children.funFact: Male orangetips use their bright orange wingtips not just for attracting mates, but also as a warning signal to other males during territorial disputes over prime nectar sources.

children.name: Pontia
children.description: Pontia is a genus of small to medium-sized white butterflies in the cabbage white family. These butterflies are characterized by their predominantly white wings with distinctive black markings, and they're closely associated with plants in the mustard family as their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pontia butterflies can be distinguished from other white butterflies by their specific wing pattern of black checkered markings along the wing edges and their preference for mustard family plants as caterpillar food sources.
children.funFact: The Checkered White's wing patterns can vary dramatically between seasons, with spring individuals showing much bolder black markings than their paler summer counterparts.

children.description: The Pieridae family includes some of New England's most recognizable butterflies, characterized by their predominantly white, yellow, or orange coloration. These medium-sized butterflies are common garden visitors and include familiar species like cabbage whites and sulphur butterflies that you'll often see fluttering around flowers and vegetable gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other butterfly families, pierids typically have bright white, yellow, or orange base colors with minimal complex patterns, and their caterpillars often feed on plants in the mustard and legume families.
children.funFact: Many white and yellow pierid butterflies have ultraviolet markings invisible to human eyes that help them recognize potential mates - what looks like a plain white butterfly to us may actually be displaying brilliant UV patterns to other butterflies!

children.name: Crambidae
Elophila
children.description: Elophila is a genus of small moths whose caterpillars have adapted to life in and around freshwater environments. These aquatic moths are part of the crambid moth family and are specially equipped to survive in wetland habitats where most other moth species cannot thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths, Elophila caterpillars are semi-aquatic and can live underwater or in waterlogged plant material. They have specialized breathing adaptations that allow them to extract oxygen from water or air-filled plant tissues.
children.funFact: The Waterlily Borer Moth caterpillars actually tunnel through the stems and leaves of aquatic plants like water lilies, creating air-filled galleries where they can breathe while living completely submerged.

children.name: Microcrambus
children.description: Microcrambus is a genus of small moths belonging to the grass-veneer family (Crambidae). These delicate moths are typically associated with grassy habitats where their caterpillars feed on various grass species. They are part of a larger group of moths known for their slender bodies and narrow wings that often display intricate patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Microcrambus moths can be distinguished from other grass-veneer moths by their particularly small size and specific wing patterns that include distinctive veining. Their forewings typically show elegant markings that give them their common name references to being 'elegant' or refined in appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being small and often overlooked, Microcrambus moths play an important ecological role as both pollinators of small flowers and as food sources for spiders, birds, and other insectivores in grassland ecosystems.

children.name: Udea
children.description: Udea is a genus of small to medium-sized moths in the crambid family, known for their distinctive wing patterns and agricultural associations. These moths are characterized by their triangular forewings and relatively broad hindwings, with many species showing intricate geometric patterns in browns, grays, and lighter tones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Udea moths can be distinguished from other crambid moths by their specific wing venation patterns and the way they hold their wings in a triangular tent-like position when at rest. Their forewings typically display distinctive cross-lines and markings that form characteristic patterns unique to the genus.
children.funFact: The Celery Leaftier Moth gets its name from its caterpillars' habit of folding and tying celery leaves together with silk to create protective shelters while they feed, making them both agricultural pests and impressive little engineers.

children.name: Crambus
children.description: Crambus is a genus of small moths known as grass-veneer moths, belonging to the larger family of crambid moths. These delicate moths are closely associated with grasses, where their caterpillars feed and develop. They are typically small, narrow-winged moths that hold their wings close to their bodies when at rest, giving them a distinctive elongated appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crambus moths can be distinguished from other grass-veneer moths by their specific wing patterns and the arrangement of veins on their forewings. They typically have pale, straw-colored or whitish wings with subtle markings that help them blend in with dried grass stems.
children.funFact: When disturbed, Crambus moths often fly in a jerky, erratic pattern close to the ground before quickly settling back into grass, where their coloration makes them nearly invisible against dried vegetation.

children.name: Nomophila
children.description: Nomophila is a small genus of moths in the grass moth family (Crambidae) that includes species commonly known as lucerne moths. These moths are typically small to medium-sized with relatively broad wings and are often found in agricultural areas and grasslands. The genus gets its name from the Greek words meaning 'pasture-loving,' reflecting their preference for open, grassy habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nomophila moths can be distinguished from other grass moths by their distinctive wing patterns featuring pale, often cream-colored forewings with darker markings and relatively broad wings compared to many other crambid moths.
children.funFact: The Lucerne Moth is considered a minor agricultural pest because its caterpillars feed on alfalfa (also called lucerne) and other legume crops, but they rarely cause significant damage to healthy plants.

children.name: Urola
children.description: Urola is a small genus of moths in the family Geometridae, commonly known as geometer moths or inchworm moths. These moths are characterized by their delicate wings and their caterpillars' distinctive looping movement as they crawl.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Urola moths are distinguished from other geometrid moths by their specific wing patterns and structural features, though detailed identification often requires examination by experts.
children.funFact: The Snowy Urola Moth gets its name from its pale, snow-white coloration that helps it blend in with birch bark and light-colored surfaces.

children.name: Blepharomastix
children.description: Blepharomastix is a small genus of moths in the grass moth family (Crambidae) that includes delicate, small to medium-sized moths with distinctive wing patterns. These moths are typically associated with wetland habitats and have larvae that feed on aquatic or semi-aquatic plants. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that can be found near marshes, ponds, and other water sources.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blepharomastix moths are distinguished by their characteristic wing markings, including translucent or "hollow" spots that give them their common name. They have relatively narrow forewings with intricate patterns that help separate them from other grass moths.
children.funFact: The name 'Blepharomastix' comes from Greek words meaning 'eyelash whip,' likely referring to the delicate, hair-like scales along their wing edges that give them a fringed appearance.

children.name: Anania
children.description: Anania is a genus of small to medium-sized moths in the grass moth family (Crambidae). These moths are typically characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and are often found in gardens, fields, and woodland edges where they are active during evening hours.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anania moths can be distinguished from other grass moths by their specific wing venation patterns and the arrangement of scales on their wings that create unique color patterns.
children.funFact: The White-spotted Sable moth gets its dramatic name from its dark wings decorated with bright white spots, making it look like it's wearing a fancy spotted fur coat!

children.name: Parapoynx
children.description: Parapoynx is a genus of aquatic moths whose caterpillars live underwater, feeding on aquatic plants like pondweeds. These small moths have adapted to life around ponds, lakes, and slow-moving waterways where their host plants grow. The adults are typically small, brownish moths that fly near water bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moth caterpillars that live on land, Parapoynx larvae are truly aquatic and can breathe underwater using special gill-like structures. The adults have relatively narrow wings and are closely associated with aquatic habitats.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Parapoynx moths are among the few lepidopteran larvae that have evolved to live completely underwater, making them more like aquatic beetles than typical moths!

children.name: Sitochroa
children.description: Sitochroa is a small genus of moths in the crambid family, with only one species found in New England. These are small, delicate moths with pale, cream-colored wings that have subtle brown markings and patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The Carrot Seed Moth has distinctive pale yellowish-white forewings with brownish lines and spots, giving it a mottled appearance that helps it blend in with dried plant material.
children.funFact: Despite its common name suggesting it feeds on carrot seeds, the Carrot Seed Moth's caterpillars actually feed on various plants in the carrot family, including wild parsnip and other umbellifers.

children.description: Crambid snout moths are a diverse family of small to medium-sized moths known for their distinctive snout-like projection formed by their elongated mouthparts. These moths are found in a wide variety of habitats throughout New England, from grasslands and gardens to wetlands and forests. Many species are active at night and are attracted to lights, while their caterpillars feed on various plants including grasses, aquatic vegetation, and garden crops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic 'snout' created by their prominent labial palps (mouthpart structures) that project forward from their head sets them apart from other moth families. Many species also hold their wings in a triangular tent-like position when at rest.
children.funFact: Some crambid moths, like those in the genus Parapoynx, have aquatic caterpillars that live underwater and feed on pond weeds, making them some of the few truly aquatic moths in New England.

children.name: Papilionidae
Papilio
children.description: Common Swallowtails are large, spectacular butterflies that belong to the genus Papilio, one of the most widespread butterfly groups in the world. These impressive insects are known for their distinctive wing extensions called 'tails' that give them their common name, along with their bold flight patterns and vibrant colors. Most species in this group are strong fliers that can be seen gliding through gardens, forests, and open areas from spring through fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other swallowtail groups, Papilio species typically have prominent tail-like projections on their hindwings and often display bright yellow, black, or blue coloration with distinctive eyespots. Many species in this genus also have a unique defensive feature as caterpillars - a retractable, orange forked organ called an osmeterium that they can push out when threatened.
children.funFact: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails have a fascinating color dimorphism where females can be either yellow like males or completely black, with the black form being more common in southern regions where it mimics the toxic Pipevine Swallowtail for protection.

children.name: Heraclides
children.commonName: New World Giant Swallowtails and Allies
children.description: Heraclides butterflies are some of the largest and most impressive swallowtails in North America, earning their common name as giant swallowtails. These butterflies are known for their striking size, bold wing patterns, and distinctive flight style that makes them easy to spot in gardens and natural areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their exceptionally large wingspan and distinctive yellow and black coloration with prominent yellow spots along the wing borders. They also have notably long 'tails' on their hindwings that are longer than those found on most other swallowtail species.
children.funFact: The Eastern Giant Swallowtail is the largest butterfly in North America, with a wingspan that can reach up to 6 inches across - larger than many small birds!

children.name: Battus
children.description: Battus is a genus of large, dark swallowtail butterflies known for their distinctive metallic sheen and specialized relationship with pipevine plants. These butterflies are famous for being both beautiful and toxic, having evolved to feed on poisonous Aristolochia vines as caterpillars, which makes them unpalatable to predators throughout their lives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Battus can be recognized by their dark wings with metallic blue or green iridescence, particularly prominent on the hindwings, and their lack of the yellow markings common in many other swallowtail genera.
children.funFact: Pipevine Swallowtails are so toxic that several other butterfly species have evolved to mimic their appearance, creating one of North America's most famous examples of protective mimicry.

children.name: Eurytides
children.description: Kite-Swallowtails are a distinctive group of large butterflies known for their elongated hindwing tails and graceful, soaring flight pattern that resembles a kite dancing in the wind. These elegant butterflies are closely tied to pawpaw trees, as their caterpillars feed exclusively on these native plants. They're considered some of the most beautiful and recognizable swallowtails in North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other swallowtail groups, Kite-Swallowtails have exceptionally long, narrow tails on their hindwings and display bold black and white striped patterns. Their flight is distinctively slow and gliding compared to the more erratic flight of other swallowtails.
children.funFact: The Zebra Swallowtail's striking appearance changes with the seasons - spring individuals are smaller and paler, while summer butterflies are larger with longer tails and more vibrant markings.

children.description: Swallowtails and Parnassians are among the largest and most spectacular butterflies you'll encounter in New England. Most species in this family are characterized by their impressive wingspan and the distinctive 'tails' that extend from their hindwings, though not all members have these projections. These butterflies are strong fliers and are often seen gliding gracefully through gardens, meadows, and forest edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets swallowtails apart from other butterfly families is their large size, often measuring 3-5 inches across, and those iconic tail-like extensions on their hindwings that give the group its name. Many species also have bold, contrasting color patterns with distinctive eyespots or bands.
children.funFact: Swallowtail caterpillars have a secret weapon called an osmeterium - a bright orange or yellow forked organ that pops out from behind their head when threatened, releasing a foul smell to deter predators!

children.name: Notodontidae
Nadata
children.description: Nadata is a small genus of moths in the prominent moth family, known for their distinctive wing patterns and robust build. These nocturnal moths are typically medium-sized with forewings that have a somewhat triangular shape when at rest. They are part of the larger group of moths whose caterpillars often have prominent humps or projections on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nadata moths can be distinguished from other prominent moths by their characteristic white or pale spots on the forewings, along with their relatively broad, sturdy appearance and specific wing venation patterns.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Nadata' comes from a Native American word, reflecting the connection between these moths and the forests of eastern North America where they have evolved alongside native tree species for thousands of years.

children.name: Gluphisia
children.description: Gluphisia is a small genus of moths in the prominent moth family (Notodontidae) that includes species with distinctive wing patterns and nocturnal habits. These moths are typically medium-sized with brownish coloration and are found in forested areas where their caterpillars feed on various deciduous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gluphisia moths can be distinguished from other prominent moths by their relatively smooth wing margins and subtle but intricate patterns of lines and shading across their forewings.
children.funFact: The Common Gluphisia Moth's caterpillars have a unique defense mechanism where they can rear up on their hind legs when threatened, making themselves appear larger and more intimidating to potential predators.

children.name: Peridea
children.description: Peridea is a small genus of moths commonly known as prominents, belonging to the family Notodontidae. These are medium-sized moths with distinctive wing patterns and caterpillars that often have unusual postures or projections. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the Angulose Prominent.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peridea moths can be distinguished from other prominent moths by their specific wing markings and the angular patterns that give some species their common names. Their caterpillars typically have a distinctive habit of raising both their head and tail ends when disturbed.
children.funFact: The name 'prominent' comes from the tufts of scales that stick up from the back edge of the forewings when the moth is at rest, giving them a distinctive silhouette.

children.name: Cecrita
children.description: Cecrita is a small genus of moths in the prominent moth family (Notodontidae) that includes just a handful of species in North America. These are medium-sized moths with distinctive wing patterns that help them blend in with tree bark during the day when they rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cecrita moths are characterized by their mottled brown and gray wing patterns with distinctive darker markings that create a saddle-like appearance across their forewings.
children.funFact: The name 'Saddled Prominent' comes from the dark markings across the moth's wings that resemble a saddle when the moth is at rest with its wings folded.

children.name: Coelodasys
children.description: Coelodasys is a small genus of moths belonging to the prominent moth family (Notodontidae). These moths are characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and are part of the larger group of night-flying moths that are attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished by their unique horn-like projection or tuft on the thorax, which gives the Unicorn Prominent its common name.
children.funFact: The name 'Coelodasys' comes from Greek words meaning 'hollow' and 'hairy,' referring to the distinctive fuzzy appearance of these moths.

children.name: Macrurocampa
children.description: Macrurocampa is a small genus of moths in the prominent moth family, known for their distinctive wing patterns and robust build. These moths are part of the larger group of nocturnal lepidopterans that are attracted to lights at night and have feathery or thread-like antennae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their mottled, bark-like wing patterns that provide excellent camouflage when resting on tree trunks during the day. They have a distinctive prominent or raised tuft of scales on their forewings that gives the prominent moth family its name.
children.funFact: The name 'Macrurocampa' literally means 'long-tailed caterpillar,' referring to the distinctive horn or spike found on the rear end of their caterpillars.

children.name: Clostera
children.description: Clostera is a genus of moths commonly known as prominents, belonging to the family Notodontidae. These medium-sized moths are characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and the habit of their caterpillars feeding on poplar and willow trees. The adults are typically brown or gray with intricate markings that help them blend in with tree bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Clostera moths can be identified by their robust build and the distinctive sigmoid (S-shaped) markings on their forewings. Unlike many other prominent moths, they tend to have more subdued coloration with subtle but characteristic curved lines across their wings.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Clostera moths are known for their unusual defensive behavior - when threatened, they can rear up and wave their front end back and forth while making clicking sounds with their mandibles.

children.description: Prominent moths are a family of medium to large-sized moths whose caterpillars are known for their unusual postures and behaviors. Many species in this group have larvae that can rear up their front or back ends when threatened, creating distinctive 'prominent' positions that give the family its name. These moths are typically brown or gray with intricate patterns that help them blend in with tree bark during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other moth families, prominent moths often have a distinctive tuft or ridge of scales on their forewings that creates a raised appearance when at rest. Their caterpillars frequently display warning postures by arching portions of their bodies upward, and many species lack the ability to roll into a ball when disturbed.
children.funFact: Some prominent moth caterpillars are such convincing mimics that they can look like bird droppings, dead leaves, or even small twigs complete with fake 'bark' textures and coloring.

children.name: Saturniidae
Dryocampa
children.description: Rosy maple moths are a small genus of colorful moths known for their striking pink and yellow coloration. These medium-sized moths are members of the royal moth family and are closely associated with maple trees, where their caterpillars feed and develop.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths which tend to be brown or gray, rosy maple moths display brilliant pink and yellow colors that make them unmistakable. Their fuzzy, wooly appearance and relatively small size also set them apart from other royal moths.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate, almost toy-like appearance, rosy maple moth caterpillars are called 'greenstriped mapleworms' and can occasionally become serious pests of maple trees when they appear in large numbers.

children.name: Actias
children.description: Moon Moths are a genus of large, spectacular moths known for their pale green coloration and distinctive long tails on their hindwings. These nocturnal beauties are among the largest moths in North America, with wingspans that can reach up to 4.5 inches. They belong to the giant silk moth family and are prized by nature enthusiasts for their ethereal, almost magical appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moon Moths are easily recognized by their characteristic long, streaming tails on their hindwings and their overall pale green coloration with translucent eyespots. Unlike other giant silk moths, they have a more delicate, moon-like appearance with their silvery-white body markings.
children.funFact: Adult Moon Moths don't have functional mouthparts and cannot eat - they live entirely off the energy stored from their caterpillar stage and typically survive only about one week as adults.

children.name: Antheraea
children.description: Tussar moths are a group of large, impressive silk moths known for their substantial size and beautiful wing patterns. These moths are part of the giant silk moth family and are characterized by their robust bodies and broad, often colorful wings that can span several inches across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tussar moths are distinguished from other silk moths by their particularly large size, distinctive eyespots on their wings, and their ability to produce wild silk that has been harvested by humans for centuries in some parts of the world.
children.funFact: The silk produced by tussar moths has a natural golden color and slightly coarser texture compared to domesticated silkworm silk, making it highly prized for luxury textiles.

children.name: Hyalophora
children.description: Hyalophora is a genus of giant silk moths that includes some of North America's largest native moths. These impressive moths are known for their substantial size, beautiful wing patterns, and the silky cocoons they spin to protect themselves during metamorphosis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hyalophora moths are distinguished by their enormous wingspan (often 5-6 inches), distinctive eyespots on their wings, and reddish-brown coloration with white and black markings that set them apart from other giant silk moth genera.
children.funFact: The silk produced by Hyalophora moths is so strong and lustrous that it was once commercially harvested in North America, though it never became as widely used as silk from Asian silkworms.

children.name: Callosamia
children.description: Callosamia is a small genus of large, beautiful moths in the giant silkmoth family. These moths are known for their impressive size and distinctive wing patterns, with females typically being larger than males. They undergo complete metamorphosis, with caterpillars that feed on various deciduous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Callosamia moths can be distinguished from other giant silkmoths by their reddish-brown coloration and distinctive white comma-shaped markings on their forewings. The males have more feathery antennae compared to females and are generally smaller in size.
children.funFact: The Promethea Silkmoth is one of the few giant silkmoths where males fly during the day to find females, while most other giant silkmoths are strictly nocturnal.

children.name: Automeris
children.description: Eyed Silkmoths are medium to large moths known for the distinctive eyespots on their hindwings that give them their name. These moths are part of the giant silkmoth family and are characterized by their fuzzy, robust bodies and broad wings. They undergo complete metamorphosis, with caterpillars that are often covered in spines or bristles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other giant silkmoths, Eyed Silkmoths have prominent circular eyespots on their hindwings that are revealed when the moth is startled or threatened. Their forewings typically lack the large transparent windows found in some related moths.
children.funFact: When threatened, Eyed Silkmoths suddenly flash their hindwings to reveal large eyespots that mimic the eyes of a much larger predator, like an owl, startling potential attackers long enough for the moth to escape.

children.description: Emperor and Giant Silk Moths are among North America's largest and most spectacular moths, with wingspans that can reach up to 6 inches across. These impressive moths are known for their vibrant colors, intricate wing patterns, and feathery antennae that help males detect female pheromones from miles away. Their caterpillars are equally striking, often large and colorful with spines or tubercles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other moth families, Saturniidae adults have no functional mouthparts and cannot feed, living only to mate and lay eggs. They're distinguished by their large size, often eyespot patterns on their wings, and the males' elaborate feathery antennae.
children.funFact: The cecropia moth, North America's largest native moth, can have a wingspan of up to 7 inches and its caterpillars can grow as thick as a human finger while feeding on over 100 different tree species.

children.name: Lasiocampidae
Malacosoma
children.description: Tent Caterpillar Moths are a small group of moths whose caterpillars are famous for creating silky shelters in tree branches. These caterpillars are social insects that live together in large groups, spinning communal webs or tents where they rest between feeding periods. The adult moths are typically brown or reddish-brown with fuzzy bodies and are active at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most caterpillars that live alone, tent caterpillars are highly social and build distinctive silk shelters in the forks of tree branches. Their communal web-building behavior and group feeding habits set them apart from other moth caterpillars.
children.funFact: Despite their name, Forest Tent Caterpillars don't actually build tents - they create silk mats on tree trunks and branches instead, while Eastern Tent Caterpillars are the true tent builders of the group.

children.name: Phyllodesma
children.description: Phyllodesma is a small genus of moths known as lappet moths, named for the distinctive wing shape and resting posture of their caterpillars. These moths are part of the family Lasiocampidae and are characterized by their robust, fuzzy bodies and broad wings. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the American Lappet Moth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phyllodesma moths can be distinguished from other lappet moths by their specific wing patterns and the unique tent-like structures their caterpillars create when resting. The caterpillars have distinctive flaps of skin along their sides that give them their 'lappet' name.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Phyllodesma moths are masters of camouflage - when disturbed, they flatten themselves against tree bark and their side flaps make them nearly invisible, looking just like a piece of rough bark or a dried leaf.

children.description: Lappet Moths are medium to large-sized moths whose caterpillars are well-known for their social behavior and distinctive shelters. Many species in this family create silk tents or mats where groups of caterpillars live together, feeding on leaves of trees and shrubs. The adult moths are typically brown or gray with fuzzy, hair-like scales that give them a woolly appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths, lappet moth caterpillars are highly social and often build communal silk structures. The adults have distinctively hairy bodies and wings, and when at rest, they hold their wings in a tent-like position over their bodies.
children.funFact: Tent caterpillars can defoliate entire trees and communicate with each other using silk trails marked with pheromones to lead their siblings to the best feeding spots.

children.name: Drepanidae
Drepana
children.description: Drepana is a genus of moths known as hooktip moths, named for their distinctive wing shape where the forewings come to a sharp, curved point or 'hook' at the tip. These medium-sized moths are part of the hooktip moth family and are known for their unique resting posture and wing structure. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species, the Arched Hooktip Moth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Drepana can be easily identified by their characteristic hooked or falcate (sickle-shaped) forewings that curve sharply at the tips. This distinctive wing shape sets them apart from most other moth families and gives them their common name.
children.funFact: Hooktip moths in the genus Drepana rest with their wings held horizontally and their bodies curved, creating a distinctive comma-like silhouette that helps them blend in with dried leaves and bark.

children.name: Pseudothyatira
children.description: Pseudothyatira is a small genus of moths in the Thyatiridae family, represented in New England by just one species - the Tufted Thyatirine Moth. These moths are characterized by their distinctive wing patterns and relatively small size compared to other members of their family. They are nocturnal creatures that are attracted to lights during their flying season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other thyatirid moths by their specific wing markings and the presence of distinctive tufts of scales on their forewings that give the Tufted Thyatirine its common name.
children.funFact: The genus name Pseudothyatira literally means 'false Thyatira,' indicating that these moths were once thought to belong to the related genus Thyatira before being recognized as distinct enough to warrant their own genus.

children.name: Habrosyne
children.description: Habrosyne is a small genus of moths known for their distinctive wing patterns that resemble handwritten letters or script. These medium-sized moths are part of the hooktip moth family and are primarily active at night. In New England, only one species from this genus is found - the Lettered Habrosyne Moth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their unique wing markings that look like cursive writing or calligraphy across their forewings. Their wings also have a slightly hooked tip shape that's characteristic of their family.
children.funFact: The name 'Habrosyne' comes from Greek words meaning 'delicate' and 'together,' while the species name 'scripta' literally means 'written,' referring to the script-like markings on their wings.

children.description: Hooktip and False Owlet Moths are a small but distinctive family of moths known for their uniquely shaped forewings that often end in curved, hook-like tips. These medium-sized moths are typically brown or gray with intricate patterns that help them blend in with tree bark and dead leaves. Most species are nocturnal and their caterpillars feed on various deciduous trees and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic hooked or curved tips of their forewings make them easily recognizable among moths. Unlike true owlet moths, they hold their wings in a distinctive tent-like position when at rest.
children.funFact: Despite their name, False Owlet Moths aren't closely related to true owlet moths at all - they were grouped together historically because of their similar appearance, but DNA studies revealed they belong to a completely different evolutionary lineage.

children.name: Limacodidae
Euclea
children.description: Euclea slug moths are a small group of moths whose caterpillars are known as slug caterpillars due to their flattened, oval shape and smooth, slug-like movement. These caterpillars are covered in stinging spines that can cause painful welts if touched, making them one of the more notorious stinging caterpillars in North America. The adult moths are relatively small and brownish, often going unnoticed compared to their more conspicuous larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euclea caterpillars can be identified by their distinctive flattened, saddle-like shape and the presence of urticating (stinging) spines arranged in clusters along their body. Unlike other slug moth caterpillars, Euclea species typically have a more pronounced saddle-shaped profile when viewed from the side.
children.funFact: The Spiny Oak-slug caterpillar's stinging spines contain venom that can cause burning pain lasting for hours, yet the caterpillar uses this defense system so effectively that it can feed openly on leaves during the day without fear of predators.

children.name: Lithacodes
children.description: Lithacodes is a genus of small moths whose caterpillars are known as slug moths due to their distinctive slug-like appearance and movement. These caterpillars lack the typical prolegs found on most moth larvae, instead gliding smoothly along surfaces using their flattened, gelatinous bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other moth caterpillars, Lithacodes larvae have a unique flattened, oval shape and move by gliding rather than crawling with legs. The adult moths are small and relatively plain compared to their more colorful slug moth relatives.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Lithacodes moths can actually change their body color and patterns to better match the leaves they're feeding on, making them masters of camouflage.

children.name: Tortricidia
children.description: Tortricidia is a small genus of moths known for their distinctive slug-like caterpillars that lack the usual prolegs found on most moth larvae. These moths are part of the larger family of micromoths, with adults that are relatively small and often overlooked. The caterpillars are the most notable stage, appearing smooth and slug-like as they feed on various plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The caterpillars of Tortricidia are unique among moths for their slug-like appearance and movement, lacking the typical prolegs that help other caterpillars grip surfaces. Adults are small, brown moths that can be distinguished from similar species by their specific wing patterns and markings.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'button slug moths,' these insects are true moths whose caterpillars have simply evolved to mimic slugs, possibly as a form of protection from predators who might find slugs less appetizing than typical caterpillars.

children.description: Slug caterpillar moths are a fascinating family of small to medium-sized moths whose caterpillars look remarkably like colorful slugs. These caterpillars have lost their typical prolegs and instead glide smoothly along leaves and branches using their flattened, gel-like bodies. The adult moths are typically brown or gray with relatively simple wing patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The caterpillars are unmistakable with their slug-like appearance, lacking the usual caterpillar legs and body segments. Many species also have stinging spines or hairs that can cause painful reactions when touched.
children.funFact: Some slug caterpillars, like the saddleback caterpillar, are covered in venomous spines that deliver a sting more painful than a bee sting, earning them the nickname 'stinging slugs.'

children.name: Pyralidae
Hypsopygia
children.description: Hayworms are a small genus of moths in the snout moth family, with delicate wings and slender bodies. These moths are typically small to medium-sized and are often found near grasses and low vegetation where their caterpillars feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hayworms can be recognized by their distinctive wing patterns with yellowish or pale fringes along the wing edges, and their habit of holding their wings in a triangular tent-like position when at rest.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'hayworms,' these are actually moths - the name refers to their caterpillars, which were historically found feeding in stored hay and dried grasses.

children.name: Pyralis
children.description: Meal moths are a genus of small to medium-sized moths known for their close association with stored food products and grain. These moths have adapted to live alongside humans, with their larvae feeding on flour, cereals, and other stored pantry items.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Meal moths can be identified by their distinctive wing patterns with reddish-brown and pale markings, and their habit of infesting stored food rather than living on wild plants like most other moths.
children.funFact: The meal moth is one of the most widespread moths in the world, having spread to every continent except Antarctica by hitchhiking in human food supplies and grain shipments.

children.description: Pyralid snout moths are a family of small to medium-sized moths known for their distinctive elongated mouthparts that form a prominent snout-like projection. These moths are typically brown or gray in color and are often found around stored food products, making some species common household pests. Their caterpillars feed on a variety of organic materials including grains, dried foods, and plant debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most notable feature of pyralid snout moths is their pronounced snout formed by extended labial palps (mouthpart segments) that project forward from the head. This snout-like appearance, combined with their tendency to hold their wings in a triangular tent-like position when at rest, makes them easily recognizable among moth families.
children.funFact: Some pyralid snout moths, like meal moths, have such a strong association with human food storage that they've spread around the world wherever people store grains and dried goods, making them some of the most cosmopolitan insects on Earth.

children.name: Riodinidae
Calephelis
children.description: Calephelis is a genus of small, delicate butterflies known as metalmarks, named for the metallic spots and lines that often decorate their wings. These butterflies are typically orange, brown, or reddish in color with intricate patterns of metallic markings that shimmer in the sunlight. They are generally small butterflies with a wingspan of about 1 inch or less.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Metalmarks can be distinguished from other small butterflies by their characteristic metallic wing markings and their habit of perching with wings held horizontally rather than vertically like many other butterfly families.
children.funFact: The Northern Metalmark is extremely rare in New England and is considered endangered in several states, making any sighting a special treat for butterfly enthusiasts.

children.description: Metalmark butterflies are small, delicate butterflies known for the distinctive metallic spots or lines that shimmer on their wings like tiny mirrors. They are typically brown, orange, or reddish in color with intricate patterns. Most species prefer open, sunny areas like meadows, grasslands, and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Metalmarks can be identified by their characteristic metallic markings that catch and reflect light, giving them their name. They have relatively short, stubby antennae compared to other butterfly families and often perch with their wings held horizontally.
children.funFact: Male metalmark butterflies have only four functional legs for walking, while females have all six legs functional - this difference between the sexes is unusual among butterflies.

children.name: Attevidae
Atteva
children.description: Atteva is a genus of small, colorful moths known for their distinctive wing patterns and feeding habits. These moths are part of the family Yponomeutidae and are characterized by their relatively small size and often vibrant coloration. Members of this genus typically have larvae that feed on specific host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Atteva moths can be distinguished from other small moths by their unique wing patterns, which often feature bright orange or yellow coloration with distinctive spots or bands. Their forewings are typically narrow and elongated compared to many other small moth species.
children.funFact: The Ailanthus Webworm Moth in this genus is actually native to Central and South America but has become established in New England, where its caterpillars feed primarily on the invasive tree-of-heaven (Ailanthus altissima).

children.description: Tropical Ermine Moths are a small family of colorful day-flying moths that are primarily found in warm climates around the world. These moths are known for their bright orange, red, or yellow wings decorated with distinctive black or white spots, giving them an almost butterfly-like appearance. Despite their tropical origins, one species has established itself in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most moths, these insects are active during the day and have vibrant warning colors with bold spot patterns. Their wings are held horizontally when at rest, and they have a distinctive fluttering flight pattern similar to butterflies.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Atteva aurea, is actually a recent arrival from the tropics that followed its host plant (tree-of-heaven) northward as this invasive tree spread across North America.

children.name: Depressariidae
Machimia
children.description: Machimia is a small genus of moths in the leafroller family, with delicate wings and intricate patterns. These moths are known for their larvae's habit of creating leaf shelters by tying or rolling leaves together, where they feed protected from predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive gold striping patterns on the forewings, which gives the Gold-striped Leaftier its common name.
children.funFact: The scientific name 'tentoriferella' literally means 'little tent bearer,' referring to the larva's behavior of creating tent-like shelters from leaves.

children.description: Flat-bodied moths are small to medium-sized moths whose caterpillars typically feed on plants in the carrot family, rose family, and other flowering plants. These moths get their name from their distinctively flattened appearance when at rest, with wings held close to their body. They are often found near their host plants during the day, becoming active at dusk and night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other moth families, flat-bodied moths have a characteristically compressed, flattened profile when resting. Their forewings are typically narrow and elongated, and they often hold their wings in a distinctive roof-like position over their flattened body.
children.funFact: Many flat-bodied moth caterpillars are leaf miners or stem borers, creating intricate tunnels and galleries inside their host plants as they feed and grow.

children.name: Tortricidae
Cenopis
children.description: Cenopis is a genus of small moths in the leafroller family, known for their intricate wing patterns and fruit-feeding caterpillars. These moths are part of a large group of insects whose larvae typically roll or fold leaves to create protective shelters while they feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cenopis moths are characterized by their reticulated (net-like) wing patterns with intricate crosshatched markings that distinguish them from other leafroller moths.
children.funFact: The caterpillars of Cenopis moths are sometimes called fruitworms because they feed inside fruits, particularly wild cherries and other stone fruits, making them important in forest ecosystems as both herbivores and food sources for birds.

children.description: Tortricid leafroller moths are a large family of small moths whose caterpillars are known for their habit of rolling or folding leaves to create protective shelters. These moths typically have bell-shaped forewings when at rest and are often brown or gray with intricate patterns that help them blend in with tree bark. The larvae feed on a wide variety of plants and can sometimes be agricultural pests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tortricids can be distinguished from other small moths by their characteristic bell-shaped wing posture when resting and their broad, often squared-off forewings. The caterpillars' distinctive behavior of creating leaf rolls or ties is also a key identifying feature of this family.
children.funFact: Many tortricid caterpillars are master architects, using silk to carefully roll leaves into tube-shaped homes where they can feed safely hidden from predators and parasites.

children.name: Psychidae
Psyche
children.description: Psyche is a genus of small moths known as bagworm moths, whose caterpillars create distinctive portable cases or 'bags' from silk and plant materials. These moths are part of the bagworm moth family and are found across temperate regions. The larvae live inside their protective cases throughout their development, dragging them along as they feed.
