children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their larvae's habit of constructing and living within protective cases made of silk woven together with bits of leaves, twigs, and other plant debris. Adult females are often wingless and remain inside their larval cases even after metamorphosis.
children.funFact: Female bagworm moths in this genus are so specialized for reproduction that they never leave their larval cases - males must find and mate with them while they remain hidden inside their protective bags!

children.description: Bagworm Moths are a unique family of moths whose caterpillars create protective cases or 'bags' made from silk and bits of plant material like twigs, leaves, or bark. The larvae live inside these portable shelters throughout their development, carrying them around as they feed on various plants. Adult females of many species are wingless and remain in their bags even after becoming moths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other moth caterpillars, bagworm larvae construct and live within distinctive protective cases made of silk and plant debris. The adult females are often flightless and may never leave their larval cases, which is unusual among moths.
children.funFact: Female bagworm moths of some species never develop wings or legs and spend their entire adult lives inside their childhood bag, mating and laying eggs without ever seeing the outside world.

children.name: Oecophoridae
Callima
children.description: Callima is a small genus of micro-moths in the family Gelechiidae, known for their tiny size and intricate wing patterns. These delicate moths are part of the large group of concealer moths, which get their name from their larvae's habit of feeding inside plant tissues or creating shelters from leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Callima can be identified by their narrow, elongated forewings with distinctive metallic markings and their characteristic resting posture with wings folded tightly against their body.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Callima moths have incredibly detailed wing scales that create shimmering metallic patterns visible only under magnification.

children.description: Concealer moths are a large family of small to medium-sized moths whose caterpillars are known for their secretive lifestyles. Many species in this family get their name because their larvae create shelters by binding leaves together, hiding in plant debris, or boring into stems and roots where they remain concealed while feeding.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These moths typically have narrow forewings and broad hindwings, with many species showing cryptic coloration that helps them blend into bark or dead plant material. Their caterpillars are distinguished by their habit of creating protective shelters or living hidden within plant tissues.
children.funFact: Some concealer moth caterpillars are so well-hidden that they can live their entire larval stage inside a single rolled leaf, emerging only as adults to mate and start the cycle again.

children.description: Butterflies and moths make up one of the largest groups of insects, all sharing the characteristic feature of having wings covered in tiny, overlapping scales that create their beautiful colors and patterns. These insects undergo complete metamorphosis, transforming from caterpillars to winged adults through a pupal stage. They include both the colorful day-flying butterflies we see in gardens and the diverse array of moths that are often active at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The microscopic scales covering their wings set Lepidoptera apart from all other insects, giving them their powdery texture and often iridescent colors. Their coiled proboscis (feeding tube) and the way their wings fold when at rest also help distinguish different groups within this order.
children.funFact: The scales on butterfly and moth wings are actually modified hairs that can create structural colors through microscopic ridges that bend light, which is why some species appear to shimmer or change color when viewed from different angles.

children.name: Coleoptera
Cerambycidae
Tetraopes
children.description: Milkweed Longhorn Beetles are a specialized group of colorful beetles that have evolved to live exclusively on milkweed plants. These medium-sized beetles have distinctively long antennae and are easily recognized by their bright red or orange coloration with black spots or markings. Both adults and larvae feed on various parts of milkweed plants, making them one of the few insects that can tolerate the plant's toxic compounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other longhorn beetles, Tetraopes species have uniquely divided eyes that wrap around the base of their antennae, giving them exceptional vision. They also produce audible squeaking sounds when handled, created by rubbing body parts together.
children.funFact: These beetles are immune to milkweed toxins and actually store them in their bodies as protection from predators, advertising their toxicity with bright warning colors just like monarch butterflies.

children.name: Prionus
children.description: Prionus beetles are large, robust longhorn beetles known for their impressive size and powerful mandibles. These beetles are wood-boring insects whose larvae develop in the roots and lower trunks of various trees, earning them the common name 'root borers.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Prionus beetles are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their exceptionally large size, thick and heavily built bodies, and prominently serrated (saw-toothed) antennae that give them a distinctive prehistoric appearance.
children.funFact: The Broad-necked Root Borer can take up to 5 years to complete its development from egg to adult, spending most of this time as a large grub feeding on tree roots underground.

children.name: Monochamus
children.description: Sawyer beetles are large, robust longhorn beetles known for their impressive size and distinctive long antennae. These wood-boring insects get their common name from the sawing or gnawing sounds their larvae make while tunneling through dead or dying coniferous trees. Adult sawyer beetles are strong fliers and are often attracted to lights at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sawyer beetles are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their particularly large size, typically measuring 1-2 inches long, and their preference for coniferous trees rather than hardwoods. They have especially prominent, forward-projecting mandibles and tend to be more robust in build than most other longhorn beetle species.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating size and loud buzzing flight, sawyer beetles are completely harmless to humans and actually play an important ecological role by helping to decompose fallen trees and create habitat for other forest creatures.

children.name: Strangalia
children.description: Strangalia is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their slender bodies and love of flowers. These beetles are commonly found visiting blooms during summer months, where adults feed on pollen and nectar while their larvae develop inside decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other longhorn beetles, Strangalia species have distinctly narrow, elongated bodies and are typically seen on flowers rather than on wood or bark during daylight hours.
children.funFact: Despite being wood-boring beetles as larvae, adult Strangalia are important pollinators that help transfer pollen between flowers as they feed.

children.name: Xylotrechus
children.description: Xylotrechus is a genus of longhorn beetles whose larvae are wood borers, tunneling through the inner bark and wood of trees. These medium-sized beetles are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping break down dead and dying trees. Both New England species are known for their distinctive markings and their role in recycling nutrients back into the forest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Xylotrechus beetles can be distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their robust build and characteristic yellow or white markings that often form bands or arrow-like patterns across their dark wing covers.
children.funFact: The Arrowhead Borer gets its name from the distinctive arrow-shaped white markings on its back that point toward its head, making it one of the most easily recognizable longhorn beetles in New England.

children.name: Saperda
children.description: Saperda is a genus of longhorn beetles whose larvae are wood-boring pests that tunnel through the stems and trunks of trees and shrubs. These beetles are known for their cylindrical bodies and relatively long antennae, and their young develop by feeding on the inner bark and wood of their host plants. Adult beetles are typically active during summer months when they mate and lay eggs on their preferred tree species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Saperda beetles can be distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their rounded heads and the way their larvae create distinctive round exit holes in wood. Their bodies tend to be more cylindrical and less flattened than many related species.
children.funFact: The Round-headed Apple Tree Borer can take up to three years to complete its development from egg to adult, spending most of that time as a larva tunneling through apple tree trunks and potentially killing young trees.

children.name: Megacyllene
children.description: Megacyllene is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their striking black and yellow banded patterns that help them mimic wasps or bees. These wood-boring beetles are closely associated with leguminous trees, particularly locust trees, where they spend their larval stage tunneling through the wood. Adult beetles are active during the day and can often be seen visiting flowers for nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their bold yellow and black striped wing covers and their specific association with locust and other legume trees. Unlike many other longhorn beetles, they are excellent wasp mimics and are active during daylight hours rather than being nocturnal.
children.funFact: The Locust Borer's larvae create distinctive oval exit holes in black locust trees, and despite being considered a pest, the adult beetles actually help pollinate goldenrod flowers in the fall.

children.name: Typocerus
children.description: Typocerus is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their distinctive banded patterns and medium size. These beetles are part of the flower longhorn group, meaning adults are commonly found visiting flowers where they feed on pollen and nectar. They have the characteristic long antennae that give longhorn beetles their name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Typocerus beetles are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their relatively robust build and distinctive color patterns, often featuring bands or stripes across their wing covers. They tend to be more compact than many other longhorn species.
children.funFact: Despite being called longhorn beetles, Typocerus species are actually important pollinators, transferring pollen between flowers as they feed, making them beneficial garden visitors.

children.name: Orthosoma
children.description: Orthosoma is a genus of large, robust longhorn beetles known as prionids. These impressive insects are among the biggest beetles in North America, with powerful mandibles and elongated antennae that give them a distinctive prehistoric appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Orthosoma beetles are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their exceptionally large size, massive heads with prominent jaws, and relatively shorter antennae compared to other members of the longhorn beetle family.
children.funFact: The Brown Prionid can live as a larva for up to 10 years, slowly developing inside decaying hardwood trees before emerging as a massive adult beetle that can reach over 2 inches in length.

children.name: Strangalepta
children.description: Strangalepta is a small genus of longhorn beetles known for their flower-visiting habits and distinctive appearance. These beetles are characterized by their elongated antennae and relatively compact bodies compared to other longhorn beetles. They are often found on flowers where they feed on pollen and nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Strangalepta beetles can be distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their shorter, more robust body shape and their preference for daytime flower-visiting behavior rather than the wood-boring habits of many relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'longhorn beetles,' Strangalepta species are actually beneficial pollinators that help fertilize wildflowers as they move from bloom to bloom feeding on nectar.

children.name: Analeptura
children.description: Analeptura is a small genus of longhorn beetles found in North America. These beetles are characterized by their elongated bodies and long antennae, typical of the longhorn beetle family, and they develop as larvae boring through the wood of dead or dying trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Analeptura can be distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their distinctive striped or lined pattern on their wing covers and their relatively slender build compared to many of their bulkier relatives.
children.funFact: The single New England species, the Lined Longhorn Beetle, gets its name from the prominent yellow or pale stripes running lengthwise down its dark wing covers, making it one of the more easily recognizable longhorn beetles in the region.

children.name: Judolia
children.description: Judolia is a small genus of longhorn beetles found in North America, with only one species calling New England home. These are medium-sized beetles that belong to the flower longhorn subfamily, meaning adults are commonly found visiting flowers where they feed on pollen and nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Judolia beetles can be identified by their relatively robust build compared to other flower longhorns, and their distinctive color patterns that often include reddish-brown or chestnut coloration with darker markings.
children.funFact: Despite being called longhorn beetles, Judolia species actually have relatively shorter antennae compared to many of their relatives in the longhorn beetle family.

children.name: Stictoleptura
children.description: Stictoleptura is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their elongated bodies and long antennae. These beetles are wood-borers, meaning their larvae develop inside tree trunks and branches, playing an important role in forest ecosystems by helping decompose dead and dying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive coloration patterns and relatively robust build compared to other longhorn beetles. They typically have prominent shoulders and specific markings that help distinguish them from closely related genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Red-shouldered Pine Borer, Stictoleptura canadensis actually prefers hardwood trees like maple and birch over pine trees for laying its eggs.

children.name: Graphisurus
children.description: Graphisurus is a small genus of marine worms that are part of the polychaete family. These segmented worms live in marine environments and have distinctive body patterns that help identify them from other similar worms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their banded or striped appearance across their segmented bodies, which gives them their distinctive visual pattern.
children.funFact: The name Graphisurus comes from Greek roots meaning 'written tail,' referring to the distinctive markings that appear like writing across their bodies.

children.name: Evodinus
children.description: Evodinus is a small genus of longhorn beetles that are specially adapted to mountainous and northern environments. These robust beetles are typically found in coniferous forests where they develop in dead or dying wood of various tree species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Evodinus beetles are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their relatively short, thick antennae and compact, heavily built body structure that helps them survive in harsh mountain climates.
children.funFact: Despite being longhorn beetles, Evodinus species have proportionally shorter antennae than most of their relatives, an adaptation that may help prevent damage from freezing temperatures in their cold mountain habitats.

children.name: Clytus
children.description: Clytus is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their distinctive rounded necks and elongated bodies. These wood-boring beetles are part of the large family of longhorn beetles (Cerambycidae) and are typically found around decaying or dead wood where they feed and reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Clytus can be identified by their characteristic rounded pronotum (the shield-like section behind the head) and their relatively short antennae compared to other longhorn beetles. They often display bold patterns of yellow, black, or white markings on their wing covers.
children.funFact: Some Clytus beetles are excellent mimics of wasps, using bright yellow and black coloration to fool predators into thinking they have a dangerous sting when they're actually harmless.

children.name: Desmocerus
children.description: Elderberry borers are specialized longhorn beetles whose larvae develop inside the stems and branches of elderberry shrubs. These medium-sized beetles have elongated bodies and long antennae typical of the longhorn beetle family. Adults are active during summer months when they can be found on elderberry flowers feeding on pollen and nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most longhorn beetles that bore into hardwood trees, elderberry borers are specialists that exclusively target the soft, pithy stems of elderberry shrubs. They can be distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their distinctive blue-black coloration with bright yellow or orange markings.
children.funFact: The Eastern Elderberry Borer has such a close relationship with elderberry plants that it's considered an indicator species - finding these beetles tells you that healthy elderberry populations are thriving in the area.

children.name: Neandra
children.description: Neandra is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their wood-boring lifestyle. These beetles spend their larval stage tunneling through dead and dying hardwood trees, playing an important role in forest decomposition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their elongated antennae and cylindrical body shape typical of wood-boring beetles, with larvae that create distinctive tunnels in hardwood.
children.funFact: The Pole Borer got its common name because its larvae were historically a major pest of wooden telephone and telegraph poles, sometimes causing them to snap unexpectedly.

children.name: Rhagium
children.description: Rhagium is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their distinctive ribbed or ridged wing covers that give them a textured appearance. These medium-sized beetles are typically found in forested areas where they develop in dead or dying coniferous trees, particularly pine species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by the prominent longitudinal ridges running down their elytra (wing covers), which create a distinctive ribbed pattern that sets them apart from other longhorn beetles.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Ribbed Pine Borer, these beetles don't actually bore into healthy living trees - they're nature's recyclers, helping decompose dead and dying wood in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Neoclytus
children.description: Neoclytus is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their distinctive wasp-like appearance and coloration. These wood-boring beetles are often found on dead or dying hardwood trees, where their larvae develop by feeding on the wood beneath the bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their bright yellow and black striped patterns that mimic wasps, along with their relatively small size compared to other longhorn beetles.
children.funFact: Despite their fearsome wasp-like appearance, these beetles are completely harmless to humans and use this mimicry as protection from predators who mistake them for stinging insects.

children.name: Enaphalodes
children.description: Enaphalodes is a genus of large, robust longhorn beetles known for their impressive size and wood-boring lifestyle. These beetles are characterized by their elongated antennae and strong, cylindrical bodies that are well-adapted for tunneling through hardwood trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Enaphalodes are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their particularly large size, reaching up to 2 inches in length, and their preference for boring into oak trees specifically.
children.funFact: The Red Oak Borer can spend 2-4 years as a larva tunneling through oak heartwood, creating galleries that can weaken trees and make distinctive oval exit holes when the adults emerge.

children.name: Cyrtophorus
children.description: Cyrtophorus is a small genus of longhorn beetles known for their distinctive ant-like appearance and behavior. These beetles have evolved to mimic ants, which helps protect them from predators who avoid the stinging insects. They are part of the large longhorn beetle family but represent a unique evolutionary adaptation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical longhorn beetles, Cyrtophorus species have a constricted, wasp-waisted body shape that closely resembles ants. They also move in quick, jerky motions similar to ant behavior rather than the steady gait of most beetles.
children.funFact: The Ant-like Longhorn Beetle is such a convincing ant mimic that it can fool both predators and casual observers, even walking among real ants without being detected.

children.name: Anelaphus
children.description: Anelaphus is a genus of longhorn beetles that are wood-boring insects found throughout North America. These beetles are characterized by their elongated bodies and distinctively long antennae that can be as long as or longer than their bodies. The adults are typically brown or grayish in color and have a somewhat cylindrical shape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their relatively robust build and the specific pattern of ridges and punctures on their wing covers. They also tend to have shorter antennae relative to body size compared to many other longhorn beetle species.
children.funFact: The Twig Pruner beetle gets its common name from the larva's unique behavior of chewing through tree branches from the inside, causing them to break off and fall to the ground where the larva can continue developing in the fallen wood.

children.name: Brachyleptura
children.description: Brachyleptura is a genus of longhorn beetles known for their relatively compact bodies compared to other longhorn beetles. These beetles are wood-boring insects whose larvae develop inside dead or dying trees, playing an important role in forest decomposition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have shorter, more robust bodies than typical longhorn beetles, with distinctive reddish wing covers and relatively short antennae for the longhorn beetle family.
children.funFact: The Red-winged Longhorn Beetle is often seen visiting flowers during summer months, where adults feed on pollen and nectar despite their larvae being wood-borers.

children.name: Bellamira
children.description: Bellamira is a small genus of longhorn beetles found in North America, with only one species calling New England home. These are medium-sized wood-boring beetles that belong to the larger family of longhorn beetles, known for their distinctively long antennae that can be as long as or longer than their bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bellamira beetles are recognized by their distinctive ladder-like markings across their wing covers, which give them their common name of ladder-marked longhorn beetles. They have a more robust, cylindrical body shape compared to many other longhorn beetle genera.
children.funFact: The larvae of Bellamira beetles spend several years developing inside dead hardwood trees, creating intricate tunnel systems as they feed on the wood before emerging as adults.

children.name: Ecyrus
children.description: Ecyrus is a small genus of longhorned beetles known for their distinctive rough, textured wing covers and moderately long antennae. These beetles are wood-borers, with their larvae developing inside dead or dying hardwood trees where they help decompose fallen timber.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ecyrus can be recognized by their densely punctured and granular wing covers that give them a distinctly rough appearance, unlike the smoother surfaces of many other longhorned beetles.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Ecyrus' comes from Greek meaning 'out of authority,' though the reason for this unusual naming choice by early taxonomists remains a mystery.

children.name: Molorchus
children.description: Molorchus is a genus of small, distinctive longhorn beetles found throughout temperate regions. These beetles are characterized by their shortened wing covers that don't fully cover their abdomen, giving them an unusual wasp-like appearance among the longhorn beetle family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most longhorn beetles, Molorchus species have abbreviated elytra (wing covers) that expose part of their abdomen, making them look quite different from their fully-covered relatives.
children.funFact: The exposed abdomen and slender build of Molorchus beetles creates such a convincing wasp mimicry that they're often mistaken for wasps by both predators and casual observers.

children.name: Etorofus
children.description: Etorofus is a small genus of marine copepods, which are tiny crustaceans that drift in ocean waters as part of the zooplankton community. These microscopic animals are important members of marine food webs, serving as food for larger organisms while feeding on even smaller particles and organisms in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive body shape and specific arrangements of swimming appendages that distinguish them from other copepod groups.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, copepods like Etorofus are among the most abundant animals on Earth and play a crucial role in ocean ecosystems by helping transfer energy from tiny phytoplankton up to fish and other marine life.

children.name: Anthophylax
children.description: Anthophylax is a small genus of longhorn beetles known for their distinctive coloration and flower-visiting behavior. These beetles are characterized by their elongated antennae and robust build typical of the longhorn beetle family, but they stand out with their unique color patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their striking metallic blue-green bodies combined with bright reddish legs, creating a dramatic color contrast that sets them apart from other longhorn beetles.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they eat flowers, Red-footed Longhorn Beetles actually visit flowers primarily for nectar while their larvae develop inside decaying hardwood trees.

children.description: Longhorn beetles are a diverse family of wood-boring beetles famous for their exceptionally long antennae, which can be longer than their entire body. Most species have elongated, cylindrical bodies and strong mandibles for chewing through wood. Their larvae develop inside trees and woody plants, where they create tunnels as they feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The extremely long antennae that give this family its name are the most reliable identifying feature, typically extending well beyond the beetle's body length. Many species also have distinctive clicking or squeaking sounds when handled.
children.funFact: Some longhorn beetle larvae can take several years to develop inside a tree, and the adult beetles that eventually emerge can live for months, making them some of the longest-lived beetles in New England.

children.name: Chrysomelidae
Charidotella
children.description: Charidotella is a genus of small, dome-shaped beetles known as tortoise beetles. These fascinating insects have transparent, shell-like wing covers that extend beyond their body like a turtle's shell, giving them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other leaf beetles, Charidotella species can actually change color from metallic gold or silver to dull brown or orange when disturbed or during different life stages.
children.funFact: The Golden Tortoise Beetle earned the nickname 'goldbug' because its metallic shine is so brilliant that early collectors thought they had discovered beetles made of actual gold!

children.name: Leptinotarsa
children.description: Potato beetles are a group of chunky, oval-shaped leaf beetles known for their distinctive striped patterns and love of plants in the nightshade family. These robust beetles are most famous for munching on potato plants, but they'll also feed on tomatoes, eggplants, and their wild relatives. Both adults and their plump, colorful larvae can quickly strip leaves from their host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Potato beetles stand out from other leaf beetles with their larger size, distinctive black and yellow or orange striped wing covers, and their dome-shaped bodies. Unlike many leaf beetles that are small and metallic-colored, potato beetles are substantial insects that are easy to spot on plants.
children.funFact: The Colorado Potato Beetle is one of the most successful agricultural pests in the world, having spread from its original home in the Rocky Mountains to colonize potato fields across North America, Europe, and Asia in just over 150 years.

children.name: Microrhopala
children.description: Microrhopala is a genus of small, metallic-colored beetles known as leaf miners. These tiny insects spend their larval stage tunneling through the leaves of plants, creating distinctive winding trails or blotches as they feed on the leaf tissue between the upper and lower surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These beetles are distinguished from other leaf miners by their compact, oval-shaped bodies and their preference for plants in the aster family, particularly goldenrod and related species.
children.funFact: The intricate maze-like patterns that Microrhopala larvae create inside leaves can be used like fingerprints to identify the exact species, even when the tiny beetle itself is nowhere to be found!

children.name: Calligrapha
children.description: Calligrapher beetles are small, colorful leaf beetles that get their name from the distinctive striped and spotted patterns on their wing covers that resemble artistic brushstrokes. These beetles are specialized plant feeders that spend their entire lives on their preferred host trees, with adults and larvae both feeding on leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other leaf beetles, calligrapher beetles have very specific host plant relationships and distinctive geometric patterns of stripes and spots that are unique to each species. Their markings are much more organized and artistic-looking than the random spots found on many other beetles.
children.funFact: Each species of calligrapher beetle has evolved alongside a specific type of tree - willow calligrapher beetles are found only on willows, while dogwood leaf beetles stick exclusively to dogwood trees throughout their entire lifecycle.

children.name: Labidomera
children.description: Labidomera is a small genus of leaf beetles that are specialists at feeding on milkweed plants. These colorful beetles have evolved to tolerate the toxic chemicals that milkweeds produce to defend themselves from herbivores. They're relatively large, robust beetles compared to many other leaf beetle species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Labidomera beetles are distinguished by their specialized diet of milkweed plants and their ability to sequester toxic cardiac glycosides from their host plants. They tend to be larger and more colorful than most other leaf beetles.
children.funFact: Like monarch butterflies, Labidomera beetles use bright warning colors to advertise their toxicity to predators - they store the poisonous chemicals from milkweed plants in their bodies, making them unpalatable to birds and other animals that might try to eat them.

children.name: Diabrotica
children.description: Diabrotica is a genus of small, colorful beetles commonly known as cucumber beetles. These insects are agricultural pests that feed on the leaves, stems, and roots of plants in the cucumber family, as well as corn and other crops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their bright yellow or greenish-yellow coloration with distinctive black spots or stripes, distinguishing them from other leaf beetles.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, cucumber beetles can cause major agricultural damage not just by eating plants, but also by spreading bacterial wilt disease as they move from plant to plant.

children.name: Chrysochus
children.description: Chrysochus is a small genus of metallic leaf beetles known for their brilliant, iridescent coloration that shimmers like jewels. These chunky, oval-shaped beetles are specialized feeders that primarily consume plants in the dogbane and milkweed families. They're considered among the most beautiful beetles in North America due to their stunning metallic sheen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chrysochus beetles are distinguished from other leaf beetles by their exceptionally bright metallic colors - typically golden, copper, or blue-green - and their robust, rounded body shape. Unlike many leaf beetles, they have notably thick antennae and are larger and more convex than most of their relatives.
children.funFact: Despite their stunning beauty, Dogbane Leaf Beetles are toxic to predators because they sequester poisonous compounds from the milkweed and dogbane plants they eat, making their brilliant colors a warning signal rather than just decoration.

children.name: Helocassis
children.description: Helocassis is a small genus of tortoise beetles known for their distinctive dome-shaped bodies that can completely cover their legs and antennae when threatened. These compact beetles are plant-eaters that feed on members of the morning glory family, including sweet potato vines and bindweeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Helocassis have particularly high, rounded shells compared to other tortoise beetles, giving them an especially turtle-like appearance. Their body shape is more globular and elevated than the flatter profile of most other tortoise beetle genera.
children.funFact: The Clavate Tortoise Beetle can retract all of its appendages under its shell-like wing covers, creating a perfect dome that makes it look exactly like a tiny golden or copper-colored bead sitting on a leaf.

children.name: Lilioceris
children.description: Lilioceris is a genus of small, colorful leaf beetles that specialize in feeding on plants in the lily family. These beetles are known for their bright red or orange bodies with black heads and legs, making them quite distinctive among garden insects. They are considered serious pests of lilies, fritillaries, and other ornamental bulb plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other leaf beetles, Lilioceris species have a characteristic habit of covering their larvae with their own feces as protection from predators. Adults also produce a distinctive squeaking sound when disturbed by rubbing body parts together.
children.funFact: The Lily Leaf Beetle was accidentally introduced to North America from Europe and has become such an effective lily destroyer that it can completely defoliate entire lily plants in just a few days.

children.name: Acalymma
children.description: Acalymma is a genus of small, colorful beetles that specialize in feeding on plants in the cucumber family. These beetles are known for their bright yellow bodies decorated with distinctive stripes or spots, making them easily recognizable garden visitors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acalymma beetles can be distinguished from other cucumber beetles by their specific stripe patterns and their exclusive preference for cucurbit plants (squash, cucumber, melon family).
children.funFact: Despite being tiny insects, Acalymma beetles can cause serious damage to cucumber crops because they not only chew on leaves but also transmit bacterial wilt disease from plant to plant as they feed.

children.name: Plagiodera
children.description: Plagiodera is a small genus of leaf beetles that specialize in feeding on willow and poplar trees. These small, metallic-colored beetles are known for their strong preference for trees in the willow family, where both adults and larvae feed on the leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plagiodera beetles can be identified by their small size, metallic sheen, and their exclusive association with willow and poplar trees. They have a more elongated body shape compared to many other leaf beetles.
children.funFact: The Willow Leaf Beetle can change color throughout its lifetime, starting as a bright metallic green when young and often becoming more bronze or copper-colored as it ages.

children.name: Deloyala
children.description: Deloyala is a genus of tortoise beetles, small rounded beetles that look remarkably like tiny shields or coins. These beetles have a distinctive dome-shaped body with expanded edges that completely cover their head and legs when viewed from above, giving them their tortoise-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Deloyala beetles are distinguished from other tortoise beetles by their specific body proportions and the unique patterns of spots or markings on their wing covers. They have a particularly flattened, broad shape with smooth, glossy surfaces.
children.funFact: When threatened, Deloyala beetles can pull their legs and antennae completely under their shell-like wing covers, making them look like small, inanimate objects that predators might overlook.

children.name: Sumitrosis
children.description: Sumitrosis is a genus of marine bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that form encrusting mats on hard surfaces like rocks, shells, and seaweed. These filter-feeding creatures build calcium carbonate skeletons and live together in colonies where each individual zooid has its own small chamber. They are commonly found in shallow coastal waters where they help filter plankton from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sumitrosis can be distinguished from other bryozoan genera by its distinctive colony growth pattern and the specific shape and arrangement of its zooid chambers. The species has characteristic pore structures and skeletal features that are unique to this genus.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Sumitrosis often get mistaken for seaweed or coral because of their plant-like or rock-like appearance when growing on underwater surfaces.

children.name: Lema
children.description: Lema is a genus of small, elongated leaf beetles that are closely related to the more familiar Colorado potato beetle. These beetles are typically slender with distinctive coloration patterns and feed primarily on plants in the nightshade family. They're known for their agricultural importance as some species can be significant crop pests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lema beetles are more slender and elongated than their stockier Colorado potato beetle relatives, with a characteristic narrow body shape. They also tend to have more pronounced striping patterns and different feeding behaviors.
children.funFact: The Three-lined Potato Beetle larvae have the unusual habit of covering themselves with their own excrement as protection from predators and to prevent dehydration.

children.name: Dibolia
children.description: Dibolia is a genus of small, jumping beetles known as flea beetles due to their ability to leap when disturbed. These tiny insects are specialized plant feeders that primarily target plantain and other broadleaf weeds. They are part of the leaf beetle family and play an important role in controlling certain weedy plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dibolia beetles can be distinguished from other flea beetles by their preference for plantain plants and their relatively robust body shape. They have enlarged hind legs that give them their characteristic jumping ability when threatened.
children.funFact: The Northern Plantain Flea Beetle can jump up to 50 times its own body length when escaping from predators, making it one of nature's most impressive tiny acrobats.

children.name: Crioceris
children.description: Crioceris is a genus of small, elongated leaf beetles that are specialized plant feeders. These beetles are known for their close relationships with specific host plants, particularly those in the lily and asparagus families. They have distinctive oval-shaped bodies and are often brightly colored with metallic sheens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crioceris beetles can be identified by their narrow, cylindrical body shape and their habit of feeding exclusively on plants in the lily family. Unlike many other leaf beetles, they often have striking color patterns with metallic blue, green, or copper highlights.
children.funFact: The Common Asparagus Beetle has been following asparagus cultivation around the world - it was accidentally introduced to North America in the 1850s and has since become the most significant pest of asparagus crops.

children.name: Baliosus
children.description: Baliosus is a small genus of tiny weevils that specialize in mining the leaves of basswood trees. These minute beetles spend their larval stage creating winding tunnels between the upper and lower surfaces of basswood leaves, feeding on the leaf tissue as they go.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size and their exclusive association with basswood trees as leaf miners. Unlike other weevils that might feed on various plant parts, Baliosus species are highly specialized for their leaf-mining lifestyle.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're often overlooked, Basswood Leafminers can create intricate serpentine patterns in basswood leaves that look like natural artwork when viewed against sunlight.

children.name: Chrysolina
children.description: Chrysolina is a genus of leaf beetles known for their metallic, often brilliantly colored bodies that can shine like polished metal in the sunlight. These small, oval-shaped beetles are plant specialists, with each species typically feeding on specific host plants throughout their entire life cycle from larva to adult.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their distinctive metallic luster and robust, dome-shaped bodies that set them apart from other leaf beetles. They have strong legs adapted for clinging to plants and powerful jaws for chewing leaves.
children.funFact: The Saint John's Wort Beetle was actually introduced to New England from Europe as a biological control agent to help manage the invasive Saint John's Wort plant, making it a beneficial non-native species that helps restore ecological balance.

children.name: Blepharida
children.description: Blepharida is a small genus of flea beetles that are specialized plant feeders. These tiny beetles are known for their jumping ability and their close relationships with specific host plants, particularly members of the cashew family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flea beetles, Blepharida species have distinctively shaped bodies and are closely associated with woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants.
children.funFact: The Sumac Flea Beetle can jump up to 100 times its own body length when disturbed, using specially modified hind legs that work like tiny springs.

children.name: Pyrrhalta
children.description: Pyrrhalta is a genus of small leaf beetles that specialize in feeding on specific host plants. These beetles are known for their close relationships with particular plant families, with different species often adapted to feed on just one type of plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their oval-shaped bodies and their highly specialized feeding habits, with each species typically associated with a specific host plant family.
children.funFact: The Viburnum Leaf Beetle found in New England is actually an invasive species from Europe that was first discovered in North America in the 1990s and has since become a significant pest of native viburnum shrubs.

children.description: Leaf beetles are a diverse family of small to medium-sized beetles that are typically found feeding on plant leaves, stems, and roots. Most species are brightly colored or metallic, and they're easily recognized by their oval-shaped bodies and relatively short antennae. Many leaf beetles are specialists, with each species often preferring specific host plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plant-feeding beetles, leaf beetles have distinctively short antennae that are less than half their body length, and their tarsi (feet) appear to have only four segments, though there's actually a tiny hidden fifth segment.
children.funFact: Some leaf beetles, like the golden tortoise beetle, can change color from gold to reddish-brown when disturbed or during mating, earning them the nickname 'goldbug.'

children.name: Coccinellidae
Coccinella
children.description: Coccinella is a genus of lady beetles that includes some of the most recognizable ladybugs in New England. These small, dome-shaped beetles are typically bright red or orange with distinct black spots, and they're beloved garden visitors known for eating aphids and other plant pests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Coccinella can be identified by their relatively large size compared to other lady beetles, their bright coloration with clearly defined spots, and their oval-shaped bodies that are more elongated than perfectly round.
children.funFact: The Seven-spotted Lady Beetle was actually introduced to North America from Europe in the 1970s as a biological pest control agent and has become so successful that it's now one of the most common ladybugs on the continent.

children.name: Hippodamia
children.description: Oblong Lady Beetles are a group of beneficial predatory beetles with distinctively elongated, oval-shaped bodies that are longer and more narrow than typical round ladybugs. These helpful garden allies are voracious hunters of aphids and other soft-bodied insects, making them valuable natural pest controllers. Both New England species display variable color patterns, often featuring combinations of red, orange, yellow, and black markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the familiar round ladybugs, Oblong Lady Beetles have noticeably elongated, oval bodies that are roughly twice as long as they are wide. Their variable color patterns and body shape make them easily distinguishable from other lady beetle genera.
children.funFact: A single Oblong Lady Beetle can consume over 5,000 aphids during its lifetime, making these small predators incredibly effective biological pest control agents.

children.name: Epilachna
children.description: Epilachna is a genus of ladybugs that breaks the typical rule of being garden helpers. Unlike most ladybugs that eat aphids and other pests, these species are plant-eaters that feed on leaves and can actually damage crops and garden plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These ladybugs can be distinguished from beneficial species by their plant-eating habits and often larger, more rounded body shape. They typically have more subdued coloring compared to the bright reds of predatory ladybugs.
children.funFact: The Mexican Bean Beetle was accidentally introduced to North America in the early 1900s and is now one of the most serious pests of bean crops, making it the 'black sheep' of the generally beloved ladybug family.

children.name: Harmonia
children.description: Greater Lady Beetles are a genus of relatively large, dome-shaped beetles known for their voracious appetite for aphids and other soft-bodied insects. These beneficial predators are characterized by their variable coloration and patterns, which can range from orange to red with varying numbers of spots. They play an important role in natural pest control in gardens and agricultural settings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Greater Lady Beetles are typically larger than most other lady beetle species and show remarkable color variation even within the same species. They can be distinguished by their more pronounced dome shape and often have more variable spot patterns than their smaller relatives.
children.funFact: A single Greater Lady Beetle can consume over 5,000 aphids during its lifetime, making it one of nature's most effective biological pest control agents.

children.name: Propylea
children.description: Propylea is a genus of ladybugs (lady beetles) that includes some of the most variable-looking members of the ladybug family. These small, dome-shaped beetles are beneficial predators that feed primarily on aphids and other soft-bodied insects. Like other ladybugs, they undergo complete metamorphosis and are considered valuable biological pest control agents.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Propylea species are distinguished by their extremely variable color patterns, which can range from yellow with black spots to nearly all black forms. This variation is much more dramatic than in most other ladybug genera, making identification challenging based on appearance alone.
children.funFact: The Fourteen-spotted Lady Beetle can have anywhere from 0 to 15 spots despite its name, and some individuals are so dark they appear almost completely black - this incredible color variation occurs even within the same population!

children.name: Coleomegilla
children.description: Coleomegilla is a genus of lady beetles that includes some of the most distinctive members of the ladybug family. These beneficial insects are known for their elongated, oval shape and their appetite for both plant pests like aphids and pollen, making them important predators in gardens and agricultural settings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the round, dome-shaped lady beetles most people recognize, Coleomegilla species have a more elongated, almost pill-shaped body. They're also unusual among lady beetles for being significant pollen feeders in addition to eating aphids and other small insects.
children.funFact: The Spotted Pink Lady Beetle can eat up to 50 aphids per day as an adult, and a single larva can consume over 300 aphids during its development!

children.name: Cycloneda
children.description: Spotless Lady Beetles are a small group of ladybugs that, as their name suggests, lack the typical spots found on most lady beetle species. These beneficial insects are predators that help control pest populations in gardens and natural areas. They have smooth, shiny wing covers and maintain the classic dome-shaped body form of all lady beetles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lady beetles which have distinctive spots or patterns, members of this genus have completely unmarked, glossy wing covers that give them a polished appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'spotless,' these lady beetles are just as effective at controlling aphids and other garden pests as their spotted relatives, sometimes eating up to 50 aphids per day.

children.name: Chilocorus
children.description: Twice-stabbed Lady Beetles are a group of small, round beetles known for their distinctive black coloration with red or orange spots. These beneficial insects are voracious predators that feed primarily on scale insects and other small plant pests, making them valuable allies in gardens and natural ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the more familiar red or orange lady beetles with black spots, these beetles are primarily black with two prominent red or orange spots on their wing covers, giving them their 'twice-stabbed' common name.
children.funFact: A single Twice-stabbed Lady Beetle can consume hundreds of scale insects during its lifetime, making it one of nature's most effective biological pest controllers.

children.name: Psyllobora
children.description: Psyllobora is a genus of small lady beetles that have broken away from the typical carnivorous lifestyle of their cousins. Instead of hunting aphids and other soft-bodied insects, these beetles specialize in feeding on fungi, particularly powdery mildews that grow on plant leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lady beetles that are predators, Psyllobora species are mycophagous (fungus-eating) and can often be found grazing on white, powdery fungal growth on plants. They tend to be smaller and more delicately built than their aphid-hunting relatives.
children.funFact: These lady beetles are actually beneficial to gardeners in a different way than typical lady beetles - instead of controlling pest insects, they help control plant diseases by eating harmful fungi!

children.name: Brachiacantha
children.description: Spurleg Lady Beetles are a small genus of tiny ladybugs that get their name from the distinctive spur-like projection on their hind legs. These diminutive beetles are typically less than 2mm long and are among the smallest members of the ladybug family. Like other lady beetles, they are beneficial predators that feed on aphids and other small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic leg spurs that give this genus its name are the key identifying feature, along with their extremely small size compared to most other lady beetles. They also tend to have more rounded, dome-shaped bodies than many of their relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being among the tiniest ladybugs in North America, Spurleg Lady Beetles are voracious aphid hunters and can consume dozens of aphids per day relative to their minuscule body size.

children.name: Anatis
children.description: Giant Lady Beetles are some of the largest lady beetles found in New England, living up to their name with their impressive size compared to typical ladybugs. These beneficial predators are excellent hunters that feed on aphids and other soft-bodied insects, making them valuable allies in controlling garden pests. They're part of the larger ladybug family but stand out as true giants in the beetle world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These lady beetles are notably larger than most other ladybug species, and they typically have distinctive eye-spot patterns on their wing covers that help distinguish them from their smaller cousins.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'lady beetles,' the Eye-spotted Lady Beetle can actually be quite aggressive hunters, capable of consuming dozens of aphids in a single day thanks to their large size and appetite.

children.name: Naemia
children.description: Naemia is a small genus of lady beetles that are specially adapted to coastal environments. These beetles are known for their ability to thrive in sandy, salt-affected habitats near the ocean where most other lady beetles cannot survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most lady beetles that live inland, Naemia species are uniquely adapted to seaside conditions and can tolerate salt spray and sandy substrates.
children.funFact: The Seaside Lady Beetle is one of the few lady beetle species that actively seeks out coastal dunes and beaches as its primary habitat, making it a true maritime specialist.

children.description: Lady beetles are small, dome-shaped beetles that are among our most beloved beneficial insects. Most species are voracious predators of aphids and other soft-bodied insects, making them natural allies in gardens and farms. They're easily recognized by their rounded bodies and bright warning colors, often featuring spots or other distinctive markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lady beetles can be distinguished from other small beetles by their distinctly dome-shaped, convex bodies and their habit of pulling their legs and antennae under their body when disturbed. Unlike many other beetles, they have clubbed antennae and their bright colors serve as warning signals to predators.
children.funFact: A single lady beetle can consume over 5,000 aphids during its lifetime, and some species like the multicolored Asian lady beetle can live for up to three years.

children.name: Scarabaeidae
Osmoderma
children.description: Typical hermit beetles are large, metallic-colored scarab beetles that spend most of their lives hidden inside rotting tree cavities, earning them their reclusive name. These robust beetles have a distinctive fruity or leather-like scent and are considered important indicators of healthy old-growth forests. They play a crucial role in breaking down dead wood and creating habitat for other forest creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other scarab beetles, hermit beetles have a uniquely flattened body shape that allows them to squeeze into narrow tree hollows, and they produce a strong, sweet fragrance that can be detected from several feet away.
children.funFact: Hermit beetles can live for up to 4 years as larvae inside the same rotting tree, and some European folklore claimed their musky scent could attract romantic partners when worn as a charm!

children.name: Euphoria
children.description: Euphoria beetles are chunky, colorful flower beetles that love to feast on pollen and nectar from blooming plants. These robust beetles are often seen buzzing around flowers during warm summer days, making them important pollinators in their ecosystems. They're part of the scarab beetle family and are known for their somewhat clumsy but endearing flight patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euphoria beetles can be distinguished from other flower beetles by their broad, flattened bodies and their habit of burrowing headfirst into flowers. Unlike many scarab beetles that are brown or black, Euphoria species often display beautiful metallic colors and distinctive markings.
children.funFact: Despite their bumbling appearance, Euphoria beetles are surprisingly strong fliers and can travel considerable distances between flower patches, though they often crash-land rather ungracefully into their target blooms.

children.name: Exomala
children.description: Exomala is a genus of scarab beetles that includes several species found across different continents. These beetles are typically small to medium-sized and are part of the larger family of scarab beetles, which are known for their robust, oval-shaped bodies and strong legs adapted for digging.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Exomala can be distinguished from other scarab beetles by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of sensory segments on their antennae. They have a distinctive club-shaped antenna tip and particular patterns of ridges and textures on their wing covers.
children.funFact: The Oriental Beetle, New England's only Exomala species, was accidentally introduced from Asia in the early 1900s and has become so well-established that it's now considered a common lawn pest, with its grubs feeding on grass roots.

children.name: Popillia
children.description: Popillia is a genus of scarab beetles that includes some of the most recognizable garden pests in North America. These metallic-colored beetles are known for their robust, oval-shaped bodies and their tendency to feed on plant leaves and flowers in large groups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Popillia can be identified by their distinctive metallic sheen, typically copper or bronze coloring, and their habit of skeletonizing leaves by eating the tissue between the veins.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Japanese Beetle, Popillia japonica was accidentally introduced to New Jersey in 1916 and has since become one of the most widespread invasive insects in eastern North America.

children.name: Pelidnota
children.description: Precious Metal Scarabs are a genus of robust beetles known for their metallic, shimmery appearance that gives them their common name. These medium to large-sized scarab beetles are part of the subfamily that includes many flower chafers and have a distinctive lustrous sheen to their wing covers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be distinguished from other scarab beetles by their metallic coloration and their preference for feeding on grape vines and other fruit plants as adults, rather than dung or decaying matter like many of their relatives.
children.funFact: Despite their beautiful metallic appearance that makes them look like living jewelry, Grapevine Beetles can be agricultural pests, with their larvae feeding on plant roots and adults munching on grape leaves and fruit.

children.name: Cotinis
children.description: Green June Beetles are large, metallic green scarab beetles that are active during summer days, unlike most of their nocturnal relatives. These chunky beetles have a distinctive velvety green sheen and are commonly seen flying around or feeding on ripening fruits in gardens and orchards. They belong to the flower chafer subfamily, which are generally day-active beetles that feed on plant materials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other June beetles that are brown and active at night, Green June Beetles are brilliantly metallic green and fly around during the day. They're also notably larger and more robust than most other scarab beetles in the region.
children.funFact: Green June Beetles are surprisingly clumsy fliers and often crash into people, earning them the nickname 'dive bomber beetles' - but they're completely harmless despite their intimidating buzz and size.

children.name: Nipponoserica
children.description: Nipponoserica is a genus of scarab beetles that are relatively small and robust, typically found in soil or leaf litter. These beetles are part of the larger family of scarab beetles, which includes many species that feed on decaying organic matter and play important roles in nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other scarab beetles by their specific body proportions and distinctive male genital structures that taxonomists use for identification.
children.funFact: Despite its Japanese-sounding name meaning 'Japanese Serica,' this genus has somehow made its way to New England, showing how beetle species can sometimes establish themselves far from their original native ranges.

children.name: Maladera
children.description: Maladera is a genus of scarab beetles that includes several species found across Asia and other regions. These beetles are typically small to medium-sized with oval, somewhat flattened bodies and belong to the larger family of scarab beetles that includes many familiar garden and agricultural pests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Maladera beetles can be identified by their distinctive antennae with club-shaped tips and their robust, oval body shape that's slightly flattened compared to other scarab beetles.
children.funFact: The Asiatic Garden Beetle, New England's only Maladera species, is actually more active at night than during the day, often being attracted to outdoor lights in summer evenings.

children.name: Polyphylla
children.description: Lined June Beetles are a group of large, robust scarab beetles known for the distinctive white or yellowish stripes that run along their wing covers. These impressive beetles are among the largest June beetles in North America, with adults emerging during summer months to feed on tree leaves and mate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other June beetles, Lined June Beetles have prominent longitudinal stripes on their elytra (wing covers) and are notably larger and more elongated in shape. Their antennae also have distinctively large, fan-like segments that help distinguish them from their smaller relatives.
children.funFact: The larvae of Lined June Beetles can take up to three years to develop underground, growing into grubs as large as a human thumb before finally emerging as adults.

children.name: Macrodactylus
children.description: American Rose Chafers are a small genus of beetles known for their distinctive long, spiny legs that give them their scientific name. These tan-colored beetles are members of the scarab beetle family and are particularly notorious for their feeding habits on roses and other garden plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be identified by their elongated legs with prominent spines, tan to light brown coloration, and their tendency to feed in groups on flower petals and leaves.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they only eat roses, American Rose Chafers will feed on over 250 different plant species, making them one of the most diverse plant feeders among scarab beetles.

children.name: Phanaeus
children.description: Burrowing dung beetles in the genus Phanaeus are robust, metallic-colored beetles that specialize in burying animal dung underground. These industrious insects work together in pairs to dig tunnels beneath dung piles, where they create brood balls of dung for their larvae to develop in. They play a crucial ecological role by recycling nutrients back into the soil and reducing fly populations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phanaeus beetles are distinguished from other dung beetles by their large size, brilliant metallic coloration, and the males' prominent head horns used for fighting over mates and dung resources.
children.funFact: A single pair of Phanaeus beetles can bury up to 200 times their own body weight in dung in just one night, making them incredibly efficient recyclers in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Xyloryctes
children.description: Xyloryctes is a genus of large, robust beetles known as rhinoceros beetles due to the prominent horn-like projections on the males' heads and thorax. These impressive insects are part of the scarab beetle family and are among the strongest creatures on Earth relative to their body size. They spend most of their lives as grubs living in rotting wood and organic matter before emerging as adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Xyloryctes can be distinguished from other rhinoceros beetles by their specific horn arrangements and their strong association with decaying hardwood trees. Males have distinctive curved horns that they use for fighting other males over territory and mates.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating appearance with prominent horns, Xyloryctes beetles are completely harmless to humans and actually help forest ecosystems by breaking down dead wood and recycling nutrients back into the soil.

children.name: Dichelonyx
children.description: Dichelonyx is a genus of scarab beetles commonly known as chafers or May beetles. These sturdy, oval-shaped beetles are typically brown or tan in color and are most active during late spring and early summer months. They are plant-feeders as both larvae and adults, with the grubs living underground where they feed on roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dichelonyx chafers can be distinguished from other scarab beetles by their relatively small size, distinctive coloration patterns (like the white collar of our New England species), and their specific timing of emergence in late May through June.
children.funFact: Adult Dichelonyx beetles are strongly attracted to lights at night and often crash into porch lights and windows during their brief mating season, earning them the nickname 'June bugs' in some regions.

children.description: Scarabs are a diverse family of beetles known for their robust, oval-shaped bodies and distinctive clubbed antennae. These beetles include many familiar species like June beetles, dung beetles, and rose chafers that you might encounter in gardens, near lights at night, or rolling balls of dung across trails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scarabs can be identified by their characteristic antennae that end in fan-like or club-shaped segments, and their strong, often metallic-looking bodies with powerful legs adapted for digging or climbing.
children.funFact: Some scarab beetles, like dung beetles, are incredible recyclers that can move balls of dung weighing 50 times their own body weight - equivalent to a human moving a car!

children.name: Curculionidae
Polydrusus
children.description: Polydrusus weevils are small, robust beetles with elongated snouts that feed on leaves and shoots of various plants. These weevils are characterized by their broad, rounded body shape and relatively short snout compared to other weevil groups. Both New England species are actually non-native insects that were introduced from Europe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctively broad snouts (hence 'broad-nosed weevil') and their habit of feeding on foliage rather than boring into plant tissues like many other weevils.
children.funFact: The Green Immigrant Leaf Weevil gets its vibrant green coloration from microscopic scales that cover its body, and these scales can wear off over time, causing older individuals to appear more bronze or copper-colored.

children.name: Otiorhynchus
children.description: Otiorhynchus is a genus of weevils known for their robust, oval-shaped bodies and characteristic long snouts called rostra. These flightless beetles are primarily plant feeders, with adults that chew on leaves and larvae that feed on roots of various plants including garden crops and ornamental plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other weevils by their inability to fly (they have fused wing covers) and their relatively broad, stocky build compared to other weevil groups.
children.funFact: All Otiorhynchus weevils in New England reproduce through parthenogenesis, meaning they are all females that can produce offspring without mating!

children.name: Phyllobius
children.description: Phyllobius weevils are small, plant-eating beetles that belong to the large weevil family. These insects are characterized by their elongated snouts and their habit of feeding on leaves and shoots of trees and shrubs. Like all weevils, they have clubbed antennae and chewing mouthparts at the end of their distinctive snouts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phyllobius weevils are distinguished from other weevil genera by their preference for woody plants and their often greenish or brownish coloration that helps them blend in with foliage. They typically have scales or fine hairs covering their bodies that give them a somewhat fuzzy appearance.
children.funFact: The Arborvitae Weevil gets its name from its close association with arborvitae trees, where both adults and larvae can cause significant damage by feeding on the foliage and inner bark.

children.name: Cyrtepistomus
children.description: Cyrtepistomus is a genus of weevils, which are beetles with elongated snouts called rostra that they use for feeding and boring into plant material. These small beetles are typically associated with oak trees and other hardwood species, where they feed on leaves, bark, and other plant tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive curved or bent rostrum and their preference for oak trees as host plants. They have a compact, oval body shape typical of many weevil species.
children.funFact: The Asian Oak Weevil was accidentally introduced to North America and has become established in parts of New England, showing how these tiny beetles can successfully colonize new continents when transported by human activities.

children.name: Pseudoedophrys
children.description: Pseudoedophrys is a small genus of weevils, which are beetles known for their distinctive long snouts called rostrums. These insects are plant-feeding beetles that use their elongated mouthparts to bore into plant tissues. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that specializes in feeding on peach tree roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Pseudoedophrys can be identified by their specific body structure and their particular association with tree roots rather than leaves or fruits like many other weevils.
children.funFact: Despite being called the Peach Root Weevil, this beetle can also attack the roots of other stone fruit trees like plums and cherries, making it a concern for orchard growers.

children.name: Pseudocneorhinus
children.description: Pseudocneorhinus is a genus of weevils, which are small beetles with elongated snouts called rostra. These weevils are plant-feeding insects that use their distinctive snouts to bore into plant tissues for feeding and egg-laying. In New England, this genus is represented by a single introduced species from Asia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other weevils by their specific body proportions and the distinctive banding patterns on their wing covers. They have relatively robust bodies and characteristic markings that help separate them from native New England weevil species.
children.funFact: The Two-banded Japanese Weevil was accidentally introduced to North America and has become established in northeastern regions, showing how some non-native insects can successfully colonize new continents.

children.name: Larinus
children.description: Larinus weevils are a group of plant-eating beetles that specialize in feeding on plants in the sunflower family, particularly thistles and knapweeds. These sturdy weevils have the characteristic long snout (called a rostrum) that all weevils possess, which they use to drill into plant stems and flower heads to lay their eggs. The larvae develop inside the plant tissues, feeding on seeds and other plant parts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Larinus weevils are distinguished from other weevil groups by their robust build and their specific association with composite flowers like thistles and knapweeds. They tend to be larger and more heavily built than many other weevil species.
children.funFact: The Blunt Knapweed Flower Weevil was actually introduced to North America as a biological control agent to help manage invasive knapweed plants that were taking over native habitats.

children.name: Sitona
children.description: Sitona is a genus of small weevils that are specialized plant feeders, particularly fond of legume plants like clover, alfalfa, and peas. These beetles have the characteristic long snout of weevils and are typically gray or brown in color with a somewhat stocky build. Both adults and larvae feed on their host plants, with adults eating leaves and larvae developing on or in the roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sitona weevils can be distinguished from other weevil genera by their preference for legume host plants and their relatively short, broad snout compared to many other weevils. They also have distinctive scales or setae (bristle-like hairs) covering their bodies that give them a somewhat fuzzy appearance.
children.funFact: Adult Sitona weevils create distinctive semicircular notches along the edges of leaves when they feed, leaving behind a telltale scalloped pattern that makes their presence easy to identify even when the beetles themselves are hidden.

children.name: Acanthoscelidius
children.description: Acanthoscelidius is a genus of seed weevils, which are small beetles that specialize in feeding on seeds. These tiny insects are part of the broader weevil family and play an important ecological role as both seed predators and pollinators in their ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other seed weevils by their specific body structure and the particular types of seeds they target for feeding and reproduction.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Acanthoscelidius acephalus, has a scientific name that literally means "headless," though like all insects, it definitely has a head!

children.name: Brachypera
children.description: Brachypera is a genus of weevils, which are beetles with distinctive elongated snouts called rostra. These small beetles are plant specialists that feed on legumes like clover, alfalfa, and other members of the pea family. They have the typical weevil body plan with a hard exoskeleton and clubbed antennae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Brachypera can be distinguished from other weevil genera by their specific host plant preferences for legumes and their relatively robust body shape. They have shorter rostra compared to some other weevil groups and show particular adaptations for feeding on clover and related plants.
children.funFact: The Clover Leaf Weevil larvae actually develop inside clover stems, creating small galls or swellings as they feed and grow, making them ecosystem engineers that modify their host plants.

children.name: Exomias
children.description: Exomias is a small genus of weevils that are characterized by their compact, robust bodies and distinctive hairy appearance. These beetles are root weevils, meaning their larvae develop by feeding on plant roots in the soil, while adults emerge to feed on foliage above ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Exomias weevils are distinguished from other weevil genera by their dense covering of hair-like scales that give them a fuzzy, grayish appearance, and their relatively short, broad snouts compared to many other weevil groups.
children.funFact: The Hairy Spider Weevil gets its common name not only from its fuzzy appearance but also from its habit of playing dead when disturbed, curling up its legs like a dead spider.

children.description: True weevils are a large family of beetles easily recognized by their distinctive elongated snouts, called rostrums, which they use like tiny drills to bore into plants. These small to medium-sized beetles are plant specialists, with different species feeding on specific host plants throughout their life cycles. Most true weevils are herbivorous, with both adults and larvae feeding on various parts of plants including leaves, stems, roots, and seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True weevils can be distinguished from other beetle families by their prominent snout-like rostrum, which has their antennae attached partway along its length rather than at the base. Their antennae are also distinctively club-shaped or elbowed, setting them apart from other snout beetles.
children.funFact: True weevils are one of the most species-rich families in the entire animal kingdom, with over 50,000 described species worldwide, making them incredibly successful plant specialists.

children.name: Carabidae
Carabus
children.description: Worm and Slug Hunters are large, impressive ground beetles known for their voracious appetite for soft-bodied invertebrates like slugs, snails, and earthworms.
