These nocturnal predators have powerful jaws and long legs that make them excellent hunters as they patrol the forest floor and garden beds at night. Both New England species display beautiful metallic colors that shimmer in the light.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These beetles are much larger than most other ground beetles, typically measuring over an inch long, and have distinctly metallic bronze or golden coloration. Their wing covers are often fused together, making them flightless but giving them extra protection.
children.funFact: A single Carabus beetle can consume over 400 slug eggs in one night, making them incredibly valuable natural pest controllers in gardens and forests.

children.name: Harpalus
children.description: Harpalus beetles are medium-sized ground beetles that are active predators and scavengers in soil and leaf litter. These robust beetles have strong legs for running and powerful jaws for catching prey like smaller insects, though some species also feed on seeds and plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Harpalus beetles can be identified by their oval-shaped bodies, prominent eyes, and distinctive grooved wing covers (elytra) that often have a metallic sheen.
children.funFact: The Strawberry Seed Beetle earned its name because adults are often found feeding on strawberry seeds, making them one of the few ground beetles that regularly consume plant material alongside their typical insect prey.

children.name: Lebia
children.description: Colorful Foliage Ground Beetles are small, brightly colored beetles that spend much of their time hunting on leaves and stems of plants rather than on the ground like most ground beetles. These active predators are known for their vibrant metallic green, blue, or bronze coloration that makes them stand out among the foliage. They are beneficial insects that help control pest populations by feeding on caterpillars, aphids, and other soft-bodied insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most ground beetles that are dark-colored and ground-dwelling, Lebia species are brilliantly colored with metallic sheens and are primarily arboreal, spending most of their time hunting in trees and shrubs.
children.funFact: Some Lebia species are specialized predators of Colorado potato beetles, with the adult beetles actually following the scent trails of their prey to locate and parasitize potato beetle larvae.

children.name: Stenolophus
children.description: Seedcorn beetles are small, fast-moving ground beetles that get their name from their habit of feeding on agricultural seeds, including corn. These slender beetles are typically brownish or yellowish in color and are active hunters that scurry quickly across the ground in search of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stenolophus beetles can be distinguished from other ground beetles by their relatively small size, pale coloration, and elongated body shape with long legs adapted for quick movement.
children.funFact: Despite being called "seedcorn beetles," these insects are actually beneficial to farmers most of the time, as they primarily hunt other small insects and only occasionally feed on seeds.

children.name: Colliuris
children.description: Long-necked Ground Beetles are a small genus of distinctive predatory beetles that get their name from their unusually elongated neck region. These sleek hunters are part of the larger ground beetle family and are active predators that hunt other small insects and invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their most notable feature is the dramatically extended pronotum (the segment behind the head) that creates their characteristic long-necked appearance, making them easily distinguishable from other ground beetles.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they stay on the ground, Long-necked Ground Beetles are excellent climbers and often hunt prey on vegetation and tree bark.

children.name: Sphaeroderus
children.description: Small Snail-eating Beetles are specialized ground beetles that have evolved to hunt and feed exclusively on snails and slugs. These beetles have uniquely modified mouthparts that allow them to extract soft-bodied mollusks from their shells. They are active nighttime hunters that patrol forest floors searching for their gastropod prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other ground beetles, these beetles have elongated, narrow heads and specialized mandibles designed specifically for reaching into snail shells. Their bodies are typically more robust and they move more slowly than their insect-hunting relatives.
children.funFact: These beetles inject digestive enzymes into snails to partially dissolve their prey before consumption, essentially pre-digesting their meal outside their own bodies.

children.name: Scarites
children.description: Scarites is a genus of large, robust ground beetles known for their impressive size and powerful build. These beetles are specialized predators that live underground, using their strong mandibles to hunt other insects in soil and leaf litter. They are among the largest ground beetles you'll encounter in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scarites beetles are easily recognized by their exceptionally large heads and powerful, prominent mandibles (jaws) that give them a fierce appearance. Their front legs are specially adapted for digging, with enlarged, spade-like segments that help them excavate burrows in the soil.
children.funFact: The Big-headed Ground Beetle can grow up to 1.5 inches long and is sometimes called a 'land lobster' due to its impressive size and powerful claws, making it one of the most formidable predatory insects in New England's soil ecosystem.

children.name: Cymindis
children.description: Cymindis is a genus of ground beetles that are active predators living in soil and leaf litter. These small to medium-sized beetles are part of the diverse ground beetle family and play important roles as hunters of other insects and small invertebrates in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cymindis beetles can be recognized by their elongated body shape and relatively long legs adapted for running and climbing. They typically have a metallic sheen and are often found on vegetation as well as on the ground, unlike many other ground beetles that stay strictly terrestrial.
children.funFact: Unlike most ground beetles that hunt exclusively on the soil surface, Cymindis species are semi-arboreal and will climb plants to hunt for prey, making them some of the most versatile hunters in the ground beetle family.

children.name: Calosoma
children.description: Caterpillar-hunter beetles are large, fast-moving ground beetles that specialize in hunting soft-bodied insects like caterpillars, moth larvae, and other garden pests. These beneficial predators are active hunters that climb trees and shrubs to seek out their prey, unlike many other ground beetles that wait for food to come to them. They have powerful jaws and can consume dozens of pest caterpillars in a single night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most ground beetles that stay on the ground, caterpillar-hunters are excellent climbers that actively pursue prey up into vegetation. They're typically larger and more colorful than their ground-dwelling relatives, with metallic sheens and iridescent colors.
children.funFact: A single Fiery Searcher beetle can eat over 300 gypsy moth caterpillars during its lifetime, making it one of nature's most effective pest control agents.

children.description: Ground beetles are a diverse family of predatory beetles that spend most of their lives hunting on or near the ground surface. These beneficial insects are voracious predators that help control garden pests by feeding on slugs, worms, caterpillars, and other small invertebrates. Most are active at night and have strong legs adapted for running down their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ground beetles can be recognized by their elongated bodies, prominent mandibles (jaws), and long, thin antennae. Unlike many other beetles, most ground beetles cannot fly well despite having wings, and they're typically dark-colored with a metallic sheen.
children.funFact: Some ground beetles can spray defensive chemicals when threatened - the bombardier beetles can actually create a boiling hot chemical explosion to deter predators!

children.name: Cicindelidae
Cicindela
children.description: Common Tiger Beetles are fast-moving, predatory beetles known for their metallic coloration and aggressive hunting behavior. These ground-dwelling insects are active during warm, sunny days and can often be seen running rapidly across sandy paths, beaches, and open areas in pursuit of prey. They have large, prominent eyes and powerful jaws that make them formidable hunters of other small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tiger beetles are distinguished by their exceptionally long legs built for speed, bulging eyes that provide excellent vision, and distinctively curved, sickle-shaped mandibles (jaws). Their metallic body colors and patterns of spots or lines are also characteristic of this genus.
children.funFact: Tiger beetles are among the fastest running insects in the world, capable of reaching speeds of up to 5 mph - so fast that they actually have to stop periodically while chasing prey because they temporarily outrun their own vision!

children.name: Cicindelidia
children.description: Cicindelidia is a genus of tiger beetles, fast-moving predatory insects known for their incredible hunting abilities. These beetles are active during the day and use their powerful mandibles (jaws) to catch and consume smaller insects. They're typically found in sandy or open habitats where they can quickly chase down their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cicindelidia can be distinguished from other tiger beetle genera by their specific body proportions and coloration patterns. They tend to have relatively robust bodies and distinctive metallic sheens that vary between species.
children.funFact: Tiger beetles in this genus are among the fastest running insects relative to their body size, capable of moving so quickly that they temporarily blind themselves and must stop to reorient before continuing their chase.

children.description: Tiger beetles are fast-running predatory beetles known for their incredible speed and hunting prowess. These sleek, often metallic-colored beetles have large eyes, long legs, and powerful jaws that they use to catch prey on the ground. They're commonly seen darting across sandy trails, beaches, and open areas during warm sunny days.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tiger beetles can be identified by their distinctively large, bulging eyes and their habit of running in short, quick bursts before stopping abruptly. Unlike most other ground beetles, they are active hunters during the day and have notably long, thin legs built for speed.
children.funFact: Tiger beetles are among the fastest insects on Earth relative to their size - some species can run so fast that they temporarily outrun their own vision and must stop to relocate their prey!

children.name: Staphylinidae
Nicrophorus
children.description: Burying beetles are fascinating insects that specialize in finding and burying small dead animals like mice, birds, and frogs. These industrious beetles work in pairs to dig beneath carcasses, creating underground chambers where they prepare the remains as food for their young. They're essential decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping recycle nutrients back into the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other carrion beetles, burying beetles actively bury their food sources rather than just feeding on surface carrion. They're typically black with distinctive orange or red markings and have a more robust build than most other carrion-feeding beetles.
children.funFact: Burying beetle parents are among the most devoted in the insect world - both mother and father stay with their young for weeks, regurgitating pre-digested food directly into their babies' mouths like bird parents do!

children.name: Necrophila
children.description: Necrophila is a genus of carrion beetles that specialize in feeding on decaying animal matter. These beetles are nature's cleanup crew, helping to decompose dead animals and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem. They have strong, robust bodies adapted for digging and burrowing into carcasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Necrophila are distinguished from other carrion beetles by their flattened, oval-shaped bodies and distinctive coloration patterns. They typically have orange or red markings on a black background, making them easily recognizable among decomposer insects.
children.funFact: The American Carrion Beetle can detect the smell of a dead animal from over a mile away using its highly sensitive antennae!

children.name: Platydracus
children.description: Platydracus is a genus of rove beetles, which are elongated beetles with shortened wing covers that leave most of their flexible abdomen exposed. These predatory beetles are typically found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist organic debris where they hunt for small insects and other prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other rove beetles by their robust build and distinctive abdominal patterns, often featuring contrasting light and dark markings.
children.funFact: When threatened, rove beetles can curve their flexible abdomen over their back like a scorpion, though they cannot sting - this dramatic pose is purely for show to intimidate predators.

children.name: Ocypus
children.description: Ocypus is a genus of large, predatory rove beetles known for their impressive size and hunting abilities. These beetles are part of the staphylinid family and are characterized by their elongated bodies, short wing covers, and powerful mandibles used for capturing prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ocypus are distinguished from other rove beetles by their exceptionally large size (often over an inch long) and robust build, making them among the largest rove beetles in North America.
children.funFact: Despite their fearsome appearance, Ocypus beetles are beneficial predators that help control populations of other insects, and they can run surprisingly fast across the ground when hunting or escaping danger.

children.name: Oiceoptoma
children.description: Oiceoptoma is a genus of carrion beetles that specialize in feeding on decaying animal matter. These beetles play an important ecological role as nature's cleanup crew, helping to break down dead animals and recycle nutrients back into the ecosystem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their flattened body shape and distinctive orange-red coloration with black markings, particularly the characteristic black margin around the edges of their wing covers.
children.funFact: Despite their somewhat gruesome diet, these beetles are excellent parents - they actually care for their young by regurgitating pre-digested carrion to feed their larvae.

children.name: Leistotrophus
children.description: Leistotrophus is a small genus of rove beetles, which are characterized by their shortened wing covers that leave most of their flexible abdomen exposed. These beetles are predatory insects that actively hunt for small prey in leaf litter and soil environments. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the gold-and-brown rove beetle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Leistotrophus can be identified by their distinctive gold and brown coloration pattern, which sets them apart from the more commonly black or dark brown rove beetles in other genera.
children.funFact: Despite having short wing covers, rove beetles like Leistotrophus are excellent fliers and can quickly fold their full-length wings beneath their abbreviated wing covers when landing.

children.name: Philonthus
children.description: Philonthus is a genus of rove beetles, which are distinctive insects with short wing covers that leave most of their flexible abdomen exposed. These predatory beetles are commonly found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist habitats where they hunt for small invertebrates. They're part of one of the largest beetle families in the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other rove beetles by their relatively large size, robust build, and specific arrangements of bristles and punctures on their head and thorax. They typically have well-developed mandibles for capturing prey.
children.funFact: When threatened, Philonthus beetles can curve their flexible abdomen over their back like a scorpion, though they don't have a stinger - this intimidating pose helps deter predators!

children.description: Rove beetles are a diverse family of beetles known for their distinctive short wing covers that leave most of their flexible abdomen exposed. They are typically elongated insects that can curl their abdomens upward when threatened, resembling tiny scorpions. Most species are predators or scavengers found in soil, leaf litter, rotting wood, and decomposing organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most beetles, rove beetles have very short elytra (wing covers) that only cover about half of their abdomen, leaving several segments visible. Their exposed, flexible abdomens allow them to maneuver easily through tight spaces in soil and debris.
children.funFact: With over 60,000 described species worldwide, rove beetles make up the largest family in the entire animal kingdom, representing about 25% of all known beetle species.

children.name: Cantharidae
Chauliognathus
children.description: Chauliognathus is a genus of soft-winged flower beetles commonly known as soldier beetles or leatherwings. These beneficial insects are frequently found on flowers during late summer and fall, where they feed on nectar and pollen while also hunting for small prey like aphids and other soft-bodied insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively soft, leathery wing covers (elytra) and elongated bodies with relatively large heads. They can be distinguished from other soldier beetles by their specific color patterns and the shape of their antennae and mouthparts.
children.funFact: Despite their name 'soldier beetles,' these insects are actually gentle beneficial predators that help control garden pests while simultaneously pollinating flowers as they feed on nectar.

children.name: Podabrus
children.description: Podabrus is a genus of soldier beetles, which are elongated, soft-bodied beetles commonly found on flowers during summer months. These beneficial insects are active predators that feed on other small insects, helping to control pest populations in gardens and natural areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Podabrus soldier beetles can be distinguished from other soldier beetle genera by their specific body proportions and the detailed structure of their antennae and leg segments, though identifying species often requires close examination by experts.
children.funFact: Despite being called soldier beetles, Podabrus species are actually peace-loving creatures that spend most of their time gently crawling on flower petals, feeding on nectar and pollen in addition to hunting small prey.

children.name: Cantharis
children.description: Cantharis is a genus of soft-winged flower beetles, commonly known as soldier beetles. These beneficial insects are elongated, soft-bodied beetles that are frequently found on flowers where they feed on nectar, pollen, and small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other beetles, Cantharis species have soft, flexible wing covers (elytra) rather than hard ones, and their bodies are typically more slender and less armored in appearance.
children.funFact: Soldier beetles got their name from their bright warning colors that resemble military uniforms, and they're considered garden heroes because both adults and larvae are voracious predators of pest insects like aphids and caterpillars.

children.name: Pacificanthia
children.description: Pacificanthia is a small genus of soldier beetles, with only one species found in New England. These are soft-bodied beetles that belong to the family Cantharidae, known for their beneficial role as predators of other insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctively rounded collar (pronotum) behind the head, which gives the New England species its common name.
children.funFact: Despite its name suggesting a Pacific origin, the Rotund-collared Soldier Beetle is found across eastern North America, including New England forests where it hunts for small insects on flowers and foliage.

children.name: Atalantycha
children.description: Atalantycha is a genus of soft-winged flower beetles, commonly known as leatherwings. These beetles have flexible, leathery wing covers and are often found on flowers where they feed on pollen, nectar, and small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Atalantycha beetles can be identified by their soft, flexible elytra (wing covers) that give them their 'leatherwing' common name, unlike the hard wing covers of most other beetles.
children.funFact: Despite being called leatherwings, these beetles are actually beneficial garden visitors that help with both pollination and pest control by eating aphids and other small harmful insects.

children.description: Soldier beetles are soft-bodied beetles that are commonly found on flowers during summer months, where they feed on nectar, pollen, and small insects. These beneficial beetles have elongated, somewhat flattened bodies and are often seen crawling actively on wildflowers and garden plants. Unlike many other beetles, they are excellent fliers and important pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Soldier beetles can be distinguished from other beetles by their soft, leathery wing covers (elytra) that don't completely cover the abdomen, and their thread-like antennae. Their bodies are much softer than most beetles, earning them the alternate name 'leatherwings.'
children.funFact: Soldier beetles get their name from the bright yellow and black coloration of some species that resembles military uniforms, and they're sometimes called 'leatherwings' because their wing covers are softer than typical hard beetle shells.

children.name: Buprestidae
Agrilus
children.description: Agrilus is a genus of small, metallic wood-boring beetles known as jewel beetles. These slender insects have larvae that tunnel through the wood of trees and shrubs, often creating distinctive galleries beneath the bark. Adult beetles are typically shiny with metallic green, bronze, or copper coloration.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Agrilus beetles are distinguished from other jewel beetles by their elongated, narrow body shape and the way their larvae create serpentine galleries that zigzag through the cambium layer of host plants.
children.funFact: The infamous Emerald Ash Borer in this genus has killed millions of ash trees across North America since its accidental introduction from Asia in the early 2000s.

children.name: Brachys
children.description: Brachys is a genus of small, metallic jewel beetles that specialize in creating distinctive leaf mines as larvae. These tiny beetles are wood-borers whose young feed between the upper and lower surfaces of leaves, creating winding tunnels or blotch-shaped mines that are often more noticeable than the adult beetles themselves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brachys beetles are distinguished from other jewel beetles by their extremely small size (usually under 3mm) and their unique larval habit of leaf mining rather than boring into wood or stems like most other members of the jewel beetle family.
children.funFact: The leaf mines created by Brachys larvae often persist long after the beetles have emerged, creating beautiful serpentine patterns in leaves that look like natural artwork.

children.name: Buprestis
children.description: Buprestis is a genus of metallic wood-boring beetles known as jewel beetles due to their brilliant, iridescent colors that shimmer like precious gems. These robust beetles have elongated, somewhat flattened bodies and are wood-borers, meaning their larvae develop inside dead or dying trees. Adult beetles are strong fliers and are often seen on sunny days visiting flowers or resting on tree bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Buprestis beetles are distinguished from other jewel beetles by their relatively large size and distinctive body shape with parallel sides. They typically have a more subdued metallic sheen compared to some of the more brilliantly colored jewel beetle genera.
children.funFact: Some Buprestis beetles can detect forest fires from miles away using specialized infrared sensors, allowing them to quickly locate freshly burned trees where they can lay their eggs in the heat-damaged wood.

children.description: Jewel beetles are a family of small to medium-sized beetles known for their brilliant metallic colors that shimmer like gems in sunlight. These beetles have hard, boat-shaped bodies and are often found on flowers, dead wood, or tree bark where they feed and lay their eggs. Their larvae are wood borers that tunnel through stems, branches, or tree trunks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jewel beetles can be identified by their distinctly metallic, iridescent coloration and their characteristic bullet-shaped body form. Unlike other metallic beetles, they have a unique clicking behavior and their antennae are typically saw-toothed or thread-like.
children.funFact: Some jewel beetle species can detect forest fires from miles away using special infrared sensors, allowing them to quickly colonize freshly burned trees before other insects arrive.

children.name: Lycidae
Calopteron
children.description: Calopteron is a genus of colorful beetles known as net-winged beetles, named for the distinctive net-like pattern of raised lines on their wing covers. These medium-sized beetles are often bright orange or red with black markings, making them quite eye-catching when spotted on flowers or vegetation. Both New England species are soft-bodied beetles that are active during the day and often found on flowering plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calopteron beetles can be distinguished from other net-winged beetles by their specific color patterns and wing markings - the Reticulated species has a net-like pattern throughout, while the End Band species has distinctive black bands at the wing tips.
children.funFact: These beetles are Batesian mimics, copying the bright warning colors of toxic fireflies to fool predators into thinking they're dangerous to eat, even though they're actually harmless.

children.name: Dictyoptera
children.description: Dictyoptera is a genus of net-winged beetles, distinctive insects known for their soft bodies and intricate wing patterns that resemble delicate lace or netting. These beetles are typically found on flowers and vegetation where they feed on nectar and other plant fluids. In New England, this genus is represented by a single beautiful species with striking coloration.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Net-winged beetles in this genus have distinctively patterned wing covers (elytra) with raised ridges that create a net-like appearance, and their bodies are notably soft compared to most other beetle families.
children.funFact: The Golden Net-winged Beetle's soft body contains chemical compounds that make it distasteful to predators, and its bright colors serve as a warning signal to potential threats.

children.name: Caenia
children.description: Caenia is a small genus of net-winged beetles, part of the larger Lycidae family known for their distinctive wing patterns that resemble fine netting. These beetles are typically found in wooded areas where they feed on other insects and play important roles as predators in forest ecosystems. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the Terminal Net-winged Beetle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caenia beetles can be distinguished from other net-winged beetles by their specific wing coloration patterns and body structure. The Terminal Net-winged Beetle has distinctive markings that help separate it from other lycid species in the region.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'net-winged' beetles, the intricate patterns on their wing covers are actually formed by raised ridges that create a mesh-like appearance, which may help confuse predators or aid in species recognition.

children.description: Net-winged beetles are small to medium-sized beetles known for their distinctive wing covers that feature a raised network pattern resembling the veins of a leaf or a net. These soft-bodied beetles are often brightly colored in reds, oranges, and yellows, serving as warning colors to predators. They are typically found on flowers, leaves, or tree bark where they feed on smaller insects or nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other beetles with hard wing covers, net-winged beetles have soft, flexible elytra with prominent raised ridges that create a distinctive net-like pattern. Their bright warning colors and soft bodies make them easy to distinguish from other beetle families.
children.funFact: Many net-winged beetles are mimicked by other insects because their bright colors advertise that they taste bad to predators - creating a whole community of imposters trying to look like these unpalatable beetles!

children.name: Elateridae
Alaus
children.description: Eyed Click Beetles are large, distinctive beetles known for their impressive size and striking appearance. They get their name from the prominent eyespots on their thorax that look like giant eyes, which help startle predators. These beetles are part of the click beetle family and can flip themselves upright with an audible clicking sound when placed on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The large, conspicuous eyespots on their thorax make them unmistakable among New England beetles. They are also notably larger than most other click beetles, reaching up to 1.5 inches in length.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating appearance with those big fake eyes, Eyed Click Beetles are completely harmless to humans and actually beneficial, as their larvae feed on wood-boring insects that damage trees.

children.name: Sylvanelater
children.description: Sylvanelater is a genus of click beetles known for their distinctive cylindrical body shape. These beetles are part of the larger click beetle family and are characterized by their ability to flip themselves upright when turned over by arching their backs and making an audible clicking sound.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sylvanelater can be distinguished from other click beetles by their notably elongated, cylindrical form rather than the more flattened oval shape typical of most click beetles.
children.funFact: The genus name Sylvanelater combines 'sylvan' meaning 'of the forest' with 'elater' meaning 'driver' or 'propeller,' reflecting both their woodland habitat and their remarkable jumping ability.

children.name: Ampedus
children.description: Ampedus is a genus of click beetles known for their distinctive clicking mechanism that helps them flip right-side up when stuck on their backs. These elongated beetles are typically found in wooded areas where they play important roles as both predators and decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their robust, oval-shaped bodies and the ability to produce an audible clicking sound by snapping a spine on their underside against a groove.
children.funFact: The name 'Ampedus' comes from Greek meaning 'girdled around,' referring to the characteristic band or collar-like markings found on many species in this genus.

children.name: Monocrepidius
children.description: Monocrepidius is a genus of click beetles, insects known for their ability to flip themselves right-side up with an audible clicking sound when placed on their backs. These beetles are typically elongated and somewhat flattened, with dark brown to black coloration that helps them blend in with soil and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other click beetles by their specific body proportions and the structure of their antennae, which are relatively short and serrated. They also have distinctive markings and textures on their wing covers that help separate them from closely related genera.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Monocrepidius lividus, is sometimes called the 'ashy click beetle' and can launch itself several inches into the air when it performs its signature clicking maneuver to escape predators.

children.description: Click beetles are a diverse family of beetles known for their unique ability to flip themselves upright when knocked onto their backs by producing an audible 'click' sound. They have elongated, somewhat flattened bodies and are found in various habitats from forests to gardens. Most species are active at night and are attracted to lights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Click beetles can be identified by their distinctive hinge mechanism between their thorax and abdomen that allows them to snap their bodies and launch into the air with a clicking sound. They also have relatively long, thread-like or saw-toothed antennae compared to many other beetle families.
children.funFact: Some click beetle larvae, known as wireworms, can live underground for several years before becoming adults, and a few species like the eyed click beetles have large eye-spots on their thorax that help startle predators.

children.name: Tenebrionidae
Capnochroa
children.description: Capnochroa is a small genus of beetles in the comb-clawed beetle family, with only one species found in New England. These are small, dark-colored beetles that live in decaying organic matter and are often found under bark or in leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive comb-like claws and dark, often blackish coloration that gives them a sooty appearance.
children.funFact: The genus name Capnochroa comes from Greek words meaning 'smoke-colored,' referring to their characteristic dark, smoky appearance.

children.name: Bolitotherus
children.description: Bolitotherus is a genus of specialized beetles that feed exclusively on bracket fungi growing on dead and dying trees. These beetles have evolved unique adaptations to live their entire lives on and around these woody fungi, making them important decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their robust, heavily armored bodies and distinctive horn-like projections on their head and thorax, which give them their common name of forked fungus beetles.
children.funFact: Bolitotherus beetles can live for several years as adults, which is unusually long for beetles, spending their extended lives slowly gnawing through tough bracket fungi that would be indigestible to most other insects.

children.name: Diaperis
children.description: Diaperis is a genus of small beetles in the darkling beetle family that are commonly found in decaying organic matter. These beetles are typically dark-colored with distinctive spotted patterns and play an important role in breaking down dead plant material in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Diaperis can be identified by their oval-shaped bodies, clubbed antennae, and characteristic light-colored spots on their dark wing covers that give them their common name.
children.funFact: Despite being called darkling beetles, many Diaperis species are actually quite active during the day, unlike their nocturnal relatives.

children.name: Dinomus
children.description: Dinomus is a small genus of metallic wood-boring beetles in the jewel beetle family (Buprestidae). These beetles are known for their brilliant, iridescent coloration that can shimmer with multiple colors depending on the angle of light.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dinomus beetles are distinguished from other jewel beetles by their relatively small size and particularly intense metallic luster that often displays rainbow-like color shifts.
children.funFact: The name 'Dinomus' means 'terrible law' in Greek, which seems ironic given that these tiny beetles are among the most beautifully colored insects in New England forests.

children.description: Darkling beetles are a diverse family of beetles known for their typically dark coloration and hard, durable bodies. Most species are scavengers that feed on decaying plant matter, fungi, or organic debris, playing important roles as decomposers in their ecosystems. They're often found under logs, stones, or in leaf litter where they help break down dead material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Darkling beetles can be identified by their fused wing covers (elytra) that often cannot open for flight, and their distinctive antennae that are usually club-shaped or beaded. Many species have a characteristic defensive behavior of standing on their heads and releasing foul-smelling chemicals when threatened.
children.funFact: Some darkling beetles are known as 'headstand beetles' because they point their rear ends up in the air when disturbed, spraying predators with noxious chemicals from special glands.

children.name: Meloidae
Lytta
children.description: Lytta blister beetles are medium to large-sized beetles known for their ability to produce a toxic chemical called cantharidin when threatened or crushed. These beetles have soft, elongated bodies and are often metallic or brightly colored, making them relatively easy to spot in their natural habitats. They're part of a fascinating group of insects that undergo a complex life cycle with multiple larval stages.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lytta beetles can be distinguished from other blister beetles by their larger size, typically metallic coloration, and robust build. They also tend to have more prominent heads and thoraxes compared to their more delicate blister beetle relatives.
children.funFact: The toxic chemical cantharidin produced by Lytta beetles was historically known as 'Spanish fly' and was mistakenly believed to be an aphrodisiac, though it's actually quite dangerous and can cause severe blistering of the skin.

children.name: Meloe
children.description: Oil beetles are large, dark beetles known for their unusual ability to release oily, toxic fluids from their joints when threatened. These flightless insects have soft, leathery wing covers and swollen abdomens that give them a distinctive bulky appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most beetles, oil beetles cannot fly as their wing covers don't meet in the middle and their wings are reduced or absent. They're easily recognized by their habit of 'bleeding' orange or yellow oil when disturbed.
children.funFact: Oil beetle larvae are parasites that must hitch a ride on bees to survive - they climb onto flowers and grab onto visiting bees, then live in the bee's nest and eat its eggs and honey stores.

children.name: Tricrania
children.description: Tricrania is a small genus of blister beetles known for their distinctive reddish wing covers that give them their common name. These beetles are part of the blister beetle family, which means they can produce defensive chemicals that cause skin irritation when handled. In New England, only one species represents this genus - the Blood-winged Blister Beetle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tricrania beetles are easily recognized by their bright red or orange-red wing covers (elytra) that contrast sharply with their darker head and thorax. This coloration pattern sets them apart from most other blister beetles in the region.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, blister beetles like those in Tricrania have complex life cycles where the larvae are parasitic on other insects, particularly bees, helping to control pest populations naturally.

children.description: Blister beetles are a family of soft-bodied beetles known for their ability to produce a chemical called cantharidin that can cause painful blisters on human skin. These medium-sized beetles have distinctive soft, flexible wing covers and elongated bodies that set them apart from other beetle families. They undergo complex life cycles and many species are plant feeders as adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most beetles with hard, rigid wing covers, blister beetles have soft, leathery elytra that don't fully protect their abdomen. Their heads are wider than their prothorax, giving them a distinctive neck-like appearance.
children.funFact: Oil beetles in this family have one of the most complex life cycles in the insect world - their larvae must first hitch a ride on a bee to reach the bee's nest, where they then eat the bee's eggs and stored honey to complete their development.

children.name: Lampyridae
Photinus
children.description: Rover Fireflies are a group of beetles known for their ability to produce flashing light through bioluminescence. These fireflies are called 'rovers' because the males actively fly around flashing their lights in specific patterns to attract mates, rather than staying in one place.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike some other firefly groups, Photinus males are strong fliers that create moving light displays as they search for females. Each species has its own unique flash pattern and timing that helps males and females of the same species find each other.
children.funFact: The Common Eastern Firefly creates the classic firefly display most people recognize - males fly in a J-shaped pattern while flashing, and females respond with a single flash from the ground or low vegetation.

children.name: Lucidota
children.description: Lucidota is a genus of fireflies that are quite different from the typical flashing fireflies most people know. These beetles are active during the day rather than at night, and the adults don't produce the familiar blinking light displays we associate with summer evenings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fireflies, Lucidota species are diurnal (day-active) and do not flash as adults, though they may glow weakly. They are typically darker in coloration compared to their night-flying relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called fireflies, adult Lucidota don't actually 'fire' - they've lost the ability to produce the bright flashing lights, though their larvae can still glow like other firefly species.

children.description: Fireflies are soft-bodied beetles best known for their ability to produce light through a chemical reaction in special organs called photophores. These nocturnal insects use their bioluminescent flashing patterns to communicate with potential mates during summer evenings. Despite their name, they are actually beetles, not flies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fireflies can be distinguished from other beetles by their ability to produce light and their soft, flexible wing covers (elytra). They have distinctive light-producing organs on their abdomen that create their characteristic glow.
children.funFact: Each firefly species has its own unique flashing pattern - like a secret morse code - that helps males and females of the same species find each other in the dark.

children.name: Lucanidae
Lucanus
children.description: Lucanus is a genus of large, impressive beetles known as stag beetles, famous for their prominent mandibles (jaws) that resemble the antlers of a stag. These robust beetles are among the largest insects in North America, with males typically larger than females and sporting more dramatic jaw structures. They spend most of their lives as larvae living in rotting wood, where they can develop for several years before emerging as adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stag beetles in the genus Lucanus are distinguished by their massive size and the males' enlarged, antler-like mandibles that can be nearly as long as their bodies. Unlike other stag beetle genera, Lucanus species have particularly robust builds and distinctive reddish-brown coloration.
children.funFact: Male stag beetles use their impressive mandibles not for feeding, but for wrestling other males over territory and mates, grappling like tiny gladiators in what looks like beetle boxing matches.

children.name: Dorcus
children.description: Dorcus stag beetles are robust, dark-colored beetles known for their impressive mandibles (jaws) that resemble deer antlers. These beetles are typically found in decaying wood where they feed and develop as larvae, playing an important role in forest decomposition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dorcus species are distinguished from other stag beetles by their generally darker coloration and more parallel-sided body shape, plus their mandibles tend to be less dramatically enlarged than those of other stag beetle genera.
children.funFact: Male Dorcus beetles use their powerful mandibles not for feeding, but for wrestling matches with other males over territory and mating rights, sometimes lifting opponents completely off the ground!

children.name: Ceruchus
children.description: Ceruchus is a small genus of stag beetles known for their association with decaying wood, particularly wood affected by red rot fungi. These beetles are specialized decomposers that play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping break down dead and dying trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other stag beetles, Ceruchus species are relatively small and have less pronounced mandibles (jaws), giving them a more compact appearance. They are specifically adapted to living in and feeding on fungus-infected rotting wood rather than fresh wood.
children.funFact: The Red-rot Decay Stag Beetle gets its name from its preference for wood that has been infected with red rot fungi, and the larvae can spend up to three years developing inside a single piece of decaying wood.

children.description: Stag beetles are a family of large, robust beetles known for their impressive mandibles (jaws) that resemble the antlers of a stag. These beetles are among the largest insects in North America, with some species reaching over two inches in length. They spend most of their lives as larvae in decaying wood, playing an important role in forest decomposition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stag beetles are easily recognized by their prominent, often branched mandibles that are especially large in males, giving them their characteristic antler-like appearance. Their bodies are typically dark brown or black and notably thick and sturdy compared to other beetle families.
children.funFact: Male stag beetles use their oversized mandibles not for feeding, but for wrestling with other males over territory and mates, much like deer sparring with their antlers.

children.name: Dermestidae
Anthrenus
children.description: Carpet beetles are small, round beetles in the genus Anthrenus that are commonly found in homes throughout New England. These tiny insects have oval-shaped bodies covered in colorful scales that create distinctive patterns of white, yellow, orange, and black markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small household beetles, carpet beetles have club-shaped antennae and their bodies are covered in tiny, overlapping scales that give them a mottled appearance. Their larvae are hairy and distinctly different from the smooth adult beetles.
children.funFact: While adult carpet beetles feed on flower pollen and nectar outdoors, their larvae are the real household troublemakers, munching on natural fibers like wool, silk, and even pet hair!

children.name: Dermestes
children.description: Skin beetles are a group of small, oval-shaped beetles that specialize in feeding on dried animal materials like skin, hair, feathers, and stored food products. These beetles are nature's cleanup crew, breaking down dead organic matter that other decomposers can't handle. They're commonly found in homes, museums, and anywhere dried animal products are stored.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Skin beetles can be identified by their compact, rounded bodies and their ability to pull their legs and antennae completely under their body when disturbed, forming a tight ball. Unlike other carrion beetles, they prefer dried rather than fresh decomposing material.
children.funFact: Museums actually use controlled colonies of skin beetles to clean delicate animal skeletons for displays, as they can strip flesh from bones without damaging even the tiniest bone structures.

children.description: Skin beetles are a family of small, oval-shaped beetles whose larvae are specialist decomposers that feed on dead organic matter like dried skin, hair, feathers, and other animal remains. These beetles play an important ecological role as nature's cleanup crew, breaking down and recycling organic materials that other organisms can't digest. Both adults and larvae are typically found in dark, undisturbed places where dried organic matter accumulates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Skin beetles can be identified by their small, compact oval bodies and distinctive clubbed antennae that can be tucked into grooves on their head when threatened. Their larvae are distinctive too, appearing as small, hairy, brownish grubs that are often more noticeable than the adult beetles.
children.funFact: Museums use dermestid beetles to clean delicate skeletons for scientific specimens because the larvae can strip flesh from bones without damaging even the tiniest bone structures that traditional cleaning methods might destroy.

children.name: Nitidulidae
Glischrochilus
children.description: Glischrochilus is a genus of small, oval-shaped beetles known as sap beetles that are commonly found around fermenting fruit, tree sap, and other decaying organic matter. These beetles are attracted to the sweet, yeasty smells of decomposition and play an important role in breaking down organic material in forest ecosystems. All three New England species are relatively small, typically measuring between 3-6 millimeters in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Glischrochilus can be distinguished from other sap beetles by their distinctive color patterns, often featuring combinations of black, red, or yellow markings. They also have characteristically short, club-shaped antennae and slightly flattened bodies that help them squeeze into tight spaces around rotting fruit and sap flows.
children.funFact: The Picnic Beetle earned its common name because it's frequently found crawling on overripe fruit at outdoor gatherings, drawn by the fermentation process that makes fruits smell like alcohol.

children.description: Sap-feeding beetles are small, oval-shaped beetles that feed primarily on tree sap, fermenting fruit, and other decaying organic matter. They are commonly found around wounded trees, overripe fruit, and flowers where they can access the sugary fluids they need to survive. These beetles play an important role as both decomposers and pollinators in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sap-feeding beetles can be identified by their flattened, oval bodies and clubbed antennae that help them detect fermenting materials. Many species have shortened wing covers that don't completely cover their abdomen, giving them a distinctive appearance.
children.funFact: Some sap-feeding beetles are so attracted to fermenting fruit that they can actually become intoxicated from the alcohol content, causing them to fly erratically or fall off their food sources!

children.name: Melyridae
Malachius
children.description: Malachius is a genus of soft-winged flower beetles known for their metallic coloration and preference for flowers. These small beetles are commonly found on blossoms where they feed on pollen and nectar, playing a role as both pollinators and predators of other small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively soft, flexible wing covers and often display brilliant metallic green, blue, or copper colors that give them their 'malachite' name.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance and flower-visiting habits, Malachius beetles are actually predators that hunt aphids and other soft-bodied insects on the flowers they visit.

children.name: Anthocomus
children.description: Anthocomus is a genus of small, colorful soft-winged flower beetles that are commonly found on flowers and vegetation. These beetles are part of the Melyridae family and are known for their striking red and black coloration that serves as a warning to predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their distinctive red and black color pattern and their soft, flexible wing covers. They have relatively long antennae and are typically found feeding on pollen and small insects on flower heads.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, Anthocomus beetles are beneficial predators that help control aphids and other small pest insects while also serving as pollinators when they visit flowers to feed.

children.description: Soft-winged Flower Beetles are small, delicate beetles that get their name from their relatively soft wing covers compared to most other beetles. These colorful little beetles are commonly found on flowers where they feed on pollen, nectar, and sometimes small insects. They play an important role as both pollinators and predators in flower ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most beetles with hard, armor-like wing covers, these beetles have softer, more flexible elytra that give them their common name. Many species are brightly colored with metallic green or blue hues and have relatively long antennae.
children.funFact: Some soft-winged flower beetles can extrude bright orange or red defensive chemicals from special glands when threatened, creating a startling display that warns predators to stay away.

children.name: Pyrochroidae
Dendroides
children.description: Dendroides is a genus of beetles commonly known as fire-colored beetles, named for their distinctive orange-red and black coloration that resembles flames. These medium-sized beetles are found in forested areas where they feed on other insects and play important roles as predators in woodland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fire-colored beetles can be identified by their bright orange-red head and thorax contrasting with dark wing covers, plus their relatively large size compared to other predatory beetles in New England forests.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting a connection to fire, these beetles are actually attracted to recently dead or dying trees, where they hunt for wood-boring beetle larvae beneath the bark.

children.description: Fire-colored beetles are a small family of beetles known for their distinctive reddish-orange to bright red coloration that gives them their common name. These medium-sized beetles are typically found on or near decaying wood, where both adults and larvae develop. They are relatively uncommon and often overlooked despite their striking appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fire-colored beetles can be distinguished from other red or orange beetles by their soft, somewhat flattened bodies and their association with dead or dying trees. Their antennae are serrated or comb-like, and they have a distinctive body shape that's more elongated than many other colorful beetles.
children.funFact: Despite their bright warning coloration that suggests they might be toxic, fire-colored beetles are actually harmless mimics that benefit from looking dangerous without actually being poisonous.

children.name: Geotrupidae
Geotrupes
children.description: Geotrupes are robust, dome-shaped beetles commonly known as earth-boring beetles or dor beetles. These chunky insects are expert diggers that spend much of their lives burrowing through soil and dung, where they feed and create tunnels for their young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Earth-boring beetles are distinguished by their heavily built, convex bodies and powerful legs adapted for digging. They have a distinctive metallic sheen and are much larger and more robust than most other dung beetles.
children.funFact: When disturbed, Geotrupes beetles can produce a loud squeaking or hissing sound by rubbing their wing covers against their abdomen, earning them the nickname 'lousy watchmen' in some regions.

children.description: Earth-boring beetles are robust, oval-shaped beetles that spend most of their lives digging tunnels in soil and decaying organic matter. These industrious insects are excellent decomposers, helping to break down dung, rotting wood, and leaf litter while aerating the soil with their extensive burrow systems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike similar dung beetles, earth-boring beetles have distinctive rows of spines on their front legs specifically adapted for digging, and their wing covers (elytra) often show prominent ridges or striations running lengthwise.
children.funFact: A single earth-boring beetle can move soil weighing up to 400 times its own body weight while constructing its underground tunnels and brood chambers.

children.name: Dytiscidae
Dytiscus
children.description: Dytiscus is a genus of large predatory water beetles that are among the most impressive aquatic insects in New England. These powerful swimmers are equipped with paddle-like hind legs and streamlined bodies that make them efficient hunters in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They are voracious predators that feed on fish, tadpoles, and other aquatic creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dytiscus beetles are notably larger than most other diving beetles, often reaching over an inch in length. They can be distinguished by their robust size, prominent eyes, and the males' distinctive sucker-like discs on their front legs used for gripping females during mating.
children.funFact: Despite being aquatic hunters, Dytiscus beetles are excellent fliers and will leave the water on warm nights to search for new ponds, sometimes crash-landing near outdoor lights in their quest for fresh hunting grounds.

children.name: Acilius
children.description: Small Flat Diving Beetles are aquatic predators that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These beetles are excellent swimmers with flattened, streamlined bodies and paddle-like hind legs that help them chase down prey underwater. They hunt small fish, tadpoles, and aquatic insects, making them important predators in freshwater ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other diving beetles, Acilius species have distinctly flattened bodies and are relatively small in size. The males often have unique suction cup-like structures on their front legs used for gripping females during mating.
children.funFact: These beetles can fly between water bodies at night to find new hunting grounds, and they navigate by using polarized light reflected off water surfaces to locate suitable ponds and lakes.

children.description: Predaceous diving beetles are aquatic hunters that spend most of their lives underwater in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These oval-shaped beetles are excellent swimmers with flattened, paddle-like hind legs that help them glide through the water as they hunt for small fish, tadpoles, and other aquatic prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other water beetles, diving beetles store air under their wing covers (elytra) to breathe underwater, creating a silvery bubble that acts like scuba gear. Their streamlined body shape and powerful swimming legs make them much more agile in water than similar-looking ground beetles.
children.funFact: When diving beetles need fresh air, they back up to the water's surface and poke just the tip of their abdomen above water to refresh their air supply, like a tiny snorkel!

children.name: Ripiphoridae
Macrosiagon
children.description: Macrosiagon is a genus of small, wedge-shaped beetles that are parasites of wasps and bees. These tiny beetles have a fascinating life cycle where their larvae attach to flowers and then hitch rides on visiting bees or wasps back to their nests, where they feed on the host's larvae and food stores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These beetles are characterized by their distinctive wedge or triangular body shape and their parasitic lifestyle. Unlike most beetles, they don't feed on plants or decaying matter as adults, instead specializing in exploiting bee and wasp colonies.
children.funFact: Macrosiagon beetles are expert hitchhikers - their tiny larvae wait on flowers with their legs outstretched, ready to grab onto any passing bee or wasp that will unknowingly transport them to a food-rich nest.

children.description: Wedge-shaped beetles are small, parasitic beetles with distinctive wedge-like body shapes that taper toward the rear. These unusual insects have complex life cycles where their larvae live as parasites inside other insects, particularly wasps and bees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their most notable feature is their wedge-shaped body form, which is quite different from most other beetle families. The males often have enlarged, fan-like antennae and reduced wing covers.
children.funFact: Female wedge-shaped beetles can produce thousands of tiny larvae that actively seek out and penetrate host insects, making them some of the most prolific parasites in the insect world.

children.name: Oedemeridae
Ischnomera
children.description: Ischnomera is a genus of beetles that belong to the false blister beetle family, despite their common name suggesting a connection to true blister beetles. These are elongated, medium-sized beetles that are often found on flowers and foliage where they feed on other insects. They get their 'false blister beetle' name because they superficially resemble true blister beetles but lack the chemical defenses of their namesakes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true blister beetles, Ischnomera species don't produce the toxic chemical cantharidin that can blister skin. They can be distinguished from similar beetles by their relatively narrow, elongated body shape and their predatory feeding habits rather than plant-feeding behavior.
children.funFact: The Red-necked False Blister Beetle is actually a beneficial predator that helps control pest insects, making it a gardener's ally despite its somewhat intimidating name.

children.description: False blister beetles are slender, soft-bodied beetles that get their name because they resemble true blister beetles but don't produce the toxic chemicals that cause skin blisters. These beetles are typically found on flowers where adults feed on pollen and nectar, while their larvae develop in decaying wood or plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true blister beetles, false blister beetles have a more elongated, narrow body shape and lack the ability to produce blistering chemicals. Their wing covers (elytra) are often softer and more flexible than those of most other beetle families.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'false' blister beetles, these insects are actually beneficial pollinators that help fertilize wildflowers as they move from bloom to bloom feeding on pollen.

children.name: Attelabidae
Synolabus
children.description: Synolabus is a small genus of weevils known for their leaf-rolling behavior. These beetles are specialized plant feeders that create distinctive rolled-up leaf shelters where they lay their eggs and their larvae develop.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their unique leaf-rolling habits and their relatively small size compared to other weevil groups. They have the typical weevil snout but are specifically adapted for manipulating leaves into protective rolls.
children.funFact: The Red-shouldered Leaf Rolling Weevil gets its name from the distinctive reddish-orange patches on its wing covers, which stand out against its otherwise dark body.

children.description: Leaf-rolling weevils are small beetles that have developed a remarkable parenting strategy involving leaves. The adults carefully cut and roll leaves into tight cylinders or tubes, creating protective nurseries for their eggs and developing larvae. These skilled architects use their elongated snouts to precisely cut leaf tissue and their legs to manipulate the leaves into perfect rolls.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other weevils that typically bore into seeds, stems, or wood, leaf-rolling weevils specialize in manipulating leaf tissue to create elaborate rolled structures. They have relatively long legs and necks compared to other weevil families, adaptations that help them in their leaf-rolling behavior.
children.funFact: The intricate leaf rolls created by these weevils can take several hours to complete and require such precision that each species often specializes on specific host plants whose leaf properties work best for their particular rolling technique.

children.name: Brentidae
Arrenodes
children.description: Arrenodes is a genus of weevils known as timber worms or bark weevils. These beetles are wood-boring insects whose larvae develop inside the bark and wood of trees, particularly hardwoods like oaks. They are small, elongated beetles with the characteristic curved snout typical of weevils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Arrenodes can be distinguished from other weevil genera by their cylindrical body shape and their specific association with hardwood trees as breeding sites. Their larvae create distinctive galleries beneath the bark of their host trees.
children.funFact: The Oak Timberworm gets its name from the intricate tunnel systems its larvae carve through oak bark and wood, which can weaken trees and make them more susceptible to wind damage.

children.description: Straight-snouted weevils are a family of beetles known for their distinctive long, straight snouts that extend forward from their heads. Unlike their curvy-snouted cousins, these weevils have remarkably linear rostrums that give them a unique appearance among beetles. They are typically wood-boring insects that spend their larval stage developing inside dead or dying trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets straight-snouted weevils apart from other weevil families is their notably straight, elongated snout that doesn't curve downward like most other weevils. They also tend to be larger and more elongated than typical weevils, with a distinctive cylindrical body shape.
children.funFact: Female straight-snouted weevils use their long, straight snouts like drills to bore deep holes into wood where they lay their eggs, and the males often have enlarged mandibles that they use to fight other males for mating rights.

children.name: Melandryidae
Dircaea
children.description: Dircaea is a genus of false darkling beetles that are typically found in decaying wood and forest environments. These beetles are part of the family Melandryidae and are known for their elongated, somewhat flattened body shape that helps them navigate through crevices in rotting logs and bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true darkling beetles, Dircaea species have distinctive spotted or mottled patterns on their wing covers and tend to be more slender in build. They also have relatively long antennae compared to their body size.
children.funFact: The Blurry-spotted False Darkling Beetle gets its name from the fuzzy, indistinct spots on its back that look like they were painted with a slightly wet brush.

children.description: False Darkling Beetles are small to medium-sized beetles that live in decaying wood and under bark of dead or dying trees. Despite their name, they are not closely related to true darkling beetles, but got their common name because of their similar dark coloration and body shape. These beetles are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping break down dead wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: False darkling beetles can be distinguished from true darkling beetles by their different antenna structure and body proportions. They typically have more elongated bodies and their antennae are often club-shaped or serrated rather than the simple segmented antennae of true darkling beetles.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Dircaea liturata, is so rarely encountered that many beetle enthusiasts consider finding one a special achievement, earning it the nickname 'the holy grail of wood-boring beetles' among collectors.

children.name: Mordellidae
Mordella
children.description: Mordella is a genus of small to medium-sized beetles known as tumbling flower beetles or mordellid beetles. These beetles are characterized by their wedge-shaped bodies that are widest at the front and taper toward the rear, giving them a distinctive humpbacked appearance. They are commonly found on flowers where they feed on pollen and nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mordella beetles can be distinguished from other flower beetles by their strongly arched back, pointed abdomen that extends beyond their wing covers, and their tendency to tumble or fall off flowers when disturbed, often landing on their backs.
children.funFact: When threatened, these beetles will curl up and drop from flowers, tumbling through the air in a seemingly helpless manner - which is how they earned their common name 'tumbling flower beetles.'

children.description: Tumbling flower beetles are small, wedge-shaped beetles that get their name from their habit of tumbling or dropping from flowers when disturbed. These beetles are typically found on flowers where they feed on pollen and nectar, playing a role as pollinators for various plants. They have a distinctive humpbacked appearance and are usually dark-colored with a metallic sheen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These beetles can be identified by their characteristic wedge-shaped body that tapers to a point at the rear, along with their tendency to curl up and fall when threatened. Their hind legs often extend beyond the tip of their abdomen, giving them an unusual silhouette among beetles.
children.funFact: When startled, tumbling flower beetles will curl into a ball and drop from their perch, hence their common name - this defensive behavior helps them escape predators by disappearing into the leaf litter below.

children.name: Cleridae
Enoclerus
children.description: Enoclerus is a genus of checkered beetles, which are predatory insects that hunt other small insects and their larvae. These beetles are typically elongated and colorful, with many species featuring bright patterns that help them blend in among flowers where they hunt for prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Enoclerus can be distinguished from other checkered beetles by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of grooves and ridges on their wing covers (elytra).
children.funFact: Enoclerus beetles are beneficial predators that help control pest populations by actively hunting wood-boring beetle larvae and other harmful insects.

children.description: Checkered beetles are small to medium-sized beetles known for their distinctive checkered or banded color patterns, typically featuring combinations of red, orange, black, and white. These active predators are commonly found on flowers and tree bark, where they hunt for other insects. Most species are beneficial to ecosystems as they help control pest populations by feeding on wood-boring beetles, flies, and other small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their checkered or striped color patterns and relatively soft, somewhat hairy bodies distinguish them from other beetle families. Unlike many beetles, they are active daytime hunters with long legs adapted for running down prey on flower heads and bark surfaces.
children.funFact: Many checkered beetles are excellent mimics of wasps or bees, using their bright warning colors and quick movements to fool predators into thinking they have a dangerous sting.

children.name: Stenotrachelidae
Cephaloon
children.description: Cephaloon is a small genus of longhorn beetles found in North America. These beetles are wood-borers that develop in dead or dying hardwood trees, with their larvae creating tunnels in the wood as they feed and grow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cephaloon beetles are distinguished from other longhorn beetles by their relatively short antennae and robust body shape, which gives them a different appearance from the typically slender, long-antennaed members of their family.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'False Leptura Beetle,' Cephaloon lepturides was originally mistaken for a member of the Leptura genus due to its similar appearance, but it's actually quite distinct genetically.

children.description: False Longhorn Beetles are small, elongated beetles that get their name from their resemblance to true longhorn beetles, though they belong to a completely different family. These beetles are typically found in decaying wood where they feed on fungi and other organic matter. They have distinctive cylindrical bodies and relatively long antennae compared to their body size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true longhorn beetles, false longhorn beetles have different antenna attachment points and leg structure. They are generally much smaller and have more robust, less graceful bodies than their longhorn beetle look-alikes.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they're mimicking longhorn beetles, false longhorn beetles evolved their similar appearance independently - a great example of convergent evolution in the insect world.

children.name: Endomychidae
Endomychus
children.description: Endomychus is a genus of small, colorful beetles that specialize in feeding on fungi. These beetles are typically found on mushrooms and other fungal growths, where both adults and larvae develop by consuming the fungal tissue. They play an important ecological role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their smooth, shiny wing covers and distinctive spotted patterns, typically featuring bright red or orange coloration with contrasting dark spots.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'handsome' beetles for their attractive appearance, these tiny fungi specialists are often overlooked because they spend most of their time hidden inside or underneath the mushrooms they're eating.

children.description: Handsome Fungus Beetles are small, colorful beetles that feed primarily on fungi, particularly molds and yeasts found in decaying organic matter. These beetles are typically shiny and often have attractive red, orange, or yellow coloration with black spots or markings. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to break down dead plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fungus-feeding beetles, Handsome Fungus Beetles have distinctively clubbed antennae and smooth, glossy wing covers (elytra) that often display bright warning colors.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting good looks, these beetles earned the title 'handsome' because their bright colors serve as a warning to predators that they may be toxic or distasteful to eat.

children.name: Cucujidae
Cucujus
children.description: Cucujus is a genus of flat bark beetles known for their extremely flattened bodies that allow them to squeeze into tight spaces under tree bark. These beetles are specialized predators that hunt for other insects living in the narrow gaps between bark and wood. They have distinctive reddish coloration and elongated body shapes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cucujus are distinguished by their remarkably flattened bodies - more so than most other flat bark beetles - and their bright reddish-orange coloration. Their bodies are so thin they can slip into cracks as narrow as a piece of paper.
children.funFact: Red flat bark beetles can survive being frozen solid during winter, with some individuals recorded surviving temperatures as low as -58°F (-50°C) by producing natural antifreeze proteins.

children.description: Flat bark beetles are extremely flattened beetles that live under the loose bark of dead or dying trees. These small predatory beetles have adapted their paper-thin bodies to squeeze into the narrow spaces between bark and wood, where they hunt for other insects and their larvae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their remarkably flattened body shape makes them easily distinguishable from other beetle families. Unlike most beetles, they are so thin they can slip into cracks that seem impossibly narrow for their size.
children.funFact: New England's single flat bark beetle species, the red flat bark beetle, is so rare that it's considered endangered in several states and can survive freezing temperatures by producing natural antifreeze proteins.

children.name: Hydrophilidae
Hydrophilus
children.description: Giant Water Scavenger Beetles are large, oval-shaped aquatic beetles that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Despite their name suggesting they only scavenge, these beetles are actually omnivorous, feeding on both decaying organic matter and small aquatic animals like snails and insect larvae. They are excellent swimmers and can often be seen coming to the water's surface to replenish their air supply.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These beetles are distinguished from other aquatic beetles by their large size (up to 1.5 inches long), shiny black coloration, and their habit of swimming with alternating leg movements rather than synchronized strokes. Unlike predatory diving beetles, they have shorter, less streamlined antennae and move more slowly through the water.
children.funFact: Female Giant Water Scavenger Beetles create remarkable silk egg cases that float on the water's surface like tiny boats, complete with a mast-like projection that helps keep the eggs properly ventilated.

children.description: Water Scavenger Beetles are aquatic beetles that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams where they feed primarily on decaying plant matter and algae. Unlike many water beetles that are predators, these beetles are mostly vegetarian scavengers that help clean up organic debris in aquatic environments. They are excellent swimmers and can often be seen coming to the surface to breathe air, which they store under their wing covers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Water Scavenger Beetles can be distinguished from other aquatic beetles by their clubbed antennae and their swimming style - they move their legs alternately rather than in unison like diving beetles do.
children.funFact: The Giant Water Scavenger Beetle is one of the largest beetles in North America, growing up to 1.5 inches long, and the females create floating egg cases that look like tiny silk purses attached to aquatic plants.

children.name: Erotylidae
Megalodacne
