children.description: Megalodacne is a genus of pleasing fungus beetles that specialize in feeding on fungi growing on decaying wood. These beetles are typically found in forested areas where they play an important role in breaking down dead organic matter and controlling fungal populations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Megalodacne beetles are distinguished by their relatively large size compared to other pleasing fungus beetles and their robust, oval-shaped bodies with distinctive coloration patterns.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Megalodacne heros, is one of the largest pleasing fungus beetles in North America and can often be found crawling on bracket fungi attached to dead trees.

children.description: Pleasing Fungus Beetles are small, colorful beetles that feed primarily on fungi, particularly the fruiting bodies of bracket fungi and other wood-decay fungi. These beetles are often brightly colored with attractive patterns of red, orange, yellow, or black, which is how they earned their common name. They play an important ecological role by helping to break down dead wood and recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small beetles, pleasing fungus beetles have distinctly clubbed antennae and smooth, shiny wing covers (elytra) that often display vibrant warning colors. Their bodies are typically oval-shaped and somewhat flattened, adapted for living in and around fungi.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, pleasing fungus beetles are some of the most colorful insects in New England forests, with their bright warning colors advertising to predators that they taste bad due to toxic compounds they obtain from eating fungi.

children.name: Cupedidae
Tenomerga
children.description: Tenomerga is a small genus of beetles in the family Tetratomidae, commonly known as polypore fungus beetles. These beetles are closely associated with bracket fungi and other wood-decay fungi that grow on dead and dying trees. They play an important ecological role as decomposers in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tenomerga beetles are distinguished from other fungus beetles by their distinctive reticulated (net-like) pattern on their wing covers and their relatively small, oval-shaped body form.
children.funFact: The Eastern Ashen Reticulated Beetle is so specialized that it's rarely found away from its fungal hosts, making it an indicator species for healthy forest fungal communities.

children.description: Reticulated beetles are an ancient family of wood-boring beetles with distinctively patterned wing covers that look like a network or mesh. These primitive beetles are considered living fossils, representing one of the oldest lineages of beetles that have remained largely unchanged for millions of years. They spend most of their lives as larvae boring through decaying hardwood trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their wing covers (elytra) have a distinctive reticulated or net-like pattern of raised lines and grooves that sets them apart from other beetle families. They also have a more primitive body structure compared to most modern beetles.
children.funFact: Reticulated beetles are so ancient that they're sometimes called "living fossils" - fossils of very similar beetles have been found that are over 200 million years old!

children.name: Synchroidae
Synchroa
children.description: Synchroa is a small genus of bark beetles that live and feed on dead or dying trees. These tiny beetles create tunnels under the bark where they lay their eggs and develop from larvae to adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Synchroa beetles are distinguished by their punctured or pitted appearance on their wing covers, which gives them a distinctive dotted texture that sets them apart from other bark beetles.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'synchronized' bark beetles, the name actually refers to their coordinated mass attacks on weakened trees rather than any synchronized movement or behavior.

children.description: Synchroa bark beetles are a small family of elongated beetles that live under the bark of dead or dying trees. These beetles are wood-borers that help break down decaying wood as part of the forest's natural recycling process. They are relatively uncommon and often overlooked due to their secretive lifestyle beneath tree bark.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Synchroa bark beetles can be distinguished from other bark beetles by their distinctive antennae, which have a loose, multi-segmented club at the tip rather than a compact club. They also tend to be more elongated and cylindrical than most other bark beetle families.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bark beetles,' Synchroa beetles are not closely related to the more familiar bark beetles in the family Curculionidae, showing how similar lifestyles can evolve independently in different beetle groups.

children.name: Tetratomidae
Penthe
children.description: Penthe is a genus of beetles that specialize in living on and feeding from fungi, particularly polypore fungi that grow on dead and decaying wood. These beetles have adapted to life in the fungal world, where both their larvae and adults depend on fungi for food and shelter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Penthe are characterized by their robust, somewhat flattened bodies and their close association with bracket fungi and polypores growing on rotting logs and stumps.
children.funFact: Penthe beetles are so closely tied to fungi that they spend their entire life cycle within or on fungal fruiting bodies, essentially living in a mushroom world from egg to adult.

children.description: Polypore fungus beetles are specialized insects that spend their lives closely associated with bracket fungi and other polypore mushrooms that grow on dead wood. These small to medium-sized beetles have developed a unique lifestyle, with both adults and larvae feeding exclusively on these shelf-like fungi. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to break down fungal material and recycle nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other beetles, polypore fungus beetles have evolved specifically to live within the porous structure of bracket fungi, with flattened bodies that allow them to navigate through the fungal tubes and chambers.
children.funFact: New England has only one species in this family - Penthe obliquata - which is sometimes called the 'oblique polypore fungus beetle' and can often be found by carefully examining bracket fungi on dead hardwood trees.

children.description: Beetles are the largest order of insects, easily recognized by their hard, shell-like wing covers called elytra that protect their delicate flying wings underneath. They undergo complete metamorphosis, developing from eggs through larval and pupal stages before becoming adults. Beetles occupy nearly every habitat imaginable and have incredibly diverse lifestyles, from predators and herbivores to decomposers and parasites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature of beetles is their hardened forewings (elytra) that meet in a straight line down the middle of their back, forming a protective shield over their body and flight wings. This distinguishes them from all other insects, which either lack wing covers entirely or have softer, overlapping wing covers.
children.funFact: One out of every four known animal species on Earth is a beetle - scientists have described over 400,000 beetle species worldwide, making them the most diverse group in the entire animal kingdom!

children.name: Odonata
Libellulidae
Libellula
children.description: Chasers and King Skimmers are robust, medium to large dragonflies known for their powerful flight and territorial behavior around ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These dragonflies are excellent hunters that patrol their territory from prominent perches, darting out to chase away intruders or capture prey before returning to the same spot. Many species show dramatic differences between males and females, with males often developing bright colors or distinctive wing patterns as they mature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dragonfly groups, Libellula species typically have broad, flattened abdomens and relatively wide wings that may feature distinctive spots, bands, or patches of color. Males often develop a waxy, powdery coating called pruinescence that can dramatically change their appearance from their juvenile coloration.
children.funFact: The Four-spotted Skimmer is one of the most widespread dragonflies in the world, found across North America, Europe, and Asia - it's even the national insect of Finland!

children.name: Sympetrum
children.description: Meadowhawks are a group of medium-sized dragonflies that are among the most commonly seen dragonflies in New England, especially during late summer and fall. These colorful insects are known for their relatively small size compared to other dragonflies and their habit of perching on low vegetation in open areas like fields, meadows, and pond edges. Most species show dramatic color differences between males and females, with males typically displaying bright reds, oranges, or yellows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Meadowhawks can be distinguished from other dragonfly groups by their smaller size, relatively narrow wings, and tendency to perch frequently rather than patrol territories by flying. They also have distinctive wing venation patterns and most species lack the bold wing patterns seen in many other dragonfly families.
children.funFact: Many meadowhawk species are the last dragonflies you'll see flying in the fall - some can remain active even after light frosts, with Autumn Meadowhawks sometimes spotted flying into November in New England.

children.name: Celithemis
children.description: Small Pennants are a group of delicate dragonflies known for their distinctive wing patterns and perching behavior. These medium-sized dragonflies typically have colorful markings on their wings and often perch on the tips of vegetation with their wings held horizontally. All species in this genus prefer sunny, open areas near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Small Pennants can be identified by their habit of perching at the very tips of plant stems and their distinctive wing patterns, which often include bands, spots, or patches of color. Unlike many other dragonflies, they frequently return to the same favorite perching spots repeatedly.
children.funFact: The Halloween Pennant gets its spooky name from the orange and black banded pattern on its wings that resembles Halloween colors, making it one of the most festively-named dragonflies in New England.

children.name: Leucorrhinia
children.description: Whitefaces are small to medium-sized dragonflies known for their distinctive white or pale facial markings that give them their common name. These compact dragonflies are typically found near ponds, bogs, and other still waters throughout New England's cooler regions. They belong to the skimmer family and are active fliers that often perch on vegetation near the water's edge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Whitefaces can be distinguished from other dragonflies by their prominent white or yellowish-white faces, combined with their relatively small size and dark wing patches or bands. Their bodies are typically black with white or yellow markings, and many species have distinctive patterns on their wings.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting white faces, juvenile whitefaces often start with yellow or pale faces that gradually turn whiter as they mature into adults.

children.name: Ladona
children.description: Corporals are a group of medium-sized dragonflies known for their broad, flattened abdomens and distinctive body markings. These sturdy dragonflies are commonly found near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England during late spring and summer. All three species share similar body shapes and flight patterns, though they can be distinguished by their unique coloration and markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Corporals have noticeably wider, more flattened abdomens compared to other dragonfly genera, giving them a robust appearance. They also tend to perch horizontally on rocks, logs, or bare ground rather than hanging vertically like many other dragonflies.
children.funFact: Male corporals are highly territorial and will chase away other dragonflies from their chosen perching spots, often returning to the exact same rock or log repeatedly throughout the day.

children.name: Tramea
children.description: Saddlebag gliders are large, powerful dragonflies named for the distinctive dark patches at the base of their hindwings that resemble saddlebags on a horse. These strong fliers are often seen patrolling open areas like ponds, lakes, and meadows, where they hunt other flying insects with impressive aerial agility. All species in this genus share the characteristic broad, dark wing patches and robust flight capabilities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The dark patches at the base of the hindwings immediately separate saddlebag gliders from other dragonfly genera. Unlike many dragonflies that have clear wings or different pattern types, the 'saddlebag' marking is unique to this group.
children.funFact: Saddlebag gliders are among the most migratory dragonflies in North America, with some individuals traveling hundreds of miles during seasonal movements, following warm weather and abundant prey.

children.name: Pantala
children.description: Rainpool Gliders are large, powerful dragonflies known for their exceptional flying abilities and wandering nature. These robust insects have broad wings and strong flight muscles that allow them to cover enormous distances, sometimes migrating across continents. They get their common name from their habit of laying eggs in temporary rainpools and other shallow water bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rainpool Gliders can be distinguished from other dragonfly genera by their unusually broad hindwings and amber or yellowish wing coloration. They also have distinctively large, prominent eyes and a more robust body structure compared to most other glider dragonflies.
children.funFact: The Wandering Glider holds the record for the longest migration of any insect, with some individuals traveling over 11,000 miles across the Indian Ocean!

children.name: Pachydiplax
children.description: Blue Dashers are a small genus of dragonflies known for their swift, darting flight patterns and distinctive coloration. The males develop a beautiful powder-blue color on their bodies as they mature, while females remain more brownish with yellow markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blue Dashers can be identified by their relatively short, broad wings and the male's striking blue coloration combined with green eyes. They're smaller and more compact than many other dragonfly species.
children.funFact: Male Blue Dashers are highly territorial and will aggressively chase away other dragonflies from their chosen perch, often returning to the exact same spot repeatedly throughout the day.

children.name: Plathemis
children.description: Whitetails are a small genus of dragonflies known for their distinctive white wing patches that develop as males mature. These medium-sized dragonflies are skilled hunters that perch on vegetation near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout their range.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male whitetails are easily recognized by their broad, chalky white wing patches and pruinose (powdery white) abdomens that develop with age. Females and young males lack the white coloration and have brown-spotted wings with darker bodies.
children.funFact: Male Common Whitetails are highly territorial and will aggressively chase away other dragonflies from their chosen perch, sometimes engaging in aerial battles that can last several minutes.

children.name: Erythemis
children.description: Pondhawks are medium-sized dragonflies known for their hunting prowess and distinctive coloration changes. These agile predators are commonly found near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams where they patrol territories and catch other flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male pondhawks undergo a dramatic color transformation from bright green to powdery blue as they mature, while females retain their green coloration throughout their lives.
children.funFact: Eastern Pondhawks are such efficient hunters that they catch their prey mid-flight with a success rate of over 90%, making them one of nature's most effective aerial predators.

children.name: Perithemis
children.description: Amberwings are small, delicate dragonflies known for their distinctive amber-colored wing patches that give them their common name. These compact dragonflies are among the smallest members of the skimmer family, with males displaying bright golden-orange wing markings that shimmer in sunlight.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amberwings can be easily identified by their small size and the characteristic amber or orange patches on their wings, which are much more prominent than the subtle wing markings found on most other skimmer dragonflies.
children.funFact: Male amberwings are highly territorial and will chase away other males from their preferred perching spots, despite being one of the smallest dragonflies in New England.

children.name: Erythrodiplax
children.description: Dragonlets are a genus of small, colorful dragonflies found primarily in the Americas. These compact dragonflies are known for their vibrant colors and relatively small size compared to other dragonfly groups. They typically inhabit areas near ponds, marshes, and slow-moving waterways.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dragonlets are distinguished by their small size, bright metallic colors, and distinctive wing venation patterns. Males often display brilliant reds, blues, or purples, while females tend to be more subdued in coloration.
children.funFact: The Seaside Dragonlet is one of the few dragonflies that can tolerate brackish water, making it well-adapted to coastal marshes and salt ponds where most other dragonflies cannot survive.

children.name: Nannothemis
children.description: Nannothemis is a genus of very small dragonflies known for their tiny size and delicate appearance. These miniature predators are among the smallest dragonflies in North America, with members rarely exceeding an inch in length. They belong to the skimmer family and are skilled aerial hunters despite their diminutive stature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nannothemis dragonflies are distinguished by their exceptionally small size compared to other skimmers, along with their relatively broad wings and compact, stocky bodies. Their petite proportions and unique wing-to-body ratio make them unmistakable among North American dragonflies.
children.funFact: The Elfin Skimmer is considered the smallest dragonfly in North America, with a body length of less than an inch, earning it the nickname 'flying jewel' among dragonfly enthusiasts.

children.name: Miathyria
children.description: Miathyria is a genus of dragonflies known for their distinctive gliding flight behavior and striking appearance. These medium-sized dragonflies are characterized by their broad, sturdy wings and ability to soar effortlessly through their preferred habitats near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Miathyria can be distinguished from other dragonfly genera by their unique combination of broad hindwings, metallic coloration, and characteristic gliding flight pattern with minimal wing beating.
children.funFact: The Hyacinth Glider gets its name from its beautiful iridescent purple-blue coloration that resembles the color of hyacinth flowers, and males are known to perform elaborate aerial courtship displays.

children.description: Skimmers are the largest family of dragonflies, known for their robust bodies and powerful flight abilities. These accomplished aerial hunters patrol territories around ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams, often seen perching on prominent spots like rocks, logs, or vegetation tips. They get their name from their habit of skimming low over water surfaces while hunting or patrolling their domains.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dragonfly families, skimmers have relatively broad, triangular hindwings and tend to be more heavily built with shorter, thicker bodies. They're also much more likely to perch frequently during flight, whereas other dragonflies like darners rarely land.
children.funFact: Many male skimmers develop a waxy blue or white coating called pruinescence as they mature, which helps them regulate body temperature and may play a role in attracting mates.

children.name: Coenagrionidae
Enallagma
children.description: Bluets are delicate damselflies that belong to the genus Enallagma, representing one of the most diverse groups of damselflies in North America. These slender insects are commonly found near ponds, lakes, streams, and wetlands throughout New England, where they spend their larval stage underwater before emerging as flying adults. Most species display beautiful blue and black coloration, though some show variations in orange, turquoise, or other hues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bluets can be distinguished from other damselflies by their relatively small size, narrow wings that fold back along their body when at rest, and typically bright blue coloration with black markings. Unlike dragonflies, they have a more delicate build and their large eyes are separated rather than touching.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bluets,' not all species in this genus are blue - the Orange Bluet displays vibrant orange coloring, the Scarlet Bluet shows red hues, and the Turquoise Bluet exhibits beautiful blue-green tones.

children.name: Ischnura
children.description: Forktails are small, delicate damselflies that get their name from the distinctive forked appendages at the tip of the male's abdomen. These slender insects are among the most common damselflies you'll encounter near ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They're weak fliers that typically stay close to water and vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Forktails can be distinguished from other damselflies by their small size (usually under 1.5 inches long) and the males' characteristic forked tail appendages. They also tend to be less colorful than many other damselfly groups, often appearing in subtle blues, greens, or oranges.
children.funFact: Female forktails often change colors dramatically as they mature - young females may be bright orange or yellow, while older females typically become blue or green, sometimes making it tricky to identify the species!

children.name: Argia
children.description: Dancers are a group of delicate damselflies that get their name from their graceful, dancing flight patterns over streams and rivers. These slender insects have narrow bodies and hold their wings vertically along their backs when at rest, unlike dragonflies which spread their wings horizontally. All dancers in this group prefer flowing water habitats and are often seen perching on vegetation near waterways.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dancers can be distinguished from other damselflies by their relatively broad wings and their preference for moving water rather than ponds or lakes. Many species in this group also display distinctive blue coloration on males, particularly on the thorax and abdomen.
children.funFact: Male dancers perform elaborate courtship displays, hovering and bobbing in front of females in what truly resembles an aerial dance performance.

children.name: Nehalennia
children.description: Sprites are tiny, delicate damselflies that are among the smallest members of their order in North America. These diminutive insects have slender bodies and narrow wings, and they're often found in wetland habitats like bogs, marshes, and areas with dense aquatic vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sprites are distinguished from other damselflies by their exceptionally small size and their preference for specific wetland microhabitats. They have relatively short, narrow wings compared to their body length and tend to stay very close to their preferred aquatic plants.
children.funFact: Despite being some of the smallest damselflies in New England, sprites are incredibly specialized - each species has evolved to live in very specific wetland conditions, with one preferring sedge-dominated areas and the other favoring sphagnum moss habitats.

children.name: Coenagrion
children.description: Northern Bluets are small, delicate damselflies that inhabit cool northern waters and bog environments. These slender insects have bright blue bodies with black markings and hold their wings vertically along their body when at rest, unlike dragonflies which hold their wings horizontally.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Northern Bluets are distinguished from other bluet damselflies by their preference for cooler, more northern habitats like bogs and taiga wetlands. They tend to be smaller and have more restricted ranges compared to their southern relatives.
children.funFact: These hardy little damselflies can survive in surprisingly cold conditions and are among the few bluet species that thrive in the harsh boreal environments of northern New England.

children.name: Chromagrion
children.description: Chromagrion is a small genus of damselflies known for their distinctive coloration and delicate build. These slender insects are part of the narrow-winged damselfly family and are characterized by their bright, contrasting body colors that often include vibrant blues and blacks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chromagrion damselflies can be distinguished from other narrow-winged damselflies by their unique color patterns and relatively small size. The males typically display brilliant metallic blue-green coloration with contrasting dark markings.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Chromagrion' literally means 'colored fierce one,' referring to the striking coloration of these small but vibrant damselflies.

children.name: Amphiagrion
children.description: Red Damsels are a small genus of delicate damselflies known for their striking reddish coloration. These slender insects are found near slow-moving waters like ponds and marshes, where they hunt small flying insects and lay their eggs in aquatic vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Red Damsels stand out from other damselflies due to their distinctive red or orange-red body coloration, which is unusual among North American damselflies that are typically blue, green, or black.
children.funFact: The Eastern Red Damsel is one of the few damselflies in North America where both males and females display prominent red coloration, making them easy to spot among the reeds and cattails of their wetland homes.

children.description: Narrow-winged Damselflies are delicate aquatic insects with slender bodies and wings that fold back along their body when at rest. These graceful fliers are commonly found near ponds, streams, and wetlands throughout New England, where they hunt small flying insects and lay their eggs in water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike dragonflies, damselflies hold their wings vertically above or alongside their body when perched, and their front and hind wings are nearly identical in shape and size.
children.funFact: Many species in this family, especially the bluets, are so similar in appearance that even experts often need to examine them closely under magnification to tell them apart!

children.name: Gomphidae
Phanogomphus
children.description: Phanogomphus clubtails are medium-sized dragonflies with the characteristic clubbed tail that gives them their name. These streamside hunters are often seen perching on rocks, logs, or vegetation near flowing water where they hunt for flying insects. All species in this genus have yellow and black markings, though the specific patterns help distinguish between different species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other clubtail genera, Phanogomphus species typically have distinctive yellow stripes on their thorax and specific patterns of yellow markings on their black abdomens. Their eyes remain separated (never touching) and males have noticeably enlarged tail segments forming the signature 'club.'
children.funFact: The Harpoon Clubtail gets its name from the harpoon-shaped yellow markings on its abdomen segments, making it one of the most distinctively patterned dragonflies in New England.

children.name: Ophiogomphus
children.description: Snaketails are a genus of dragonflies known for their distinctive club-shaped abdomens that narrow at the base and widen toward the tip, resembling a snake's tail. These medium-sized dragonflies are typically found near fast-flowing streams and rivers throughout New England, where their nymphs develop in clean, well-oxygenated water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dragonfly groups, snaketails have eyes that are widely separated on top of their heads rather than touching, and their characteristic club-shaped abdomen makes them easily recognizable in flight.
children.funFact: Snaketail nymphs are excellent indicators of water quality - they can only survive in clean, unpolluted streams, making them valuable species for monitoring the health of New England's waterways.

children.name: Stylurus
children.description: Hanging Clubtails are a group of dragonflies known for their distinctive resting behavior - they typically hang vertically from branches, twigs, or other vegetation rather than perching horizontally like many other dragonflies. These medium to large-sized dragonflies have the characteristic clubbed tail that gives them their name, with the tip of their abdomen expanded into a paddle-like shape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other clubtail dragonflies that often rest on rocks or the ground, Hanging Clubtails prefer to hang vertically from vegetation. They also tend to be more secretive and harder to spot than their relatives, often staying well-hidden in wooded areas near streams and rivers.
children.funFact: Hanging Clubtails are sometimes called 'ghost dragonflies' by enthusiasts because they can be incredibly difficult to find and photograph due to their secretive nature and excellent camouflage when hanging motionless among branches.

children.name: Gomphurus
children.description: Gomphurus is a genus of dragonflies commonly known as clubtails, named for the distinctive club-shaped widening at the tip of their abdomens. These are medium to large dragonflies that are strong fliers and active hunters, patrolling territories along rivers and streams. All three New England species are swift aerial predators that catch other flying insects on the wing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gomphurus clubtails are distinguished from other clubtail genera by their robust build, prominent club-shaped abdominal tips, and typically bold yellow and black coloration patterns. They tend to be larger and more powerfully built than many other clubtail species.
children.funFact: The Cobra Clubtail gets its dramatic name from the male's especially pronounced abdominal club that flares out like a cobra's hood when viewed from above.

children.name: Arigomphus
children.description: Pond Clubtails are a small genus of dragonflies that specialize in living around ponds, slow streams, and other quiet waters. These medium-sized dragonflies are part of the clubtail family, getting their name from the distinctive club-shaped widening at the tip of their abdomen. Both New England species prefer areas with muddy or sandy bottoms where their larvae can burrow and develop.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other clubtails that often prefer flowing water, Pond Clubtails are specifically adapted to still or very slow-moving waters. They can be distinguished from other clubtails by their preference for pond habitats and their relatively robust build.
children.funFact: The larvae of Pond Clubtails are accomplished burrowers that dig backwards into the muddy bottom of ponds, leaving only their eyes and the tip of their abdomen exposed to ambush passing prey.

children.name: Lanthus
children.description: Pygmy Clubtails are small, delicate dragonflies that belong to the clubtail family. As their name suggests, they are among the tiniest dragonflies in New England, with slender bodies and relatively narrow wings. These petite predators are often found near streams and small rivers where they hunt for even smaller flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pygmy Clubtails are distinguished from other clubtails by their remarkably small size and more delicate build. Unlike their larger clubtail relatives, they have less prominent club-shaped tail ends and tend to be more secretive in their behavior.
children.funFact: Despite being the smallest dragonflies in their family, Pygmy Clubtails are still fierce hunters that can catch prey while flying at speeds up to 15 miles per hour.

children.name: Hylogomphus
children.description: Hylogomphus is a genus of dragonflies known as clubtails, characterized by their distinctive club-shaped abdomens that widen toward the tip. These medium-sized dragonflies are typically found near streams and rivers, where they perch on rocks, logs, or sandy shores. Like other clubtails, they have separated eyes and tend to rest with their wings held horizontally.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hylogomphus can be distinguished from other clubtail genera by their specific combination of facial markings, thoracic stripes, and abdominal patterns. The two New England species show distinctive features on their faces - the Mustached Clubtail has prominent mustache-like markings, while the Spine-crowned Clubtail has characteristic spines on its head.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'clubtails,' the enlarged tip of their abdomen is actually more pronounced in males and helps distinguish them from females during identification.

children.name: Dromogomphus
children.description: Spiny-legged Clubtails are robust dragonflies known for the distinctive spines along their legs, which help them grip prey while hunting. These medium to large dragonflies have wide heads with prominent eyes and club-shaped tails that expand at the tip. They are strong fliers that patrol territories along rivers and streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The prominent spines on their legs set them apart from other clubtail dragonflies, giving them their common name. Their legs appear noticeably bristly or thorny compared to the smoother legs of related species.
children.funFact: The spines on their legs aren't just for show - they work like tiny fishing hooks to help these dragonflies catch and hold onto flying insects while eating them in mid-air.

children.name: Hagenius
children.description: Hagenius is a genus of large, powerful dragonflies known for their impressive hunting abilities. These robust insects are among the largest dragonflies in North America, with strong flight capabilities and fierce predatory behavior that earned them their common name of dragonhunters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hagenius dragonflies are distinguished by their exceptionally large size, thick robust bodies, and distinctive yellow and black coloration. They have notably strong legs positioned forward on their thorax, making them excellent at catching other dragonflies in mid-flight.
children.funFact: Dragonhunters are so named because they specialize in hunting other dragonflies, and can take down prey nearly as large as themselves while flying at speeds up to 35 miles per hour.

children.name: Stylogomphus
children.description: Least Clubtails are a small genus of dragonflies known for being among the tiniest members of the clubtail family. These delicate dragonflies have the characteristic club-shaped tip at the end of their abdomen, but in a much more petite package than their larger clubtail relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They are distinguished from other clubtails by their exceptionally small size and more slender build. Their clubbed abdomen tip is proportionally smaller and less pronounced than in other clubtail genera.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Least Clubtails are skilled hunters that can catch prey nearly as large as themselves while flying at speeds up to 25 miles per hour.

children.name: Progomphus
children.description: Sanddragons are medium-sized dragonflies known for their preference for sandy-bottomed streams and rivers. These dragonflies have robust bodies and are skilled hunters, catching other insects while flying through their riparian habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sanddragons can be identified by their yellowish-brown coloration with dark markings and their habit of perching on sandy or rocky surfaces near flowing water. They have distinctive club-shaped appendages at the tip of their abdomen.
children.funFact: Sanddragon nymphs burrow into sandy stream bottoms where they can remain hidden for several years before emerging as adults.

children.description: Clubtails are a diverse family of dragonflies named for the distinctive club-like widening at the tip of their abdomens. These medium to large dragonflies are commonly found near streams, rivers, and ponds throughout New England, where they hunt for insects both as aquatic nymphs and flying adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dragonfly families, clubtails have eyes that are separated on top of their heads rather than touching, and most species have that characteristic swollen 'club' at the end of their abdomen that gives them their name.
children.funFact: Clubtail nymphs are accomplished burrowers that live buried in the sand or mud at the bottom of waterways, sometimes for several years before emerging as adults.

children.name: Corduliidae
Somatochlora
children.description: Striped Emerald Dragonflies are a diverse group of medium to large dragonflies known for their metallic green bodies that often display distinctive yellow or pale stripes. These fast-flying predators are commonly found near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's forests and wetlands. All members of this genus share similar body shapes and hunting behaviors, though they can be tricky to identify without close examination.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other emerald dragonflies, Somatochlora species typically have distinctive striped patterns on their thorax and often show less brilliant metallic coloration. Many species in this genus also have unique tail appendages that vary dramatically between species, from clamp-like to brush-like tips.
children.funFact: The tip of a male's abdomen is so distinctive in this group that many species are named after their unique tail appendages - from the Clamp-tipped to the Brush-tipped to the unusual Ski-tipped Emerald!

children.name: Epitheca
children.description: Baskettails are medium to large dragonflies known for their distinctive flight pattern of hovering and patrolling over ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They get their common name from the female's unique egg-laying behavior, where she carries her eggs in a basket-like structure at the tip of her abdomen before dipping down to release them into the water. All baskettails are strong fliers that are often seen cruising back and forth over their aquatic territories during late spring and summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Baskettails can be identified by their robust build, clear or lightly tinted wings, and the females' characteristic egg-carrying basket at the end of their abdomen. Unlike many other dragonflies, they tend to fly in regular patrol patterns rather than perching frequently.
children.funFact: Female baskettails are like living egg dispensers - they can carry up to 1,000 eggs in their specialized abdominal basket and strategically release them in prime aquatic nursery spots!

children.name: Neurocordulia
children.description: Shadowdragons are medium-sized dragonflies known for their dusky, brownish coloration and preference for flying in dim light conditions like dawn and dusk. These elusive insects are typically found near forested streams, ponds, and wetlands where they patrol for smaller flying insects. They get their name from their shadowy appearance and secretive behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other dragonflies, shadowdragons have distinctly darker, more muted wing patterns and body coloration, making them blend well with shaded environments. Their flight pattern is also more erratic and less predictable than their brighter-colored relatives.
children.funFact: Shadowdragons are most active during twilight hours when most other dragonflies have settled down for the night, giving them less competition for prey and making them the 'night shift' hunters of the dragonfly world.

children.name: Dorocordulia
children.description: Lesser Emerald Dragonflies are small, delicate dragonflies with bright metallic green bodies that shimmer in sunlight. These woodland species prefer to hunt along forest streams and ponds rather than large open waters. Both New England species are relatively small compared to other emerald dragonflies, earning them their 'lesser' designation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be distinguished from other emerald dragonflies by their smaller size and preference for shaded, forested waterways. Their flight pattern tends to be more delicate and less aggressive than their larger emerald relatives.
children.funFact: The Racket-tailed Emerald gets its name from the distinctive club-shaped tip of the male's abdomen, which looks like a tiny tennis racket when viewed from above.

children.name: Williamsonia
children.description: Boghaunters are medium-sized dragonflies that specialize in living around acidic wetlands like bogs, swamps, and slow-moving streams. These dragonflies are known for their relatively secretive behavior and preference for shaded, wooded waterways rather than open ponds or lakes. They get their name from their habit of patrolling and 'haunting' boggy areas where few other dragonflies venture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boghaunters can be distinguished from other dragonflies by their dark coloration, relatively stocky build, and their preference for perching on vegetation rather than hovering continuously. They also have distinctively patterned abdomens and tend to fly closer to the water surface than many other dragonfly species.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'boghaunters,' these dragonflies are actually quite beneficial predators that help control mosquito populations in wetland areas where mosquitoes are most abundant.

children.name: Cordulia
children.description: Common Emerald Dragonflies are medium-sized dragonflies with brilliant metallic green bodies that shimmer in sunlight. They are strong fliers that patrol territories over ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams, hunting for smaller insects on the wing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These dragonflies can be identified by their bright emerald-green metallic sheen and relatively robust build compared to other dragonfly families. Unlike some dragonfly groups, they rarely perch and are almost always seen flying.
children.funFact: American Emerald dragonflies are sometimes called 'flying jewels' because their metallic green bodies can appear to change color from emerald to bronze depending on the angle of sunlight.

children.name: Helocordulia
children.description: Sundragons are medium-sized dragonflies known for their distinctive flight patterns and preference for patrolling over rivers and streams. These dragonflies get their name from their habit of flying in sunny areas, often seen darting back and forth along waterways during warm afternoons.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sundragons can be identified by their metallic green eyes, dark brown to black bodies with yellow markings, and their characteristic territorial behavior of patrolling specific stretches of flowing water.
children.funFact: Uhler's Sundragon males are highly territorial and will chase away other dragonflies from their chosen river territory, sometimes engaging in aerial battles that can last several minutes.

children.description: Emerald Dragonflies are a family of medium to large dragonflies known for their brilliant metallic green eyes and often iridescent bodies that shimmer in sunlight. These skilled hunters patrol wetland areas, flying with strong, steady wingbeats as they search for mosquitoes, flies, and other small insects. Most species in this family prefer clean, pristine waters like forest ponds, bogs, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dragonfly families, Emerald Dragonflies have distinctively bright metallic green eyes that really make them stand out. Many species also have a triangular marking on the top of their head and tend to hold their wings perpendicular to their body when perched.
children.funFact: Some Emerald Dragonflies, like the Boghaunters, are excellent indicators of healthy ecosystems - they only live in the cleanest, most pristine wetlands and disappear when water quality declines.

children.name: Aeshnidae
Aeshna
children.description: Aeshna darners are large, powerful dragonflies that are among the most impressive aerial hunters in New England's wetlands. These robust insects are characterized by their strong flight capabilities and relatively large size, making them formidable predators that patrol territories around ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aeshna darners can be distinguished from other dragonfly groups by their typically larger size, strong and direct flight patterns, and their habit of patrolling defined territories rather than perching frequently like some other dragonfly families.
children.funFact: Many Aeshna darners are capable of long-distance migration, with some species traveling hundreds of miles between breeding and overwintering areas, rivaling the famous migrations of Monarch butterflies.

children.name: Anax
children.description: Anax dragonflies are among New England's largest and most impressive dragonflies, known for their powerful flight and striking appearance. These robust insects are excellent hunters that patrol territories over ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Both species in this genus are strong fliers that can cover great distances during migration or while hunting.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anax dragonflies are distinguished by their large size, bright green eyes, and distinctive flight pattern of patrolling back and forth over water. They have clear wings and tend to be much larger and more aggressive than most other dragonfly species in the region.
children.funFact: Common Green Darners are incredible migrants that can travel over 900 miles, with some individuals flying from Canada all the way to the southern United States and back in a multi-generational journey similar to monarch butterflies.

children.name: Gomphaeschna
children.description: Pygmy Darners are a small genus of medium-sized dragonflies that are surprisingly elusive despite their relatively large size. These darners are known for their secretive nature and preference for flying in shaded areas near wooded ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Both New England species are accomplished hunters that patrol their territories with swift, darting flight patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other darner groups, Pygmy Darners are notably smaller and more compact, with distinctive pale markings on their dark bodies. They can be distinguished from other darners by their habit of flying closer to vegetation and their tendency to perch more frequently than their larger cousins.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'pygmy' darners, these dragonflies are still quite large by general dragonfly standards, with wingspans reaching over 3 inches - they're only small when compared to the giant darners in their family!

children.name: Boyeria
children.description: Spotted Darners are large, robust dragonflies known for the distinctive spotted patterns along their bodies and wings. These powerful fliers are typically found near wooded streams, rivers, and ponds where they hunt for flying insects. They are among the larger dragonflies you'll encounter in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other darner groups, Spotted Darners have prominent dark spots or markings on their wings and thorax, giving them their common name. They also tend to be more associated with shaded, forested waterways compared to the open-water habitats preferred by many other darners.
children.funFact: Spotted Darners are crepuscular hunters, meaning they're most active during dawn and dusk when their spotted camouflage helps them blend into the dappled light filtering through forest canopies.

children.name: Epiaeschna
children.description: Epiaeschna is a genus of large, powerful dragonflies known for their impressive hunting abilities and preference for wooded aquatic habitats. These dragonflies are among the largest in North America, with strong flight capabilities that make them formidable aerial predators. They typically patrol territories around ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams surrounded by forest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Epiaeschna are distinguished by their exceptional size, dark coloration with distinctive markings, and their habit of flying at dusk when most other dragonflies have settled down for the night. They have particularly robust thoraxes and powerful wing muscles that enable their strong, sustained flight.
children.funFact: The Swamp Darner can fly at twilight and even into near darkness, earning it the nickname 'shadow darner' for its ability to hunt when other dragonflies cannot see well enough to fly.

children.name: Basiaeschna
children.description: Basiaeschna is a small genus of dragonflies known as darners, which are among the largest and most powerful flying dragonflies. These impressive insects are characterized by their robust build and strong flight capabilities, making them formidable aerial predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Basiaeschna darners are distinguished from other darner genera by their relatively compact body structure and specific wing vein patterns. They tend to be smaller and more stocky compared to the larger, more slender darners in related genera.
children.funFact: The Springtime Darner gets its name because it's one of the earliest dragonflies to emerge each year, often appearing when many other dragonfly species are still dormant.

children.name: Rhionaeschna
children.description: Neotropical Darners are a small genus of large dragonflies that are primarily found in Central and South America, with just one species reaching into North America. These impressive dragonflies are powerful fliers with robust bodies and clear wings, typically found near slow-moving waters like ponds and marshes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other darner genera, Neotropical Darners have distinctive wing venation patterns and unique coloration, with the Spatterdock Darner showing bright green eyes and a brown thorax with yellow stripes.
children.funFact: The Spatterdock Darner gets its name from its habit of laying eggs in the stems and roots of spatterdock (yellow pond lily), making it one of the few dragonflies closely associated with a specific aquatic plant.

children.name: Nasiaeschna
children.description: Nasiaeschna is a small genus of large dragonflies known as darners, with only one species found in New England. These impressive dragonflies are among the larger members of the darner family, with powerful flight capabilities and distinctive markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their robust build and unique thoracic markings that help distinguish them from other darner genera.
children.funFact: The Cyrano Darner gets its common name from its distinctively long, prominent nose-like projection, reminiscent of the famous fictional character Cyrano de Bergerac.

children.description: Darners are large, powerful dragonflies that are among the most impressive aerial hunters in New England's wetlands. These fast-flying insects have long, slender bodies and large eyes that meet at the top of their heads, giving them excellent vision for catching prey on the wing. Most species patrol territories along ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Darners are typically much larger than other dragonfly families, with most species having wingspans over 3 inches. Their eyes touch each other at the top of their head, unlike many other dragonfly families where the eyes are separated.
children.funFact: Green Darners are incredible migrants that can travel over 900 miles, with some individuals flying from Canada to Mexico in a multigenerational journey similar to Monarch butterflies.

children.name: Lestidae
Lestes
children.description: Pond Spreadwings are slender, delicate damselflies that hold their wings horizontally away from their bodies when at rest, giving them their distinctive 'spreadwing' name. These elegant insects are commonly found near ponds, marshes, and slow-moving waterways throughout New England, where they hunt small flying insects and mate during the warmer months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other damselflies that fold their wings back along their bodies, spreadwings hold their wings perpendicular to their body when perched. They also tend to be more metallic in coloration and have a more robust build compared to other damselfly groups.
children.funFact: Many spreadwing species insert their eggs directly into plant stems above the waterline, and the eggs can survive through winter, hatching when spring flooding brings them into contact with water.

children.name: Archilestes
children.description: Stream Spreadwings are large, elegant damselflies that prefer flowing water habitats like streams and rivers. Unlike most damselflies that hold their wings vertically when at rest, these insects hold their wings horizontally spread out from their body, giving them their distinctive name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They are among the largest damselflies in North America and are the only damselflies that consistently hold their wings spread horizontally when perched, similar to dragonflies.
children.funFact: Great Spreadwings are late-season fliers that emerge in summer and can live for several months, often being seen well into autumn when most other damselflies have disappeared.

children.description: Spreadwings and allies are a family of slender damselflies known for their distinctive resting posture - they hold their wings partially spread at an angle rather than folded back along their body like most other damselflies. These delicate insects are commonly found near ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they hunt small flying insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other damselflies that fold their wings completely back when at rest, spreadwings hold their wings at a distinctive angle away from their body, giving them their common name.
children.funFact: Many spreadwing species lay their eggs directly into plant stems above the water line, and the eggs can survive through winter, hatching when spring floods bring them into contact with water.

children.name: Calopterygidae
Calopteryx
children.description: Jewelwings are large, elegant damselflies known for their brilliant metallic green bodies and distinctive broad, colorful wings. Unlike most damselflies, the males have dark, iridescent wings that shimmer with blue and green hues, while females typically have smoky or clear wings with white spots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jewelwings can be distinguished from other damselflies by their exceptionally broad wings and the males' distinctive dark, metallic wing coloration. They also have more robust bodies compared to typical narrow-winged damselflies.
children.funFact: Male jewelwings perform elaborate courtship displays, fluttering their shimmering dark wings like tiny flags to attract females along stream banks.

children.name: Hetaerina
children.description: Rubyspots are broad-winged damselflies known for the brilliant ruby-red patches at the base of their wings, particularly prominent in males. These elegant insects are typically found near flowing streams and rivers where they hunt for small flying insects and engage in elaborate courtship displays.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other damselflies, rubyspots have distinctively broad wings with metallic red coloration at the base, and they hold their wings partially open when at rest rather than folded completely back along their body.
children.funFact: Male rubyspots perform an intricate wing-flashing courtship dance, using their brilliant red wing patches like tiny stained glass windows to catch sunlight and attract females.

children.description: Broad-winged damselflies are a family of large, robust damselflies known for their exceptionally wide wings and metallic, iridescent bodies that shimmer with brilliant greens, blues, and reds. Unlike most damselflies, they hold their wings out from their body when at rest, similar to dragonflies. These stunning insects are commonly found along streams and rivers throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their wings are much broader than typical damselflies and often have colorful patches or bands, while their bodies display intense metallic colors that can appear almost jewel-like in sunlight. Males typically have darker, more colorful wing markings than females.
children.funFact: Male broad-winged damselflies perform elaborate courtship flights, showing off their colorful wings like tiny stained glass windows to attract females along sunny stream banks.

children.name: Cordulegastridae
Zoraena
children.description: American Spiketails are large, robust dragonflies known for their distinctive club-shaped tails that end in a pointed spike-like projection. These impressive insects are strong fliers that prefer wooded areas near streams and rivers, where they patrol territories and hunt for smaller flying insects. All four New England species share similar body structures and behaviors, though they can be distinguished by their unique wing spot patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other dragonfly groups, spiketails have that characteristic enlarged, club-like end to their abdomen with a prominent spike. They also tend to be larger and more robust than most other dragonflies, with particularly strong flight capabilities.
children.funFact: Spiketail larvae can take up to 5 years to develop in stream sediments, making them some of the longest-lived dragonfly juveniles in New England.

children.description: Spiketails are large, robust dragonflies known for their impressive size and distinctive flight patterns. These powerful fliers are among the biggest dragonflies you'll encounter in New England, with females possessing a prominent egg-laying spike (ovipositor) that gives the family its common name. They're often seen patrolling woodland streams and rivers where they hunt for insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spiketails can be identified by their large size, dark bodies with bright yellow stripes or spots, and clear wings with distinctive venation patterns. Unlike other dragonfly families, they have widely separated compound eyes that don't touch at the top of their heads.
children.funFact: Female spiketails use their namesake spike to drill eggs directly into sandy or muddy stream bottoms, repeatedly jabbing the substrate while hovering just above the water surface.

children.name: Macromiidae
Macromia
children.description: River Cruisers are large, powerful dragonflies that patrol rivers and streams throughout New England. These impressive insects are known for their swift, direct flight patterns as they hunt for smaller flying insects along waterways. All members of this genus are closely tied to flowing water habitats where they spend their larval stage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: River Cruisers can be distinguished from other dragonflies by their robust build, dark bodies with yellow or green markings, and their habit of flying in long, straight patrol routes over rivers rather than hovering in one spot.
children.funFact: River Cruiser larvae can live underwater for 2-3 years before emerging as adults, making them some of the longest-lived dragonfly juveniles in New England.

children.description: Cruisers are large, powerful dragonflies known for their impressive flying abilities and territorial behavior. These robust insects are typically found near rivers and streams, where they patrol their territory with strong, steady flight patterns that give them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cruisers can be distinguished from other dragonflies by their large size, dark coloration with bright yellow or green markings, and their habit of flying in long, straight courses rather than hovering like many other dragonfly families.
children.funFact: River Cruisers are among the fastest flying dragonflies in North America, capable of reaching speeds of up to 35 miles per hour during their territorial patrols.

children.description: Dragonflies and damselflies are ancient flying insects with two pairs of large, transparent wings covered in intricate networks of veins. They are skilled aerial predators that catch other insects on the wing, and spend their juvenile years as aquatic nymphs in ponds, streams, and wetlands before emerging as winged adults.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other winged insects, dragonflies and damselflies cannot fold their wings back along their body - they hold them perpendicular to their bodies at rest. Dragonflies hold their wings horizontally when resting, while damselflies typically fold theirs vertically above their backs.
children.funFact: Dragonflies are some of nature's most efficient hunters, catching up to 95% of the prey they pursue - a success rate that puts even the best human athletes to shame!

children.name: Orthoptera
Acrididae
Melanoplus
children.description: Melanoplus grasshoppers are the most common and diverse group of grasshoppers you'll encounter in New England fields, meadows, and forests. These medium to large-sized hoppers get their name from the distinctive spur-like projection found on their throat, and they're known for their powerful jumping abilities and varied diet of grasses and plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key identifying feature is the prominent spur or spine on the throat (prosternum) between the front legs. Most species in this genus also have relatively short wings compared to their body size, and males often produce distinctive chirping sounds by rubbing their hind legs against their forewings.
children.funFact: The Migratory Grasshopper, despite its name, rarely migrates today, but historically formed devastating swarms that could darken the sky and strip entire fields bare in a matter of hours.

children.name: Spharagemon
children.description: Spharagemon grasshoppers are medium-sized band-winged grasshoppers known for their distinctive crackling flight sounds and colorful hind wings. These ground-dwelling insects prefer open, sandy or rocky habitats where their mottled brown and gray coloration provides excellent camouflage against bare soil and stones. They are strong fliers that make short, buzzing flights when disturbed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their prominent flight sounds, relatively broad bodies, and tendency to inhabit dry, open areas with sparse vegetation. Their hind wings typically show bright yellow or orange bands that flash during flight.
children.funFact: These grasshoppers are sometimes called 'crackling grasshoppers' because males produce distinctive rattling or crackling sounds during their courtship flights by rapidly beating their wings.

children.name: Schistocerca
children.description: Bird grasshoppers are large, robust grasshoppers that get their name from their impressive flying abilities and tendency to take long, bird-like flights when disturbed. These grasshoppers are among the biggest you'll encounter in New England, with strong hind legs for jumping and well-developed wings for sustained flight. They're typically found in open areas like fields, meadows, and grasslands where they feed on various plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bird grasshoppers are notably larger than most other grasshoppers in the region, often measuring 1-2 inches long. They can be distinguished by their powerful flight capabilities and tendency to fly considerable distances rather than just making short hops like smaller grasshopper species.
children.funFact: The American Bird Grasshopper can fly up to 40 feet in a single flight and has been known to travel several miles in search of food or mates.

children.name: Arphia
children.description: Arphia is a genus of band-winged grasshoppers known for their colorful hind wings that flash bright yellow or orange when they fly. These medium-sized grasshoppers are excellent jumpers and fliers, often startling observers when they suddenly take off and reveal their vibrant wing colors. They're commonly found in open areas like fields, roadsides, and woodland edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arphia grasshoppers can be identified by their distinctly colored hind wings - either bright sulfur yellow or golden yellow - that contrast sharply with their more camouflaged brown and gray forewings and bodies. Unlike many other grasshoppers, they often make crackling or clicking sounds during flight.
children.funFact: These grasshoppers use their brightly colored wings as a defense mechanism - when threatened, they flash their vivid colors to startle predators, then quickly land and fold their wings to seemingly disappear against the ground.

children.name: Trimerotropis
children.description: Trimerotropis grasshoppers are band-winged grasshoppers known for their distinctive flight displays and sounds. These medium-sized grasshoppers have well-developed hind wings that often feature bold patterns or bright colors that flash when they fly, then disappear when they land and fold their wings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasshoppers, Trimerotropis species are known for the crackling, rattling, or buzzing sounds they make during flight, produced by their specialized wing structures. They also tend to have more robust bodies and stronger flight capabilities than typical ground-dwelling grasshoppers.
children.funFact: The Seaside Grasshopper is one of the few grasshoppers specially adapted to live in coastal dune environments, where it can tolerate salt spray and shifting sands that would be inhospitable to most other grasshopper species.

children.name: Orphulella
children.description: Orphulella is a genus of small to medium-sized grasshoppers known for their slender build and preference for grassy habitats. These grasshoppers are commonly found in fields, meadows, and pastures throughout New England, where they feed on grasses and other low-growing plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Orphulella can be distinguished from other grasshoppers by their relatively narrow bodies, long antennae, and distinctive wing patterns that often include spots or bands.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'Pasture Locust,' Orphulella speciosa is actually a true grasshopper, not a locust - the common name is a historical misnomer that has stuck over time.

children.name: Stethophyma
children.description: Stethophyma is a small genus of grasshoppers that specialize in living among sedges and other wetland grasses. These medium-sized grasshoppers are well-adapted to marshy habitats where they blend in perfectly with the vegetation they call home.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many grasshoppers that prefer dry fields, Stethophyma species are specifically adapted to wet, marshy environments and are most commonly found in sedge meadows and along pond edges.
children.funFact: The name Stethophyma comes from Greek words meaning 'chest swelling,' referring to a distinctive enlarged area on their thorax that helps distinguish them from other grasshopper genera.

children.name: Dissosteira
children.description: Dissosteira is a genus of band-winged grasshoppers known for their distinctive flight displays and cryptic coloration. These grasshoppers are ground-dwellers that blend seamlessly with bare soil, rocks, and sandy areas when at rest. They're most noticeable when they take flight, revealing brightly colored hindwings that flash during their short, buzzing flights.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their mottled brown and gray forewings that provide excellent camouflage, and their characteristic flight pattern of short bursts with audible wing rattling. Their hindwings typically display bold black bands with yellow or clear borders that are only visible during flight.
children.funFact: Carolina Grasshoppers create their distinctive crackling sound not by rubbing body parts together like crickets, but by snapping their hindwings during flight - a behavior called crepitation that may startle predators or attract mates.

children.name: Chortophaga
children.description: Chortophaga is a small genus of grasshoppers known for their distinctive striped patterns and medium size. These grasshoppers are typically found in grassy areas and open fields where they feed on various plants and grasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their prominent green or yellowish stripes running along their bodies, which help distinguish them from other grasshopper species in the same habitats.
children.funFact: The Green-striped Grasshopper can change its body color seasonally, appearing more green in summer and shifting to brown or tan tones in fall to better match its surroundings.

children.name: Dichromorpha
children.description: Dichromorpha is a small genus of grasshoppers known for their compact size and distinctive wing characteristics. These grasshoppers are typically found in grassy habitats where they blend in well with vegetation due to their coloration and behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably short wings that don't extend fully over their abdomen, making them poor fliers compared to other grasshoppers. They tend to be smaller and more slender than many other grasshopper species.
children.funFact: Despite having short wings that make them weak fliers, Dichromorpha grasshoppers are excellent jumpers and can leap many times their body length to escape predators.

children.name: Pseudochorthippus
children.description: Pseudochorthippus is a small genus of grasshoppers that includes species adapted to moist, marshy habitats. These grasshoppers are typically found in wet meadows, marshes, and other areas with high moisture levels where they feed on grasses and sedges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their preference for wetland environments and their relatively short wings compared to many other grasshopper species. They have specialized adaptations that allow them to thrive in the humid conditions of marshes and wet meadows.
children.funFact: The name Pseudochorthippus means 'false grass-hopper,' referring to certain structural differences that distinguish this genus from the more typical Chorthippus grasshoppers.

children.name: Booneacris
children.description: Wingless Mountain Grasshoppers are a unique group of grasshoppers that have evolved to live in high-altitude, rocky environments. As their name suggests, these grasshoppers have lost their ability to fly and instead rely on their powerful legs for jumping and climbing over mountain terrain.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasshoppers, members of this genus are completely flightless with greatly reduced or absent wings. They are specially adapted for life on rocky mountain slopes and alpine environments.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Booneacris glacialis, is found only in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and is so rare that it wasn't scientifically described until 1974.

children.name: Psinidia
children.description: Psinidia is a genus of band-winged grasshoppers known for their distinctive flight displays and wing patterns. These grasshoppers are typically found in open, sandy or rocky habitats where they blend in well with their surroundings when at rest.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished by their clear or lightly colored hind wings with dark bands, and their ability to produce crackling sounds during flight displays.
children.funFact: When threatened, Psinidia grasshoppers will leap into the air and flash their colorful hind wings while making clicking sounds, then suddenly drop down and seemingly disappear against the ground.

children.name: Chloealtis
children.description: Chloealtis is a small genus of grasshoppers known for their distinctive mottled appearance and preference for grassy habitats. These medium-sized locusts are characterized by their brownish coloration with scattered darker spots that help them blend in with dried vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other grasshoppers by their speckled or 'sprinkled' pattern of dark spots across their wings and body, which gives them excellent camouflage among grasses and low vegetation.
children.funFact: The name 'Chloealtis' comes from Greek words meaning 'green grasshopper,' even though these insects are typically brown and blend in perfectly with dead grass and plant litter.

children.name: Paroxya
children.description: Swamp Grasshoppers are specialized grasshoppers that have adapted to life in wetland environments. These insects are excellent swimmers and can even dive underwater to escape predators, unlike most other grasshoppers that prefer dry habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical grasshoppers, Swamp Grasshoppers have modified legs and body structure that allow them to move efficiently through water and wet vegetation. They also tend to be more robust and have different coloration patterns adapted to marshy environments.
children.funFact: Swamp Grasshoppers can hold their breath underwater for several minutes and will dive beneath the surface when threatened, making them some of the most aquatic grasshoppers in North America.

children.name: Hesperotettix
children.description: Hesperotettix is a small genus of grasshoppers found primarily in western North America, with only one species reaching into New England. These are medium-sized grasshoppers that are well-adapted to living among shrubs and low vegetation in open habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively robust build and their association with specific host plants, particularly in the sunflower family.
children.funFact: The Snakeweed Grasshopper gets its name from its preference for feeding on snakeweed and other desert shrubs, making it unusual among grasshoppers for specializing on woody plants rather than grasses.

children.name: Encoptolophus
children.description: Encoptolophus is a small genus of band-winged grasshoppers known for their distinctive clouded or mottled wing patterns. These medium-sized grasshoppers are well-adapted to blending in with rocky, sandy, or disturbed ground habitats where they spend most of their time.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their clouded or smoky wing membranes and their preference for bare or sparsely vegetated ground rather than dense grasslands.
children.funFact: The name Encoptolophus means 'hindered crest,' referring to the reduced or interrupted ridge (crest) on top of their heads that helps distinguish them from other band-winged grasshoppers.

children.name: Pardalophora
children.description: Pardalophora is a genus of band-winged grasshoppers known for their distinctive colorful hind wings that are revealed during flight. These grasshoppers are ground-dwelling insects that blend in well with their surroundings when at rest, but flash bright colors when they take to the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their prominent colored bands on the hind wings, particularly coral or reddish hues, and their preference for sandy or gravelly habitats where their mottled brown and gray coloration provides excellent camouflage.
children.funFact: The bright wing colors that give these grasshoppers their name are thought to startle predators during takeoff, giving the grasshopper a crucial split second to escape before it lands and seemingly vanishes against the ground.

children.name: Eritettix
children.description: Eritettix is a small genus of grasshoppers found in North America, with only one species calling New England home. These grasshoppers are part of the band-winged grasshopper family and are typically found in grassy areas and meadows. They are moderate-sized grasshoppers known for their distinctive markings and coloration.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their velvet-like striped patterns and relatively compact body structure compared to other band-winged grasshoppers. They have shorter wings relative to their body size and distinctive color patterns that help distinguish them from similar species.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Eritettix' comes from Greek roots meaning 'beloved grasshopper,' reflecting early naturalists' appreciation for these distinctively marked insects.

children.name: Pseudopomala
children.description: Pseudopomala is a genus of slender grasshoppers known for their preference for bunch grasses and their relatively small size compared to other locusts. These grasshoppers are typically found in grasslands and prairies where they blend in remarkably well with their grassy surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have notably short wings and are much less likely to take flight than other grasshoppers, preferring to hop or crawl through grass clumps. Their bodies are particularly narrow and elongated, helping them navigate between grass stems.
children.funFact: Despite being called locusts, Pseudopomala grasshoppers are actually quite sedentary and rarely form the large migrating swarms that true locusts are famous for.

children.name: Camnula
children.description: Camnula is a genus of grasshoppers that includes just one species found in New England: the Clear-winged Grasshopper. These grasshoppers are characterized by their relatively transparent wings and are part of the band-winged grasshopper family. They are typically found in open, grassy habitats where they blend in well with their surroundings.
