children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature of Camnula grasshoppers is their notably clear, transparent wings that lack the colorful bands or patterns found in many other grasshopper genera. This gives them their common name and helps distinguish them from their more brightly marked relatives.
children.funFact: Clear-winged Grasshoppers are excellent fliers and can travel considerable distances, sometimes appearing in large numbers during migration events across New England.

children.description: Short-horned Grasshoppers are the classic grasshoppers most people think of when they picture these jumping insects. They get their name from their relatively short antennae, which are shorter than their body length, and they're known for their powerful hind legs that allow them to leap many times their body length. This diverse family includes everything from tiny grasshoppers in meadows to large, colorful species that inhabit various habitats from grasslands to rocky slopes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their long-horned grasshopper relatives, these insects have antennae that are shorter than their bodies and typically stouter. They also produce sound by rubbing their hind legs against their forewings, rather than rubbing their wings together.
children.funFact: Many short-horned grasshoppers can produce and hear ultrasonic calls beyond human hearing range, allowing them to communicate secretly while avoiding detection by bats and other predators.

children.name: Tettigoniidae
Conocephalus
children.description: Lesser Meadow Katydids are slender, green grasshopper relatives that live in grassy habitats like meadows, fields, and marshes. They have long, thread-like antennae and produce distinctive chirping songs, especially at night. These katydids are smaller and more delicate than their tree-dwelling cousins, with pointed heads and relatively long legs for hopping through grass.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true katydids that live in trees, Lesser Meadow Katydids are ground-dwellers with more streamlined bodies and shorter wings. Their cone-shaped heads and preference for grassy habitats help separate them from other katydid groups.
children.funFact: Each species of Lesser Meadow Katydid has its own unique song pattern and frequency, allowing males to attract only females of their own species even when multiple species live in the same meadow.

children.name: Orchelimum
children.description: Orchelimum katydids are slender, green insects that are masters of grassy habitats throughout New England. These musical insects are known for their chirping songs that fill meadows, wetlands, and coastal areas during summer evenings. All members of this genus are excellent jumpers with long hind legs and thread-like antennae that can be longer than their bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their tree-dwelling katydid cousins, Orchelimum species prefer ground-level habitats and have more streamlined bodies adapted for navigating through dense grass and sedges. They can be distinguished from other meadow katydids by their relatively small size and the specific patterns of their songs.
children.funFact: Each Orchelimum species has its own unique song pattern and frequency, allowing researchers to identify different species just by listening to their calls in the field.

children.name: Scudderia
children.description: Scudder's Bush Katydids are a group of large, green insects that live in trees and shrubs throughout New England. These musical crickets are known for their loud, rhythmic calls that fill summer evenings, produced by males rubbing their wings together to attract mates. They have long antennae, powerful hind legs for jumping, and leaf-like wings that help them blend perfectly with foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other katydid groups, Scudder's Bush Katydids have distinctive tail projections (cerci) that vary in shape between species - some are forked, others curved, and some are broad and flat. Their calls also tend to be more continuous and musical compared to the shorter, choppier sounds of other katydid genera.
children.funFact: Each species in this genus has its own unique song pattern and rhythm, allowing you to identify them by sound alone even when they're perfectly camouflaged in the trees above you.

children.name: Neoconocephalus
children.description: Common Coneheads are a group of katydids known for their distinctive pointed, cone-shaped heads that give them their name. These green or brown insects are excellent jumpers and are often found in tall grasses, meadows, and weedy areas throughout New England. They're active at night and are known for their loud, continuous chirping songs that can be heard from late summer into fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other katydids, coneheads have distinctly pointed, conical heads and longer, more slender bodies. Their wings typically extend well beyond their body length, and males have specialized sound-producing structures that create their characteristic high-pitched, sustained calls.
children.funFact: The Slightly Musical Conehead gets its amusing name because its song sounds less melodious compared to other musical insects - it produces a continuous, buzzy trill that some find less pleasant than the songs of crickets or other katydids.

children.name: Amblycorypha
children.description: Round-headed Katydids are a group of green, leaf-like insects known for their broad, rounded heads and relatively short antennae compared to other katydids. These nocturnal musicians are excellent camouflage artists, blending seamlessly into foliage during the day while producing distinctive chirping songs at night to attract mates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their long-horned katydid cousins, Round-headed Katydids have noticeably shorter antennae and more compact, oval-shaped bodies. Their heads are distinctively wide and rounded, giving them their common name.
children.funFact: Each species in this genus has its own unique song pattern - the Rattler Round-winged Katydid even gets its name from its distinctive rattling call that sounds like a tiny maraca being shaken!

children.name: Microcentrum
children.description: Angle-winged katydids are large, leaf-green insects with distinctive angular wing shapes that give them their name. These nocturnal musicians are known for their loud, rhythmic calls that echo through summer evenings. They're excellent mimics of leaves, with broad, flat wings that help them blend seamlessly into foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their wings have sharp, angular edges rather than the rounded wings of most other katydids, and they're notably larger than many of their relatives. The angular wing shape combined with their bright green coloration makes them easy to distinguish from other katydid species.
children.funFact: Male angle-winged katydids produce their famous "katy-did, katy-didn't" calls by rubbing specialized structures on their wings together, and each species has its own unique rhythm and timing.

children.name: Atlanticus
children.description: Eastern Shieldbacks are large, robust katydids known for their distinctive shield-like structure on their back (called a pronotum) that gives them their common name. These impressive insects are flightless, with reduced wings, and are primarily ground-dwelling crickets that prefer woodland habitats. They're among the largest orthopterans (grasshoppers and crickets) you'll encounter in New England forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other katydids, Eastern Shieldbacks cannot fly and have notably shortened wings that don't extend beyond their prominent shield-shaped back plate. They're also much larger and more heavily built than typical katydids, with powerful legs adapted for walking rather than jumping.
children.funFact: Despite being in the katydid family, Eastern Shieldbacks are carnivorous hunters that will catch and eat other insects, making them unusual predators among their mostly plant-eating relatives.

children.name: Meconema
children.description: Meconema is a genus of delicate bush-crickets known for their slender build and long, thread-like antennae. These small insects are typically found on trees and shrubs, where they feed on aphids and other soft-bodied insects rather than plant material like many other crickets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most crickets, Meconema species are primarily predatory and have reduced or absent wings in females, making them flightless.
children.funFact: The Oak Bush-cricket is actually a recent arrival to New England, having been accidentally introduced from Europe and slowly expanding its range across North America since the 1950s.

children.name: Pterophylla
children.description: Pterophylla is a genus of large, green katydids known for their broad, leaf-like wings and distinctive calls. These robust insects are among the most recognizable katydids in eastern North America, with bodies that can reach up to 2 inches in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have exceptionally wide, rounded forewings that look remarkably like leaves, and they produce a distinctive harsh, rasping call that sounds like 'katy-did, katy-didn't.'
children.funFact: The Common True Katydid's scientific name 'camellifolia' means 'camellia-leaved,' referring to how perfectly its wings mimic the broad, oval leaves of camellia plants.

children.name: Roeseliana
children.description: Roeseliana is a small genus of bush-crickets (katydids) that includes just one species found in New England. These are medium-sized insects with powerful hind legs for jumping and long antennae that help them navigate their grassland and meadow habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively short wings and are primarily ground-dwelling, unlike many other bush-crickets that are more arboreal. They produce their characteristic chirping sounds by rubbing their wing covers together.
children.funFact: Roesel's Bush-cricket was originally a European species that has successfully established itself in North America, making it one of the few katydid species to successfully cross the Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Phaneroptera
children.description: Sickle-bearing Bushcrickets are delicate, green katydids named for the distinctive curved, sickle-shaped structures (cerci) at the tip of their abdomen. These slender insects are primarily found in shrubs and low vegetation where they blend in perfectly with their leafy surroundings. They are skilled jumpers and produce soft chirping sounds, particularly during evening hours.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The curved, sickle-like appendages at the end of their abdomen set them apart from other katydid groups. They also tend to be more delicate in build compared to their robust cousins in other genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Mediterranean Katydids,' these insects have successfully established populations in New England, likely arriving as stowaways on imported plants or through natural range expansion northward.

children.name: Leptophyes
children.description: Leptophyes is a genus of delicate bush-crickets known for their slender build and distinctive spotted patterns. These small insects are typically found among shrubs and low vegetation, where they blend in remarkably well with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their heavily speckled appearance and relatively small size compared to other bush-crickets. They have notably long, thin antennae and lack fully developed wings in adults.
children.funFact: Despite being called crickets, Leptophyes species are actually more closely related to katydids and produce their chirping sounds by rubbing their wing covers together rather than their legs.

children.name: Montezumina
children.description: Montezumina is a small genus of katydids, which are singing insects related to crickets and grasshoppers. These katydids are part of the broader family of long-horned grasshoppers, known for their distinctive chirping calls and long, thread-like antennae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are typically smaller and more modest in appearance compared to many other katydid species, with subtle coloration that helps them blend into their surroundings.
children.funFact: The genus name Montezumina honors the Aztec emperor Montezuma, reflecting the historical connection between many katydid species and the Americas.

children.description: Katydids are leaf-green insects known for their melodic chirping sounds that fill summer evenings across New England. These relatives of grasshoppers have long, thread-like antennae and powerful hind legs for jumping, with most species perfectly camouflaged to blend in with foliage where they feed on leaves and smaller insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike grasshoppers, katydids have much longer antennae (often longer than their body) and typically hold their wings roof-like over their backs. Most species are also more slender and have flattened bodies compared to their stockier grasshopper cousins.
children.funFact: Male katydids create their signature songs by rubbing their wings together, with each species having its own unique rhythm and pitch - some even got their name from calls that sound like 'katy-did, katy-didn't!'

children.name: Trigonidiidae
children.commonName: Trigs, Sword-tailed Crickets, and Ground Crickets

children.name: Allonemobius
children.description: Robust Ground Crickets are small, brown crickets that live close to the ground in leaf litter, grass, and low vegetation. They are active from late summer through fall, producing distinctive chirping songs that help identify different species. These crickets are smaller and more compact than their tree-dwelling relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crickets that live in trees or bushes, these species stay near ground level and have shorter, more robust bodies. Their songs are also typically higher-pitched and more musical than those of larger cricket species.
children.funFact: The Tinkling Ground Cricket gets its name from its bell-like song that sounds remarkably similar to wind chimes on a gentle breeze.

children.name: Neonemobius
children.description: Small Ground Crickets are tiny, dark-colored crickets that live close to the ground in moist habitats like wetlands, forest floors, and grassy areas. These diminutive insects are much smaller than the house crickets most people are familiar with, typically measuring less than half an inch long. All members of this group prefer humid environments and are most active during warm months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cricket groups, Small Ground Crickets are characterized by their very small size, preference for ground-level microhabitats, and their association with specific moisture-loving plants like sphagnum moss. They also have proportionally shorter wings compared to other crickets.
children.funFact: The Sphagnum Ground Cricket is so specialized that it's almost exclusively found living among sphagnum moss in bogs and wetlands, making it one of the most habitat-specific crickets in New England.

children.name: Anaxipha
children.description: Brown Sword-tail Crickets are tiny, delicate crickets known for their distinctive sword-like ovipositors (egg-laying tubes) that extend from the females' abdomens. These small insects are commonly called 'trigs' and are among the tiniest crickets you'll encounter in New England. They typically live in grassy areas and produce high-pitched chirping sounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These crickets are much smaller than most other crickets, usually less than half an inch long, and have proportionally long, sword-shaped ovipositors in females. Their chirping is notably high-pitched and tinkling compared to the deeper calls of larger cricket species.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, male Brown Sword-tail Crickets can produce calls so high-pitched that some people, especially older adults, cannot hear them at all due to age-related hearing loss.

children.name: Phyllopalpus
children.description: Phyllopalpus is a small genus of bush crickets known for their distinctive appearance and behavior. These crickets are characterized by their compact size and preference for shrubby vegetation where they feed on plant matter and small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their relatively large, flattened heads and unique palps (sensory appendages near the mouth) that give the genus its name, which means 'leaf palps.'
children.funFact: The Red-headed Bush Cricket is one of the smallest crickets in North America, measuring only about 6-8 millimeters in length, making it smaller than many ants!

children.name: Eunemobius
children.description: Even-spurred Ground Crickets are small, brownish crickets that live close to the ground in leaf litter, under logs, and in grassy areas. They get their name from the paired spurs on their hind legs that are roughly equal in length. These crickets are part of the larger ground cricket family and are known for their quiet, subtle chirping sounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that sets them apart from other ground crickets is having two spurs of nearly equal length on their hind tibiae (lower leg segments), rather than having one spur notably longer than the other.
children.funFact: Despite being crickets, Even-spurred Ground Crickets produce such soft chirping sounds that they're often called 'whisper crickets' and can be easily overlooked even when they're right underfoot.

children.name: Cyrtoxipha
children.description: Green Trigs are small, delicate crickets known for their bright green coloration that helps them blend perfectly with grass and low vegetation. These tiny insects are part of the tree cricket family and are among the smallest crickets you'll encounter in New England. They spend most of their time in grassy areas and meadows, where their green bodies make them nearly invisible among the plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Green Trigs can be distinguished from other crickets by their exceptionally small size and vivid green color throughout their entire body. Unlike many other cricket species that are brown or black, these insects maintain their bright green appearance as adults.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, male Green Trigs produce surprisingly loud chirping sounds to attract mates, and their calls can often be heard on warm summer evenings even when the crickets themselves are impossible to spot in the grass.

children.description: Trigonidiidae is a diverse family of small crickets that includes ground crickets, sword-tailed crickets, and trigs. These crickets are generally much smaller than house crickets and are often found living close to or on the ground in various habitats from forests to grasslands. Most species produce soft, high-pitched chirping sounds that can be quite different from the loud songs of their larger cricket relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are typically smaller and more delicate than other cricket families, with many species having distinctive sword-like projections on their abdomens or specialized wing structures. Ground crickets in particular are adapted for life at soil level, while trigs often have modified wings for their unique acoustic displays.
children.funFact: Some sword-tailed crickets produce songs so high-pitched that many people can't hear them, chirping at frequencies above the range of human hearing to communicate with potential mates.

children.name: Oecanthidae
Oecanthus
children.description: Common tree crickets are delicate, pale-colored crickets that live in trees, shrubs, and tall grasses throughout New England. These slender insects are best known for their melodious chirping songs that fill summer evenings, with males producing their calls by rubbing their wings together to attract mates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike ground crickets, tree crickets have long, thin antennae and are typically light green or whitish in color with translucent wings. They're also much more arboreal, spending most of their lives above ground in vegetation.
children.funFact: The snowy tree cricket is known as the 'thermometer cricket' because you can estimate the temperature in Fahrenheit by counting its chirps in 13 seconds and adding 40!

children.name: Hapithus
children.description: Hapithus is a small genus of bush crickets known for their active, energetic behavior. These crickets are characterized by their excellent jumping ability and restless nature, spending much of their time moving through vegetation rather than staying in one place.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other bush crickets by their particularly strong hind legs adapted for jumping and their notably active behavioral patterns.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they live in bushes, Hapithus crickets are equally at home in tall grasses and can leap distances up to 20 times their body length when startled.

children.name: Neoxabea
children.description: Smooth-legged Tree Crickets are a small genus of delicate, pale green crickets that live in trees and shrubs. They get their name from their notably smooth hind legs, which lack the spines found on many other cricket species. These nocturnal insects are known for their clear, musical chirping calls that fill New England evenings during late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tree crickets, Neoxabea species have completely smooth hind legs without any spines or bristles. They also tend to be smaller and more delicate than their spiny-legged relatives.
children.funFact: The Two-spotted Tree Cricket is sometimes called the 'pin-head cricket' because of the tiny dark spots on its head that look like pinpricks.

children.description: Tree crickets and bush crickets are delicate, pale-colored insects that are excellent climbers, spending most of their lives in shrubs, trees, and tall grasses. Unlike their ground-dwelling cricket cousins, these insects have long, thin legs and antennae that help them navigate through vegetation. They're known for their melodious chirping songs, which are often heard on warm summer evenings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tree crickets are much more slender and pale than other crickets, with translucent or light green coloration that helps them blend in with leaves. Their wings are typically broader and more delicate than ground crickets, and they hold their bodies more horizontally when at rest.
children.funFact: Male tree crickets are nature's thermometers - you can estimate the temperature by counting their chirps! Count the number of chirps in 13 seconds and add 40 to get the approximate temperature in Fahrenheit.

children.name: Rhaphidophoridae
children.commonName: Camel Crickets, Cave Crickets, and Cave Wēta

children.name: Ceuthophilus
children.description: Camel crickets are wingless insects with distinctively humped backs that give them their common name. These nocturnal creatures have extremely long antennae and powerful hind legs that allow them to jump impressive distances when disturbed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true crickets, camel crickets cannot chirp because they lack the wing structures used to produce sound. Their arched backs and spider-like appearance make them easily recognizable among other cricket relatives.
children.funFact: Camel crickets are excellent recyclers in nature, feeding on decaying organic matter, fungi, and even fabric or paper when they venture into human dwellings.

children.name: Diestrammena
children.description: Diestrammena is a genus of camel crickets, also known as cave crickets, that are characterized by their humpbacked appearance and long, spindly legs. These wingless insects are typically found in dark, humid places like basements, caves, and under logs. Members of this genus are originally from Asia but have established populations in other parts of the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Diestrammena camel crickets can be distinguished from native North American camel crickets by their more robust build and distinctive leg banding patterns. They also tend to be larger and have more pronounced humped backs than most local species.
children.funFact: Despite being called crickets, camel crickets in the genus Diestrammena don't chirp because they lack the wing structures that other crickets use to make their characteristic sounds.

children.name: Tachycines
children.description: Tachycines is a genus of camel crickets that are native to Asia but have spread to other parts of the world through human activity. These crickets are characterized by their humpbacked appearance, long antennae, and powerful jumping legs, though they lack wings and cannot fly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tachycines crickets can be distinguished from other camel crickets by their relatively robust build and specific leg and antenna proportions. They also tend to be more tolerant of cooler temperatures than many related species.
children.funFact: The Greenhouse Camel Cricket earned its name because it was first discovered in North America hiding in heated greenhouses, where it found the perfect warm, humid conditions to survive harsh winters.

children.name: Euhadenoecus
children.description: Appalachian Crevice Crickets are specialized cave-dwelling insects that have adapted to life in the dark cracks and crevices of rocky areas throughout the Appalachian Mountains. These pale, wingless crickets have lost their ability to fly and instead rely on their long antennae and legs to navigate their underground world. They are perfectly suited for squeezing through narrow spaces in caves, rock formations, and deep soil crevices.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical crickets, crevice crickets are wingless, nearly colorless, and have exceptionally long, thin legs and antennae that help them feel their way through tight spaces. Their bodies are more elongated and flattened compared to surface-dwelling crickets, allowing them to slip into narrow rock crevices.
children.funFact: These crickets are so well-adapted to cave life that they can live for several years, much longer than most surface crickets, and they communicate through vibrations rather than the chirping sounds we associate with their above-ground relatives.

children.description: Camel crickets and cave crickets are humpbacked, wingless insects that look like a cross between a cricket and a spider. These silent jumpers have extremely long antennae and powerful hind legs that help them navigate in dark environments like caves, basements, and forest leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true crickets, these insects cannot chirp because they lack wings and sound-producing organs. Their distinctively arched backs and disproportionately long, thread-like antennae make them easy to identify.
children.funFact: Cave crickets are so good at jumping that they can leap several times their own body length to escape predators, often startling people when they suddenly bound toward them instead of away!

children.name: Gryllidae
Gryllus
children.description: Gryllus is a genus of field crickets that are among the most familiar chirping insects in New England. These medium-sized, dark-colored crickets are the ones you typically hear singing on warm summer and fall evenings from grassy areas, gardens, and fields. All three New England species are ground-dwelling crickets that create their characteristic songs by rubbing their wings together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Field crickets in the genus Gryllus are larger and more robust than house crickets, with longer antennae and stronger hind legs for jumping. They're distinguished from other cricket genera by their dark brown to black coloration and their preference for living outdoors in natural habitats rather than in buildings.
children.funFact: Each species of Gryllus field cricket has its own unique chirping pattern and song frequency, allowing you to identify which species is singing just by listening carefully to the rhythm and pitch of their calls.

children.name: Velarifictorus
children.description: Velarifictorus is a genus of burrowing crickets known for their underground lifestyle and distinctive chirping songs. These crickets are excellent diggers that create elaborate tunnel systems in soil where they spend most of their lives. They are relatively recent arrivals to New England, having been introduced from Asia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These crickets can be distinguished from other cricket groups by their robust, cylindrical bodies adapted for digging and their preference for living almost entirely underground rather than on the surface.
children.funFact: The Japanese Burrowing Cricket was first discovered in New England in the 1950s and has since become established in the region, with males producing their mating calls from deep within their underground burrows.

children.name: Gryllodes
children.description: Gryllodes is a genus of crickets that includes species adapted to warm, indoor environments around the world. These crickets are typically associated with human habitation and can be found in heated buildings, greenhouses, and other structures where they can survive year-round.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Gryllodes are distinguished from other cricket genera by their relatively small size, pale coloration, and their preference for indoor environments over natural outdoor habitats.
children.funFact: The Tropical House Cricket can produce offspring continuously throughout the year when living in heated buildings, unlike most New England crickets that have seasonal life cycles.

children.name: Miogryllus
children.description: Miogryllus is a small genus of crickets known for their distinctive striped patterns and musical chirping abilities. These crickets are typically found in grassy areas and meadows where they feed on plant matter and small insects. They are most active during warm evenings when their characteristic songs can be heard across the landscape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Miogryllus can be identified by their bold longitudinal stripes running down their bodies and their relatively small size compared to other cricket genera. They also have a unique wing structure that produces a distinctively pitched chirp.
children.funFact: The Eastern Striped Cricket's chirp rate is so closely tied to temperature that you can estimate the air temperature by counting its chirps per minute and using a simple mathematical formula!

children.name: Acheta
children.description: Acheta is a genus of crickets that includes some of the most familiar chirping insects found around human habitations. These medium-sized crickets are known for their distinctive musical calls produced by males rubbing their wings together. In New England, this genus is represented by the common house cricket, which has become closely associated with human dwellings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acheta crickets are distinguished from other cricket genera by their robust build, relatively large size, and strong jumping ability. They typically have well-developed wings and produce loud, clear chirping sounds that are more musical than the calls of many other cricket species.
children.funFact: House crickets have been kept as pets and good luck charms in many cultures for over 1,000 years, and their chirping rate can actually be used as a natural thermometer - count the chirps in 15 seconds and add 40 to get the approximate temperature in Fahrenheit!

children.description: True crickets are the classic chirping insects that create the soundtrack of summer evenings across New England. These small to medium-sized insects have long antennae, powerful hind legs for jumping, and most males produce their distinctive songs by rubbing their wings together. They're found in a variety of habitats from fields and forests to your basement or garden.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True crickets can be distinguished from other cricket-like insects by their flattened bodies, long thread-like antennae that are often longer than their bodies, and their characteristic chirping songs. Unlike grasshoppers, they hold their wings flat over their backs and have different wing structures specialized for sound production.
children.funFact: Each species of true cricket chirps at a different rate, and you can actually estimate the temperature by counting a cricket's chirps - the snowy tree cricket is so accurate it's sometimes called the 'thermometer cricket'!

children.name: Tetrigidae
Tetrix
children.description: Tetrix is a genus of tiny grasshoppers known as groundhoppers or grouse locusts that are among the smallest members of the grasshopper family. These miniature insects are typically less than half an inch long and have a distinctive cone-shaped extension of their back plate that extends well beyond their abdomen. They're often found hopping around in moist soil, leaf litter, and along stream banks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grasshoppers, Tetrix species have greatly reduced or completely absent hind wings, and their pronotum (back plate) extends far beyond the tip of their abdomen like a pointed cap. They also lack the ability to produce sound through stridulation, unlike most of their singing grasshopper relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being grasshoppers, Tetrix species are excellent swimmers and can actually walk on water surfaces using the surface tension, making them one of the few grasshopper groups adapted for aquatic environments.

children.name: Tettigidea
children.description: Tettigidea is a genus of tiny grasshoppers known as pygmy grasshoppers or grouse locusts. These small insects are characterized by their greatly extended pronotum (the shield-like plate behind the head) that covers most or all of their abdomen. They are typically found in moist habitats near water sources, muddy areas, and along stream banks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Tettigidea can be distinguished from other pygmy grasshoppers by their specific body proportions and the shape of their extended pronotum. The pronotum in this genus typically has a distinctive pointed or rounded rear projection that extends well beyond the tip of the abdomen.
children.funFact: Despite being called grasshoppers, Tettigidea species are actually omnivorous and will eat algae, fungi, and decaying organic matter in addition to plant material, making them important decomposers in wetland ecosystems.

children.name: Nomotettix
children.description: Nomotettix is a genus of tiny grasshoppers known as pygmy grasshoppers or grouse locusts. These diminutive insects are characterized by their small size and distinctive crested appearance, typically measuring less than an inch in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their prominent crest or ridge running along the top of their pronotum (the shield-like plate behind their head), which gives them their "crested" common name.
children.funFact: Despite being called grasshoppers, pygmy grasshoppers like Nomotettix are more closely related to crickets and are among the smallest members of the grasshopper family.

children.name: Paratettix
children.description: Paratettix is a genus of small, ground-dwelling grasshoppers known as grouse locusts or pygmy locusts. These tiny insects are characterized by their distinctive hood-like extension of the pronotum (the shield-like plate behind the head) that covers much of their body. They are among the smallest grasshoppers in North America, typically measuring less than half an inch long.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Paratettix can be distinguished from other grouse locusts by their particularly pronounced hood-like pronotum that extends well beyond the tip of the abdomen. The hood often has a peaked or ridged appearance that gives them their characteristic silhouette.
children.funFact: Despite being grasshoppers, Paratettix species are poor jumpers compared to their larger relatives and often rely more on running and hiding among leaf litter and moss to escape predators.

children.description: Pygmy grasshoppers are tiny, ground-dwelling insects that are easily overlooked due to their small size and excellent camouflage. These miniature hoppers have a distinctive shield-like extension of their back plate (pronotum) that often extends past their abdomen, giving them a unique armored appearance. They're commonly found in moist areas like stream banks, pond edges, and boggy soils where they feed on algae, moss, and decaying plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike regular grasshoppers, pygmy grasshoppers have their pronotum (the shield behind their head) dramatically extended backward, often covering most or all of their tiny wings. They're also much smaller than typical grasshoppers, usually measuring less than half an inch long.
children.funFact: Some pygmy grasshoppers are excellent swimmers and can actually dive underwater to escape predators, using air bubbles trapped under their extended back shield to breathe while submerged.

children.name: Gryllotalpidae
Gryllotalpa
children.description: Gryllotalpa is a genus of large, robust crickets known as mole crickets that spend most of their lives underground. These insects have evolved powerful, shovel-like front legs that make them exceptional diggers, allowing them to tunnel through soil in search of plant roots and small insects to eat. They are among the most fossorial (underground-dwelling) members of the cricket family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mole crickets are easily distinguished from other crickets by their enlarged, spade-shaped front legs adapted for digging, their cylindrical body shape, and their reduced wings. Unlike typical crickets that hop on the surface, these insects are built like tiny moles for life underground.
children.funFact: Male mole crickets are acoustic engineers that construct horn-shaped burrows to amplify their mating calls, which can be heard up to a mile away and sound more like a trill than typical cricket chirping.

children.name: Neocurtilla
children.description: Neocurtilla is a genus of mole crickets that are specially adapted for life underground. These robust insects have powerful front legs modified for digging and spend most of their time burrowing through soil in search of plant roots and other organic matter to eat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crickets, Neocurtilla species have enlarged, shovel-like front legs with strong claws perfectly designed for excavating tunnels in soil. Their bodies are also more cylindrical and streamlined compared to surface-dwelling crickets.
children.funFact: Mole crickets are surprisingly good swimmers and can even fly, despite spending most of their lives underground in tunnel systems they excavate with their specialized digging claws.

children.description: Mole crickets are unusual underground insects that spend most of their lives tunneling through soil and plant roots. These robust crickets have powerful front legs specially adapted for digging, making them excellent excavators in lawns, gardens, and agricultural fields. Unlike their chirping cousins above ground, mole crickets are built for a subterranean lifestyle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mole crickets can be distinguished from other crickets by their cylindrical, mole-like bodies and their dramatically enlarged, shovel-shaped front legs used for digging. They also have small eyes and shortened wing covers compared to surface-dwelling crickets.
children.funFact: Mole crickets are among the loudest insects in North America - males create their mating calls by singing from specially constructed underground burrows that act like megaphones, amplifying their chirps so they can be heard from over a mile away.

children.name: Myrmecophilidae
Myrmecophilus
children.description: Myrmecophilus is a genus of tiny crickets that have evolved to live exclusively with ants in their colonies. These minute insects are specialized ant guests, spending their entire lives within ant nests where they feed on scraps and secretions. They represent one of nature's most remarkable examples of social parasitism among insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crickets, Myrmecophilus species are wingless, extremely small (only 2-3mm long), and have reduced eyes since they live in the darkness of ant colonies. Their bodies are also more rounded and less flattened than typical crickets, helping them navigate through ant tunnels.
children.funFact: Ant crickets are so well-adapted to their hosts that they can chemically mimic ant pheromones, allowing them to move freely through the colony without being attacked by their much larger roommates.

children.description: Ant crickets are tiny, wingless insects that have evolved to live exclusively inside ant colonies. These unusual crickets are so small they can easily fit on your fingernail, and they spend their entire lives as guests in ant nests, feeding on ant secretions and nest debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other crickets, ant crickets are completely wingless, have greatly reduced eyes, and possess a humpbacked appearance. Their small size and specialized body shape allow them to move freely among their ant hosts without being detected as intruders.
children.funFact: Ant crickets are so well-adapted to underground life that they can't survive outside of ant colonies - they're completely dependent on their hosts for food, shelter, and protection.

children.name: Gryllacrididae
Camptonotus
children.description: Camptonotus is a genus of crickets known for their distinctive leaf-rolling behavior. These crickets create shelter by cutting and rolling leaves into tube-like structures where they hide during the day and lay their eggs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most crickets that live on the ground or in vegetation crevices, Camptonotus crickets are specialized leaf-rollers that actively modify their environment by creating cylindrical leaf shelters.
children.funFact: The Carolina Leafroller Cricket can roll leaves so tightly that the finished shelter looks like a green cigar, and they're so well-hidden inside that they're rarely seen despite being fairly common in wooded areas.

children.description: Raspy crickets are nocturnal insects that get their name from the rough, raspy sound they make when communicating. Unlike true crickets, they are typically wingless or have very short wings, and they have long, thread-like antennae that can be longer than their bodies. These insects are usually found in leaf litter, under logs, or in caves where they feed on decaying plant matter and small insects.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Raspy crickets differ from true crickets by lacking fully developed wings for flight and having extremely long antennae. They also have a more humpbacked appearance and produce their distinctive raspy calls using different body parts than regular crickets.
children.funFact: Despite being called crickets, raspy crickets are more closely related to katydids and wetas, and some species can live for several years, which is unusually long for most cricket-like insects.

children.name: Tridactylidae
Neotridactylus
children.description: Neotridactylus is a genus of tiny grasshoppers known as pygmy mole grasshoppers. These small insects are excellent diggers that spend much of their time burrowing in moist soil near streams, ponds, and other wet areas. They get their name from their diminutive size and mole-like habit of living underground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical grasshoppers, pygmy mole grasshoppers have shortened wings and powerful front legs adapted for digging. They also lack the long jumping hind legs that most grasshoppers are famous for.
children.funFact: Despite being called grasshoppers, these tiny insects are actually more closely related to crickets and spend most of their lives tunneling through muddy soil rather than hopping through grass.

children.description: Pygmy mole crickets are tiny insects that live along the edges of streams, ponds, and other wet areas. They are excellent diggers with powerful front legs adapted for burrowing into sandy or muddy soil. These small crickets are also surprisingly good swimmers and can even jump on water surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike regular crickets, pygmy mole crickets have enlarged, shovel-like front legs for digging and greatly reduced hind legs that are not suited for jumping. They are much smaller than typical mole crickets and lack the ability to produce sound.
children.funFact: Pygmy mole crickets can actually walk on water by using surface tension, making them one of the few insects that can effectively move across water surfaces without swimming.

children.name: Mogoplistidae
Cycloptilum
children.description: Common Scaly Crickets are a small genus of tree crickets known for their distinctive scale-like wing covers and relatively quiet chirping compared to other cricket species. These delicate insects are typically found in shrubs and low vegetation where they feed on small insects and plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be identified by their unusually scaly or roughened wing texture and their tendency to be less active than other crickets, often remaining motionless when disturbed.
children.funFact: The genus name Cycloptilum means 'round wing,' referring to the distinctive rounded shape of their wing covers that gives them their scaly appearance.

children.description: Scaly crickets are small, delicate insects that get their name from the tiny scales covering their wings and body, giving them a somewhat moth-like appearance. Unlike their larger cricket cousins, these diminutive musicians are typically found in leaf litter, under bark, or in other hidden microhabitats where they blend in remarkably well with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These crickets are distinguished from other cricket families by their distinctive scaly wing covers and much smaller size, typically measuring less than half an inch long. They also tend to be more secretive and less likely to be heard chirping compared to field crickets or tree crickets.
children.funFact: Despite being called crickets, scaly crickets are so quiet and secretive that many people live their entire lives without ever knowingly encountering one, even though they may be present in nearby leaf litter and garden debris.

children.name: Romaleidae
Romalea
children.description: Horse Lubbers are large, robust grasshoppers known for their impressive size and colorful appearance. These hefty insects are among the biggest grasshoppers in North America, with thick bodies and relatively short wings that make them poor fliers but excellent walkers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Horse Lubbers are distinguished from other grasshoppers by their exceptionally large size, bright warning colors (often yellow, orange, and black), and their inability to fly due to reduced wing development.
children.funFact: Despite being grasshoppers, Eastern Lubber Grasshoppers are terrible jumpers and instead rely on walking slowly while displaying bright warning colors to advertise their toxic nature to predators.

children.description: Lubber grasshoppers are large, robust grasshoppers known for their impressive size and often colorful appearance. These heavy-bodied insects are poor fliers, with wings that are typically too small or underdeveloped for sustained flight, so they rely on walking and jumping to get around.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasshoppers, lubbers are notably large and bulky with reduced wings that make them flightless or nearly flightless. They're also known for their bright warning colors and ability to produce defensive chemicals when threatened.
children.funFact: When threatened, many lubber grasshoppers can spray a foul-smelling, irritating foam from their thorax as a defense mechanism, earning them the nickname 'stink grasshoppers.'

children.description: Orthoptera includes the jumping and singing insects we commonly hear on summer evenings - grasshoppers, crickets, and katydids. These insects are famous for their powerful hind legs built for jumping and their ability to produce sounds by rubbing body parts together, a process called stridulation. Most have straight, narrow wings and undergo incomplete metamorphosis, developing from egg to nymph to adult without a pupal stage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other insects, Orthoptera have enlarged hind legs specialized for jumping and most males can produce distinctive chirping, clicking, or buzzing sounds for communication. Their front wings are typically leathery and narrow, while their hind wings fold like fans beneath them.
children.funFact: You can estimate the temperature by counting a cricket's chirps - count the number of chirps in 14 seconds and add 40 to get the approximate temperature in Fahrenheit!
